World.title: Brazil Electoral Court Decides If Bolsonaro AI Video Is a Banned Deepfake
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

BRAZIL · ELECTIONS 2026

Key Facts —The case: The Superior Electoral Court (TSE) judges on Tuesday evening whether the AI-generated video of Jair Bolsonaro endorsing his son Flávio at the PL convention was an illegal deepfake. —The split: One wing of the court sees no violation because the video was labeled as AI-made; another, led by Justice Estela Aranha, wants all deepfake content removed from the electoral debate. —The test: Vice-president André Mendonça has proposed that deepfake status requires realism capable of producing a false perception of authenticity. —The rules: Already in force for 2026: mandatory AI labeling, a 72-hour blackout around each vote, a ban on chatbots recommending candidates, and joint liability for platforms. —The stakes: Sanctions range from content removal and fines to the cancellation of a candidacy registration.

One-stop reference Company Intelligence Every listed company in Latin America — financials, ownership and structure for 1,450+ companies across 26 exchanges, in one place. Browse the directory →

Five weeks before the first round, Brazil’s electoral court is about to draw the line between legal AI content and an illegal deepfake — in a case starring Jair Bolsonaro, a father barred from campaigning who appeared on a convention screen anyway.

Ask Rio Times This story and the bigger picture. RT Ask Open the full Ask Rio Times → RTAsk Rio TimesWhat this means, and what's next› Ask Rio Times This story and the bigger picture. × RT Economy impact Key players Stability What's next Tap a question, or type your own — the answer appears right here. Ask Open the full Ask Rio Times →

The video that forced the question

On 25 July, at the national convention that confirmed Senator Flávio Bolsonaro as the Liberal Party’s presidential candidate, the party played a video in which former president Jair Bolsonaro — under house arrest and barred from political statements by Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes — appears to declare support for his son. The figure on screen was generated by artificial intelligence, and the event was streamed live on YouTube.

The Workers’ Party (PT) took the case to the Superior Electoral Court the next day, arguing that the recording uses technology to distort image and voice and therefore fits the definition of a deepfake, which the court’s resolutions ban from electoral propaganda.

Flávio Bolsonaro’s campaign answered that the video broke no law because it never hid the use of the technology — the piece was openly labeled as AI-made. The defense of the former president added that he did not know the video would be produced or shown at his son’s launch event.

The case lands on the desk of the court’s president, Justice Kassio Nunes Marques, who is its rapporteur and has told colleagues he wants the ruling to set a precedent for future episodes. Judgment is scheduled for Tuesday evening, 1 September.

A court split over what a deepfake is

Inside the TSE, two readings compete. One wing sees little gravity in the episode: since the video carried an AI warning, there was no attempt to deceive the voter. Another current, led by Justice Estela Aranha, has argued for the removal of all deepfake content from the electoral context, labeled or not.

Last week, the court’s vice-president, Justice André Mendonça, proposed objective criteria to close the gap: content should be treated as a deepfake when its realism is capable of producing a false perception of authenticity in the viewer — a test that looks at the effect on the audience, not at the intent of the producer.

The political context adds voltage. Because Jair Bolsonaro is prohibited from manifesting himself during the election period, Supreme Court Justice Flávio Dino published a text after the convention drawing a parallel between totalitarianism and trickery — widely read in Brasília as a warning that the AI video may have been an end-run around Moraes’s ban.

The rules already in force

Whatever the verdict, Brazil’s 2026 campaign already runs under the strictest AI rulebook in the country’s electoral history, approved by the TSE in early March and effective for the entire general election.

Every campaign piece that uses AI to create or alter image, voice or content — printed or digital — must carry an explicit, prominent and accessible warning, and must say which technology was used. Avatars and chatbots talking to voters must identify themselves as machines.

In the 72 hours before each round and the 24 hours after it, publishing or boosting any new AI-produced or AI-altered content about candidates is absolutely banned — the court’s answer to the classic “election-eve slander” problem, now supercharged by generative tools.

The rules also reach the technology industry. AI providers may not recommend candidacies, even when users ask them to — a clause designed to prevent algorithmic interference in the voter’s decision. Platforms that fail to remove unlabeled or prohibited synthetic content immediately share liability and face fines and other sanctions. Sexualized deepfakes against female candidates are treated as gender-based political violence under a 2021 law.

Sanctions scale from immediate takedown to fines and, in the gravest cases, cancellation of the candidacy registration or loss of an elected mandate.

The caseload is already here

The pre-campaign has kept the three justices assigned to electoral propaganda — Nunes Marques, Mendonça and Aranha — busy. Both the PT-led federation and the PL have won emergency orders forcing platforms to take down posts within 24 hours.

In one case, Aranha ordered Instagram to remove a Flávio Bolsonaro video associating PT lawmaker Gleisi Hoffmann with “violence and criminality,” treating it as early negative campaigning. In another, the TSE upheld a R$5,000 (about US$965, at roughly 5.19 reais to the dollar on 1 September) fine issued by the Paraná regional court over an AI video spread in a WhatsApp group during the 2024 municipal elections.

Behind the scenes, court technicians are studying AI-detection tools for use this cycle, in house or from the market. The working understanding, reported by the legal outlet JOTA, is that detectors work on probability and never reach full accuracy — so their output can inform a ruling but never decide one alone.

What comes next

If the court classifies the convention video as a deepfake, the PL risks sanctions and every campaign inherits a narrow definition of what AI can do in the final five weeks. If it accepts the labeling defense, labeled synthetic endorsements become a lawful — and certainly copied — campaign tool.

Either way, the first round on 4 October will be the first national stress test of the framework built in 2024 and hardened in March. The ruling expected on Tuesday night tells campaigns exactly how much room they have left.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the TSE deciding about the Bolsonaro AI video? The court is judging whether the AI-generated video of Jair Bolsonaro endorsing his son Flávio at the PL convention of 25 July fits the legal definition of a deepfake, which is banned from electoral propaganda, and whether it constituted irregular campaigning. Are deepfakes banned in Brazil’s 2026 election? Yes. Electoral rules prohibit deepfakes used to harm or favor candidacies. AI-made campaign content in general is allowed only with explicit labeling, and it is completely banned in the 72 hours before and 24 hours after each vote. Can AI chatbots recommend candidates in Brazil? No. AI providers are barred from recommending candidacies, ranking candidates or suggesting votes, even when a user asks — a rule meant to prevent algorithmic interference in the vote decision. What are the penalties for illegal AI content in the campaign? They range from immediate content removal and fines to cancellation of the candidacy registration or loss of an elected mandate. Platforms that fail to remove illegal synthetic content immediately share liability. Why was the Jair Bolsonaro video controversial? The former president is under house arrest and barred from political statements, so an AI simulation of him endorsing his son was seen by critics as a way to circumvent the ban. The PL says the video was openly labeled as AI-made and therefore legal.

Sources: Poder360; g1; CNN Brasil; Valor Econômico; Estadão; JOTA; Gazeta do Povo; TSE resolutions 23.610/2019, 23.732/2024 and the March 2026 amendment. FX basis: USD/BRL 5.1866, Investing.com, 1 September 2026.

World.title: Uruguay River: Green Hydrogen Deal Nears as New Pulp Mill Revives Old Fears
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

URUGUAY–ARGENTINA · POLITICS

Key Facts —The de-escalation: HIF Global’s US$5.385 billion green hydrogen and e-fuels plant will be moved away from the Uruguay River shoreline opposite Colón, Argentina, to an industrial site in Nuevo Paysandú, Uruguayan media reported in July and August. —The tariff: State utility UTE has agreed an energy price close to US$45 per megawatt-hour, El Telégrafo reported on 19 July; President Orsi said on 28 August that the numbers “had moved closer.” —The legal front: An Argentine federal court in Concepción del Uruguay admitted a pre-emptive evidence case over the plant in April and ordered environmental studies; the case remains open. —The echo: A Uruguayan investor group, Amberplan, is studying a US$800 million tissue-paper mill on the same river — reviving memories of the 2005–2010 Botnia pulp-mill conflict. —The stakes: The HIF project would be the largest private investment in Uruguay’s history, with up to 3,200 construction jobs in one of its poorest departments.

The Uruguay River is quietly testing whether two countries that once fought a five-year diplomatic war over a pulp mill have learned to de-escalate — just as a new paper plant appears on the horizon.

De-escalation on the Uruguay River

The Uruguay River dispute that has strained Montevideo and Buenos Aires for more than a year is moving toward a negotiated landing. The US$5.385 billion green hydrogen and synthetic-fuels plant that HIF Global plans in the department of Paysandú will be relocated away from the riverbank site at Constancia — barely three kilometers across the water from the Argentine resort city of Colón — to an industrial property further inland, Uruguayan media reported in July and August.

El Telégrafo of Paysandú reported on 19 July that the government had settled on a site belonging to state oil company Ancap in Nuevo Paysandú, next to its portland cement plant, and that state utility UTE had agreed with the company on an electricity price close to US$45 per megawatt-hour. Infobae reported on 12 August that the leading option is a 48-hectare, industrially zoned property controlled by Ancap’s biofuels arm ALUR — whose ethanol plant would also supply the project’s captured biogenic CO2. Lawmaker Juan Gorosterrazú said in early July that HIF had accepted the move, which removes the “visual contamination” objection raised from Colón: the new location sits roughly ten kilometers from the Argentine city, no longer directly opposite its beaches.

The economics are converging too. President Yamandú Orsi said on 28 August that the price numbers “had moved closer” — the gap between UTE’s offer and the US$40 per megawatt-hour HIF has sought since 2023 has narrowed, as we reported on 30 August. Industry Minister Fernanda Cardona cautioned on 22 July that “there is no contract with HIF yet”: the parties are closing a memorandum with public agencies, after which the company would seek financing and take its final investment decision in 2027. The project — a 1.1-gigawatt electrolyser fed by roughly 2,300 megawatts of new solar and wind capacity — would be the largest private investment in Uruguay’s history, a bet we examined in August.

How the Conflict Played — and Why It Stayed Civil

The dispute escalated fast after Uruguay granted the project location viability in November 2025. On 2 November, hundreds of Colón residents, environmental groups and tourism operators marched to the General Artigas international bridge; a second caravan followed on 16 November. The protests were explicitly backed by Fundavida, the Gualeguaychú assembly that led the historic fight against the Botnia pulp mill, and its playbook was visible: bridge caravans, cross-border networks, and demands routed through the Administrative Commission of the Uruguay River (CARU), the binational body created by the 1975 river statute.

The conflict also acquired a judicial dimension. In April, federal judge Hernán Viri in Concepción del Uruguay partially admitted a pre-emptive evidence petition — case 3276/2026 — filed by Entre Ríos legislators Guillermo Michel, Marianela Marclay and Adán Bahl. He ordered Uruguay’s environmental agency Dinacea to hand over the project’s authorization request and impact study, asked CARU whether the venture had been formally notified, and appointed a court biologist, MercoPress reported. La Nación reported in June that the Argentine judiciary had advanced in the case. Entre Ríos governor Rogelio Frigerio had threatened in March to take the matter to The Hague if the plant went ahead opposite Colón.

What did not happen is as notable as what did. Foreign ministers Mario Lubetkin and Pablo Quirno met twice in six months; at their 12 May meeting in Montevideo — joined by Frigerio, Colón mayor José Luis Walser and Uruguay’s environment and industry ministers — Uruguay formally put “other possible locations” on the table in a joint communiqué. Quirno’s line set the tone: Argentina “will never oppose investments in Uruguay,” he said, describing a “conciliatory, pro-investment position” aimed at win-win solutions. Paysandú mayor Nicolás Olivera confirmed after the meeting that Argentina had never asked to delay the project — only to move it. Uruguay’s environment ministry had already included Colón in the plant’s official zone of influence, forcing cross-border impacts into the full environmental study HIF must still file.

The Botnia Shadow

Every actor in this story measures itself against 2005–2010. Back then, the installation of the Botnia (later UPM) pulp mill in Fray Bentos triggered a blockade of the Gualeguaychú–Fray Bentos bridge that lasted years, poisoned bilateral relations and landed before the International Court of Justice. The ICJ ruled in 2010 that Uruguay had breached the procedural obligations of the 1975 river statute but had not been proven to cause environmental harm; the mill stayed. Former president Tabaré Vázquez later admitted he had considered armed-conflict scenarios during the crisis, AFP recalled in May.

This time, the procedural channel worked early: CARU was seized, the impact zone was widened to Argentine soil, and the site was moved before positions hardened. The contrast is the strongest evidence that both governments absorbed the lesson of the pulp-mill war.

Enter the Next Paper Mill

The test of that lesson may come sooner than expected. In February, Uruguayan deputy Walter Verri confirmed that the investor group Amberplan is studying a new paper plant on the Uruguay River — a US$800 million facility producing 144,000 tonnes of tissue paper a year, mainly for export to Argentina, with Paysandú and neighboring Soriano as candidate locations, according to El Telégrafo, El Once and Gualeguaychú’s El Día. “I want to roll out the red carpet for them to set up in Paysandú,” Verri said, confirming coordination with mayor Olivera.

The project is at study stage and no environmental filing exists. But the fact that Argentina’s Entre Ríos press covered it under headlines like “another paper mill opposite our shores” shows how quickly the old reflexes return. A pulp or paper plant is precisely the asset class that started the 2005 war — and unlike hydrogen, it carries the word that still mobilizes Gualeguaychú.

What to Watch

Three milestones will show whether the de-escalation holds: the signature of the HIF investment agreement, which Olivera said in July was “days, not weeks” away; the company’s full environmental impact study, which must now assess effects on Colón and include public hearings; and the final investment decision, expected in 2027. On the Argentine side, the Concepción del Uruguay court case remains open and could reactivate if the process stalls.

And then there is Amberplan. If the tissue mill advances to a formal filing, the 1975 statute obliges Uruguay to notify CARU before authorizing it — the exact procedural step whose omission lit the fuse two decades ago. The river has seen this movie before; the sequel, both governments insist, will be different.

World.title: Raízen Closes US$1.42 Billion Sale of Argentina Business to Mercuria
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

BRAZIL · BUSINESS

Key Facts —Deal closed: Raízen completed the sale of its Argentina downstream business to Switzerland’s Mercuria Energy Group on Tuesday, 1 September, for R$7.3 billion (US$1.42 billion). —What changed hands: The Dock Sud refinery (14% of Argentina’s fuel output), 894 Shell-branded service stations (17.9% market share), a lubricants plant, airport fueling platforms and fuel terminals. —Why it sold: The cash funds Raízen’s capital-structure management inside Brazil’s largest-ever out-of-court debt restructuring, covering about R$65 billion (US$12.6 billion). —The buyer’s angle: Mercuria, partnered with Argentine businessman José Luis Manzano’s Integra Capital, deepens its Argentine footprint beyond Vaca Muerta. —Still under pressure: Raízen shares trade at R$0.26 (US$0.05), down 68% in 2026, and leverage peaked at 5.3 times net debt to EBITDA.

Raízen has closed the US$1.42 billion sale of its Argentine operations to Mercuria, turning June’s agreement into cash for the biggest debt workout in Brazilian corporate history.

From Signing to Closing in Three Months

Raízen, the sugar, ethanol and fuel-distribution joint venture between Cosan and Shell, announced on Tuesday, 1 September, that it has completed the sale of its Argentine operations to Mercuria Energy Group. The transaction, valued at R$7.3 billion (US$1.42 billion), was first signed on 4 June and closed after all precedent conditions were met, including the applicable regulatory approvals.

The final price remains subject to customary post-closing adjustments based on closing financial statements, with the net amount to be determined once those are concluded. Raízen said the net proceeds will go to managing its capital structure.

“The transaction is aligned with Raízen’s strategy of optimizing its asset portfolio, simplifying its operational structure and disciplined capital allocation, with a focus on priority markets and geographies,” the company said in its market notice. With the closing, Raízen no longer holds the Argentine operations, which had already been reported as a discontinued operation in its latest quarterly results.

What Mercuria Bought

The package is a strategic piece of Argentina’s fuel infrastructure. It includes the Dock Sud refinery in Buenos Aires province, responsible for about 14% of the country’s fuel production, and a network of 894 Shell-branded service stations holding 17.9% of the retail market — second only to state-controlled YPF, with 58.1%.

Also transferred: a lubricants plant in the city of Buenos Aires, aviation-fueling platforms at the Ezeiza and Aeroparque airports, and fuel terminals at Arroyo Seco and Santa Fe. The buyers — Latam Downstream Holdings and Silver Projects I, entities controlled by Mercuria — also assumed the debt of Raizen Argentina S.A.U.

For Mercuria, one of the world’s largest independent commodity traders, the acquisition scales up an Argentine bet it had already made upstream: the Swiss group operates in the Vaca Muerta shale formation through Phoenix Resources. Both there and in the Raízen deal, its local partner is José Luis Manzano, founder and president of Integra Capital, whose participation in the purchase was reported by Bloomberg Línea at signing.

What Raízen does. Raízen S.A. operates as an integrated energy company in Brazil, Argentina, rest of Latin America, North America, Asia, Europe, and internationally. The company trades in and markets fossil fuels and franchises network of service stations under the Shell brand name. It also engages in the production, origination, marketing, and trading of ethanol…

One Piece of a Record Restructuring

The Argentina exit is the single largest divestment in Raízen’s extrajudicial recovery, a restructuring of about R$65 billion (US$12.6 billion) in debt — the largest of its kind in Brazilian corporate history. São Paulo’s 3rd Bankruptcy and Judicial Recovery Court homologated the plan in late July, after creditors representing 81.6% of covered claims signed on.

The plan converts 45% of restructured debt into equity at R$0.25 (US$0.05) per share and refinances the remaining 55% through new instruments split between the company’s two future units. Shell is injecting R$3.5 billion (US$680 million), and Aguassanta, the Ometto family’s investment vehicle behind Cosan, may add R$500 million (US$97 million).

Asset sales have run in parallel. In July, Raízen sold the Caarapó mill in Mato Grosso do Sul to Adecoagro for R$760 million (US$148 million); earlier disposals included the Leme mill for R$425 million (US$83 million) and the Rio Brilhante and Passa Tempo mills for a combined R$1.54 billion (US$299 million). Including smaller non-core assets, divestments had raised roughly R$5 billion (US$971 million) before the Argentina closing. The company now operates 23 mills with crushing capacity of about 69 million tonnes of cane per crop.

The pressure that forced the fire sale is visible in the numbers. Leverage reached 5.3 times net debt to EBITDA in the quarter ended December, far above the 2.0 to 2.5 times management considers healthy. Raízen posted a net loss of R$1.64 billion (US$318 million) in the April–June quarter, narrower than a year earlier, and its shares — at R$0.26 (US$0.05), down 68% this year — value the whole company at roughly R$2.68 billion (US$520 million), less than twice the price of the Argentine unit just sold.

What Comes Next

With Argentina off the books, Raízen’s reorganization enters its execution phase. By the end of 2027 the company plans to split into two independent units: Raízen Energia, housing sugar, ethanol and bioenergy, and Raízen Combustíveis, concentrating fuel distribution and Shell-branded lubricants. The plan’s full closing is scheduled for up to 31 March 2027 and remains conditioned on several factors.

Analysts caution that even billion-dollar sales do not, by themselves, fix the balance sheet. Citi wrote after the Caarapó deal that such disposals are positive for simplification but insufficient for meaningful deleveraging — a verdict that applies, at larger scale, to the Mercuria proceeds as well. Meanwhile, asset manager IG4 Capital, fresh from taking control of petrochemical maker Braskem, has proposed buying Raízen credits to lead the restructuring, adding a contest for influence over what emerges from the process.

For Mercuria and Manzano, the bet is the mirror image: Argentina’s fuel market, its second-largest refinery network and its shale boom, acquired from a motivated seller. Which side of the trade pays off first is now a matter of execution on both sides of the border.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did Raízen sell in Argentina and for how much? Raízen sold its entire Argentine downstream business to Mercuria Energy Group for R$7.3 billion (US$1.42 billion): the Dock Sud refinery, 894 Shell service stations, a lubricants plant, airport fueling platforms and fuel terminals. The deal closed on 1 September 2026. Why did Raízen sell its Argentine operations? To raise cash for the largest out-of-court debt restructuring in Brazilian history, covering about R$65 billion (US$12.6 billion). Proceeds go to capital-structure management as the company cuts leverage that peaked at 5.3 times net debt to EBITDA. Who is Mercuria and what is its role in Argentina? Mercuria is a Swiss commodity-trading group already active in Argentina’s Vaca Muerta shale through Phoenix Resources. It bought the Raízen assets through controlled entities, partnered with José Luis Manzano’s Integra Capital, and assumed the Argentine unit’s debt. What happens to Raízen now? The court-approved plan converts 45% of debt into equity, injects R$3.5 billion (US$680 million) from Shell and splits the company into Raízen Energia and Raízen Combustíveis by end-2027. Shares remain down 68% in 2026, and IG4 Capital is bidding to lead the restructuring.

World.title: Can Tourism Really Push Out Drug Trafficking in Costa Rica’s South Pacific?
World.content:
Local officials and business leaders in Costa Rica’s South Pacific are betting on tourism to change the image and economic trajectory of communities long associated with drug trafficking, illegal mining and other illicit activity. More than 200,000 tourists visit the region each year, drawn by its natural beauty even as police investigations continue to identify the area as a corridor for cocaine shipments moving north before leaving the country.

Golfito mayor Freiner Lara says his locality has chosen to invest in security and infrastructure specifically to support that tourism growth. Security cameras are being installed in downtown Golfito, with monitoring handled by the Ministry of Public Security. Lara said the effort has involved close coordination with that ministry and with the United States Embassy, and that a monitoring center should be operational by October.



He pointed to a continued Coast Guard presence and joint patrols as evidence the approach is working, while acknowledging Golfito remains vulnerable given its coastline and proximity to Panama. A local business owner, went further, crediting tourism development with transforming the image of towns including Sierpe, Drake, Puerto Jiménez and Uvita.

He described crime and trafficking problems in those communities as far smaller today than in the past, attributing the shift to sustained cooperation among local institutions. That optimistic framing runs against a body of reporting and research suggesting the relationship between tourism and drug trafficking in Costa Rica is far more tangled than a simple trade off.

The United States State Department has named Costa Rica the top transshipment point for cocaine moving from South America toward the United States and Europe in recent years, and security analysts have pointed to the country’s remote forested terrain, the same terrain that draws tourists, as exactly what traffickers exploit to avoid detection.

In other tourism dependent Pacific towns, prosecutors have directly linked local drug micro trafficking to harm against the visitor economy itself, citing thefts from tourists and open drug dealing in areas meant to attract them. A national study on drug use once found that in provinces with heavy tourist traffic, a meaningful share of residents reported knowing many people who use illegal drugs, complicating any claim that tourism simply displaces trafficking rather than sometimes accompanying it.

The renewed push around Sierpe also arrives alongside a much older and still unresolved promise, an international airport for the Zona Sur, planned for that same district. Costa Rican presidents have pledged the project since the early 2000s, and President Rodrigo Chaves revived it during a tour of the region, targeting a runway near Sierpe on state owned land.

Two years later, government progress tracking shows the project at zero percent, with only an archaeological study completed, and Chaves himself has suggested 2027 as a more realistic horizon. Critics have raised serious concerns about the site’s proximity to the internationally protected Térraba Sierpe wetland and its flood exposure, questions that have followed the project for over a decade without resolution.

World.title: US Demands Nicaragua Release Brooklyn Rivera’s Relatives
World.content:
The United States on Monday demanded that Nicaragua’s government release relatives of Indigenous leader Brooklyn Rivera, who died in prison three months ago. Rivera, a longtime leader of the Miskito people, died on May 30 at the age of 73 after being detained since 2023.

The government of President Daniel Ortega and his wife, Rosario Murillo, showed Rivera hospitalized and in critical condition for the first time just days before his death. About six relatives and other people who traveled to Managua to claim his body were arrested. Their whereabouts have remained unknown ever since, according to human rights groups and Rivera’s exiled daughter, Tininiska Rivera.

“The dictatorship forcibly disappeared Rivera’s relatives and members of his community when they asked for his remains,” and for the “crime” of “trying to mourn his death,” said U.S. Assistant Secretary of State for Western Hemisphere Affairs Juan Pablo Segura. “This is tyranny in its cruelest and most cowardly form. Murillo, Ortega: unconditionally release Brooklyn’s family and all political prisoners,” Segura demanded.

In June, Washington imposed visa restrictions on more than 100 Nicaraguan officials in response to Rivera’s death. He was buried without his relatives present. A network of human rights organizations and prisoners’ relatives counts at least 60 political prisoners in Nicaragua. Of those, 23 remain victims of “enforced disappearance,” including Rivera’s relatives.

Ortega, an 80-year-old former leftist guerrilla, and his wife, who is five years younger, rule with absolute power and maintain tight control over Nicaraguan society. That control has intensified since the 2018 protests, when a government crackdown left about 300 people dead, according to the United Nations, and forced hundreds of thousands into exile.

On September 21, the National Assembly is scheduled to vote on a constitutional reform that would exclude opposition parties from elections despite objections from numerous countries.

World.title: BEL says temporary generation capacity to begin operations by mid-September
World.content:
BEL says temporary generation capacity to begin operations by mid-September

By Zoila Palma: Belize Electricity Limited (BEL) says temporary generation capacity currently being installed at the Westlake Facility is expected to begin operations by mid-September as the company moves to strengthen electricity supply and reduce the risk of further disruptions to the national grid.

In a press release, BEL said recent power outages have highlighted the importance of maintaining adequate generation reserves, particularly when electricity supply from Mexico’s Comisión Federal de Electricidad (CFE) is temporarily unavailable.

“Belize Electricity Limited (BEL) informs its Customers and the public that the Company continues to actively manage available generation and advance measures to strengthen electricity supply and the reliability of the National Grid.”

BEL said that on August 25, available in-country generation stood at approximately 103 megawatts (MW), while evening demand reached 122 MW. On August 31, available generation was approximately 109 MW against demand of 117 MW.

“On both occasions, the temporary loss of electricity supply from Mexico’s Comisión Federal de Electricidad (CFE), at a time when local generation was already below demand, resulted in temporary loss of power to the National Grid.”

The company said available in-country generation continues to be affected by seasonal conditions, scheduled maintenance and reduced output from some generating facilities. BEL said it is closely managing these conditions while working to ensure adequate supply is available to meet customer demand.

BEL also pointed to measures taken following an anticipated electricity supply shortfall identified in 2025.

“As part of these efforts, BEL advised in October 2025 of a potential electricity supply shortfall in 2026, following which Cabinet made a declaration of emergency under the Public Utilities Commission (PUC) (Request for Proposals) Regulations, 2024.”

The company said the emergency declaration allowed it to procure temporary generation capacity, which is now being installed at the Westlake Facility and is expected to begin operations by mid-September 2026 for an initial six-month period. “

This additional generation will provide important support to the National Grid, particularly during periods of high demand or when another source of power becomes temporarily unavailable.”

BEL further noted that its August 26, 2026 letter to the PUC forms part of its ongoing regulatory responsibility to assess electricity supply requirements for the upcoming 12 months and ensure appropriate measures are taken to support Belize’s growing energy needs.

While BEL continues to strengthen available generation, it warned that controlled power interruptions or load shedding may still be necessary to maintain grid stability, particularly if a significant source of supply becomes unexpectedly unavailable. “BEL will continue taking all available measures to minimize any impact on Customers.”

World.title: Lords Bank man charged after alleged assault on common-law wife and 13-year-old stepdaughter
World.content:
Lords Bank man charged after alleged assault on common-law wife and 13-year-old stepdaughter

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 36-year-old Lords Bank man has been granted bail after being charged in connection with an alleged domestic dispute in which his common-law wife and her 13-year-old daughter were reportedly assaulted.

Cesar Alexander Mazariegos, a fisherman of the Hollywood area in Lords Bank Village, was arraigned in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on two counts of common assault.

Mazariegos appeared unrepresented before Senior Magistrate Mannon Dennison, where he initially pleaded guilty with an explanation. After hearing his account of the incident, however, the magistrate determined that his explanation amounted to a possible defence and entered not guilty pleas on his behalf.

With no objection from the prosecution, Mazariegos was granted bail in the sum of $3,000 plus one surety of the same amount. As conditions of his bail, he is prohibited from contacting either complainant and must remain at least 150 feet away from them.

Police say the incident occurred at around 9:30 p.m. on August 28 at a residence in the Hollywood area.

According to police allegations, the 31-year-old woman was breastfeeding her baby inside a bedroom when Mazariegos entered and became involved in an argument with her. She alleged that he grabbed her around the neck in a choking position, causing difficulty breathing.

Her 13-year-old daughter allegedly intervened and was herself grabbed around the neck, slammed against a wall and slapped twice in the face.

The woman further alleged that when she attempted to protect her daughter, Mazariegos again placed her in a chokehold and punched her repeatedly to the head, face and back, causing pain, swelling, bruising and scratches. She also reportedly suffered a cut to her finger during the confrontation.

Police arrived shortly afterward, and the mother and daughter were issued medico-legal forms and taken to the Karl Heusner Memorial Hospital for treatment.

Mazariegos was detained later that night and subsequently charged.

In court, he disputed the allegations, saying he had arrived home after receiving upsetting news and claimed his wife and her daughter rushed toward him, prompting him to push them away.

He was able to post bail and is expected to return to court in early November.

World.title: Minister of Foreign Affairs welcomes Secretary General of the Organization of American States
World.content:
Minister of Foreign Affairs welcomes Secretary General of the Organization of American States

By Zoila Palma: On August 31, 2026, Foreign Minister Francis Fonseca, welcomed Albert Ramdin, Secretary General of the Organization of American States (OAS), to Belize for a working visit.

Minister Fonseca and Secretary General Ramdin, together with their respective delegations, held bilateral discussions on matters of mutual interest.

Discussions included the important role and operations of the OAS Office in the Adjacency Zone, the current state of bilateral relations between Belize and Guatemala, and the upcoming ruling of the International Court of Justice (ICJ) on the Belize–Guatemala territorial, insular and maritime claim.

“Belize values its longstanding partnership with the OAS and its continued support for peace, dialogue and cooperation in the region,” a statement from the Ministry said.

World.title: Belize and Guatemala Foreign Ministers meet with OAS
World.content:
Belize and Guatemala Foreign Ministers meet with OAS

By Zoila Palma: Today, the Foreign Ministers of Belize and Guatemala, Francis Fonseca and Carlos Ramiro Martínez, joined OAS Secretary General Albert Ramdin and the Ambassadors of the Group of Friends for an important meeting at the OAS Adjacency Zone Office.

The Ministry of Foreign Affairs said that the meeting provided an opportunity for frank and constructive exchanges on the way forward, including continued economic assistance and the role of the OAS in promoting peace, stability and constructive engagement between Belize and Guatemala following the ICJ decision.

The session also reaffirmed the value of continued dialogue, cooperation and the active support of the Group of Friends in advancing positive relations between the two countries.

Minister Francis Fonseca was supported by Oscar Arnold, Chief Executive Officer for Foreign Affairs and Foreign Trade; Ayesha Borland, Director of International Affairs (Multilateral); Alfonso Gahona, Director of International Affairs (Bilateral); and Idelso Leslie, Foreign Service Officer.

World.title: Gun case against Dixon Cayetano adjourned to October 8
World.content:
Gun case against Dixon Cayetano adjourned to October 8

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Thirty-eight-year-old Dixon Montero Cayetano remains on remand at the Belize Central Prison after making his second appearance in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on firearm and ammunition charges.

Cayetano, a Taylor’s Alley resident who remains unrepresented, appeared before Magistrate Newshad Mohammed in Court #5 on Monday, where the matter was adjourned until October 8, 2026.

He was first arraigned on July 8, 2026, on charges of keeping an unlicensed firearm and keeping unlicensed ammunition. He pleaded not guilty and was remanded due to the nature of the offences.

Police allege that Cayetano was found in possession of a black Daewoo-brand 9mm pistol along with 13 live rounds of 9mm ammunition during an encounter in the Taylor’s Alley area.

Cayetano, a Honduran national who has claimed that he is a naturalized Belizean, remains behind bars pending his next court appearance.

World.title: Benque Viejo Town Council hoists flag marking commencement of September Celebrations
World.content:
Benque Viejo Town Council hoists flag marking commencement of September Celebrations

By Zoila Palma: The Benque Viejo Town Council held its National Flag Raising Ceremony this morning at the Benque Viejo flagpole along the George Price Highway, marking National Flag Day and the start of the September Celebrations under the theme “Look at Me, I Am Belize @45.”

The ceremony brought together residents and members of the community to celebrate Belize’s national identity and reflect on the country’s journey since Independence.

Mayor Jorge Rosales used the occasion to reflect on Belize’s progress over the past 45 years and extended warm September Celebrations greetings to the residents of Benque Viejo del Carmen.

He encouraged the community to embrace the spirit of patriotism and togetherness as the country celebrates its 45th year of Independence.

The Benque Viejo Town Council also joined Belizeans across the country in celebrating National Flag Day, encouraging residents to proudly display the national flag and participate in the activities planned throughout the September Celebrations.

World.title: THE 786 PROBLEM
World.content:
THE 786 PROBLEM

The views expressed in this article are those of the writer and not necessarily those of Breaking Belize News.

The crowd was bigger than the electorate — but Belize City is bigger than both

By Lennox Lamb: I didn’t watch this convention from Facebook.

I mi deh deh.

Standing on Freetown Road Sunday afternoon, looking across the ITVET area, one thing was impossible to miss:

The PUP still know how fi bring people out.

Blue tents. Blue shirts. Flags. Banners. Food. DJs. Live music. Campaign workers everywhere.

Di machinery mi out full force.

From the stretch of Freetown Road and the convention area I could see, my estimate is that the crowd moving through and gathering around the event was somewhere in the 2,500-to-3,000 range.

That is my estimate, not an official count.

But you neva need no calculator fi see di thing.

The machine mi working.

Published convention reporting put the delegate universe at 787. The detailed result sheet records 786 ballots counted.

And right deh so, the real story starts.

The crowd measures machinery.

The delegates measure internal power.

March 2027 will measure Belize City.

Those are three different things.

Miller won. Full stop.

Eluide Miller beat Allan Pollard Jr.

Miller — 427.

Pollard — 341.

That gives us 768 recorded mayoral selections from 786 ballots counted.

Among those 768 selections, Miller won 55.6% to 44.4%.

Margin:

86 votes.

Clear victory.

No asterisk required.

Miller is the PUP’s mayoral candidate.

But now that everybody finish saying who win, let’s look at what really happened under the tent.

Because there is another number sitting there.

18.

I got that number with simple subtraction.

786 ballots counted.

768 recording a choice between Miller and Pollard.

786 minus 768 equals 18.

Nobody has publicly explained what those 18 ballots were.

So I won’t.

I will not call them blank ballots.

I will not call them spoiled ballots.

I will not call them undervotes.

I don’t know.

What I know is that eighteen ballots went into a two-man mayoral contest without recording either man’s name in the final totals.

In a room of 786, that is worth noticing.

No conspiracy.

No motive.

Just subtraction.

Mahler beat Hyde?

The convention was widely discussed as something bigger than Miller versus Pollard.

Anthony Mahler behind Miller.

Cordel Hyde behind Pollard.

7News reported that alignment before the vote.

So naturally, when Miller won, the easiest analysis became:

Mahler beat Hyde.

Nice headline.

Easy morning show.

Good Facebook beef.

I’m just not convinced it’s that simple.

Kareem Musa pushed back on that interpretation himself, telling 7News the contest was between Miller and Pollard.

The numbers give Musa’s argument some weight.

Under the PUP’s delegate formula, Lake Independence had roughly 192 delegates.

Pollard received 341 votes.

So even if every Lake Independence delegate had voted for Pollard — and we absolutely do not know that they did — Pollard still received at least 149 votes from outside Lake I.

That matters.

It means the arithmetic does not prove Hyde failed to “deliver” his constituency.

It proves Pollard had support beyond Hyde’s constituency.

So maybe Sunday’s result tells us less about one political general defeating another than people would like.

Sometimes Belize politics loves a kingmaker story.

Sometimes the voters spoil it.

Pickstock leaves us with a gap

Anthony Mahler was returned unopposed in Pickstock in the 2025 general election.

That means there was no 2025 PUP vote total there to divide by 25 under the normal delegate formula.

How Pickstock’s convention allocation was ultimately calculated has not been publicly explained in the material available to me.

That’s the fact.

So I leave it there.

And Miller did not arrive alone either

The same scrutiny has to apply to the winner.

If we are looking at Pollard’s political support structure, we have to look at Miller’s too.

7News reported Mahler’s support for Miller, and after the convention Miller publicly thanked Anthony Mahler and Francis Fonseca for standing with him.

Breaking Belize News has also reported that Miller is the son-in-law of outgoing Mayor Bernard Wagner.

None of that invalidates Miller’s 427 votes.

It simply reminds us that he, like Pollard, entered the convention with political relationships around him.

And those relationships matter in a delegate election.

Then there is Allan Pollard

This may be the most interesting number story of the entire convention.

According to published municipal results, Allan Pollard received:

10,886 votes in 2021.

Top of the poll.

Then in 2024:

12,574.

Top of the poll again.

He even outpolled Mayor Bernard Wagner in both elections.

Then Sunday:

341.

And he lost.

That does not mean 12,574 people suddenly stopped liking Allan Pollard.

It means these numbers measure different kinds of political power.

Pollard has repeatedly demonstrated strength with the public electorate.

Miller has repeatedly demonstrated strength inside the delegate structure.

Miller topped the PUP councillor convention in 2023.

Now he has won the mayoral delegate convention.

One man’s strongest numbers have appeared outside the party room.

The other’s have appeared inside it.

Sunday was an inside election.

Miller won it.

March 2027 won’t be.

Winning the people who control the PUP in Belize City and winning Belize City itself are two different elections.

That, to me, is the real lesson.

Then El Toxico walked in

While everybody mi busy counting Mahler and Hyde, perhaps somebody shoulda been counting followers.

Kristian “El Toxico” Alpuche:

564 votes.

More than Miller.

More than Pollard.

More than anybody else on the published result sheet.

Second place received 466.

That’s a 98-vote gap.

For an electoral newcomer.

But “newcomer” only tells half the story.

New to electoral politics?

Yes.

New to people?

Not even close.

Before anybody handed him a ballot number, Alpuche already had a recognizable social-media and public profile. News 5 had previously reported on his online reach and community activities.

So one possible reading is something we may need to start paying more attention to:

digital political capital.

Build the audience first.

Ask for the vote later.

But hold on.

There is another possible explanation.

Alpuche appeared first on a nineteen-name councillor ballot, and delegates could select ten candidates.

Ballot position can matter in long multi-selection contests.

How much did his social-media recognition matter?

How much did ballot position matter?

I don’t know.

So I won’t pretend I do.

And there is an even bigger limitation.

These 786 delegates are not Belize City.

So Alpuche’s result may tell us something interesting about name recognition and internal PUP politics.

It cannot, by itself, tell us where Belizean politics generally is heading.

Still:

Watch it.

Dem mi di choose — but how much?

Across all nineteen councillor candidates, the published results total 6,935 selections.

With 786 ballots and up to ten councillor choices per ballot, the theoretical maximum was 7,860.

That means approximately 88% of all available selections were used.

Average:

8.82 councillor selections per ballot.

One interpretation is that delegates were editing their tickets.

Dem neva just automatically tick ten names.

But let’s be fair.

Eighty-eight percent usage is also high enough to suggest considerable slate discipline.

Maybe delegates followed recommended tickets and left off one or two people.

Maybe they selected individual names.

Maybe both happened.

The mathematics cannot tell us.

So we don’t force it.

What the mathematics can tell us is this:

Darwin “Puppy” Leslie:

384.

Malcolm Nunez:

383.

One vote.

One likkle vote.

Benque gave us nine.

San Ignacio/Santa Elena gave us a coin toss.

Belize City gave us one.

Tell me again why Belize politics boring.

Now here is the number that really matters

Not 427.

Not 341.

Not 564.

20,197.

According to the published 2024 municipal results, that is how many ballots were cast in Belize City.

Sunday’s 786 convention ballots represent less than 4% of that number.

And the PUP delegate system is built around PUP votes.

That makes perfect sense.

It is a PUP convention.

But it also means the internal electorate is not designed to mirror Belize City.

The convention answers:

Who does the PUP want?

March asks:

Who does Belize City want?

Different electorate.

Different mathematics.

Different fight.

History whispers

I originally went searching for a nice clean rule.

Maybe parties that win two consecutive general elections become vulnerable in the next Belize City municipal election.

Sounded good.

The numbers said:

No sah.

The UDP won nationally in 2008 and 2012 and continued winning Belize City afterward.

So scratch that.

But another pattern remains worth watching.

Belize City moved from PUP to UDP in 2006.

The country followed in 2008.

Belize City moved from UDP to PUP in 2018.

The country followed in 2020.

Now, the obvious objection is fair.

Municipal elections fall roughly mid-term, and mid-term swings against governments happen all over democratic politics.

Exactly.

Two examples do not create an electoral law.

But they do leave us with an interesting possibility:

Belize City has twice moved before the national political tide.

Not prophecy.

Not prediction.

A warning light.

And now Bernard Wagner is leaving City Hall.

That makes 2027 even more interesting.

And the UDP?

There is one hole in this analysis I won’t hide.

March 2027 will not be a PUP convention.

There will be an opposition on the ballot.

What exactly is the UDP building in Belize City?

Who will carry its ticket?

What organization will it have?

Where can it realistically grow?

I do not have verified answers to those questions in front of me, so I won’t manufacture them.

That conversation is still coming.

For now, the point is narrower:

PUP strength cannot be measured only by PUP internal strength.

Back to Freetown Road

Sunday looked impressive.

Di thing look strong.

Di machine look well-oiled.

Confidence mi high.

Maybe that confidence is justified.

Maybe.

But political parties get themselves into trouble when they begin measuring their strength by their own crowd instead of by the electorate waiting outside the party structure.

And there is another danger.

A weak opponent can be an advantage.

It can also become a narcotic if a party begins using the condition of its opposition as the main measurement of its own strength.

Look how weak they are.

is not the same question as:

How strong are we?

That difference may matter more in March 2027 than anything that happened under the tent Sunday.

THE NUMBER: 786

Ballots counted at the PUP Belize City convention.

THE CHOICE: 768

Recorded mayoral selections for Miller or Pollard.

THE UNEXPLAINED: 18

The arithmetic difference.

Nobody has publicly explained what those ballots represented.

I won’t guess.

THE MARGIN: 86

Miller’s 427 to Pollard’s 341 — 55.6% to 44.4% of the 768 recorded mayoral selections.

THE OUTLIER: 564

Kristian “El Toxico” Alpuche.

First on the ballot.

First in the count.

THE MARGIN THAT HURTS: ONE

Leslie 384.

Nunez 383.

THE WARNING: 20,197

The number of ballots cast in the last Belize City municipal election.

Because those are the people who ultimately matter.

Not 786 delegates.

Not a minister.

Not an area representative.

Not a Facebook beef.

Belize City.

Sunday decided who leads the PUP ticket.

It did not decide City Hall.

The crowd measures machinery.

The delegates measure power inside the party.

March 2027 measures everything else.

And Belize City has taught both red and blue one lesson over the years:

Don’t count the City until the City counts you.

Lennox Lamb

World.title: Public Utilities Commission reviews BEL’s submission declaring emergency due to anticipated generation shortfall
World.content:
Public Utilities Commission reviews BEL’s submission declaring emergency due to anticipated generation shortfall

By Zoila Palma: The Belize Electricity Limited (BEL) has notified the Public Utilities Commission (PUC) of an anticipated material shortfall in electricity generation services, prompting the PUC to review BEL’s submission for a possible emergency declaration.

The PUC announced that BEL has formally submitted a notice declaring an anticipated emergency concerning generation services.

This comes following ongoing concerns over the reliability and availability of electricity generation to meet the country’s demand.

According to the PUC, BEL’s submission is being reviewed in accordance with the Request for Proposals (RFP) Regulations, 2024, under Statutory Instruments Nos. 137 and 153. The regulations establish the legal framework for addressing situations where additional generation services may be required.

The PUC said the RFP Regulations “provide clear guidelines for the process, promote transparency, and establish the roles and responsibilities of participants in this RFP process.”

The Commission added that its role is to “apply these frameworks consistently and transparently” while reviewing BEL’s submission.

This comes as Belize has experienced heightened pressure on its electricity system, including recent load shedding and power supply disruptions.

BEL has previously warned that generation availability and demand pressures could require measures to maintain stability of the national grid.

World.title: Tents? No Way!
World.content:
The tent at Middle Quarters Primary and Infant School in St Elizabeth where some classes were held

MIDDLE QUARTERS, St Elizabeth — Describing tents as heat traps, Middle Quarters Primary and Infant School Principal Pauvine Watson-Barrett is insisting that all of her 252 students must be housed in ventilated classrooms when the new academic year opens next Monday.

“The tent cannot be used; it is extremely hot. We tried to use the tent last academic year. We had grade one initially in the tent and after the [Primary Exit Profile] exam we had grade six going to the tent and giving grade one a feel of a classroom space,” she told the Jamaica Observer on Monday.

“However, due to the heat the children were not able to use the tent for the entire day. They had to be out of it by midday. Right now it is hotter than what we were experiencing last academic year, so I don’t see where I can use that tent to host the classroom,” she added.

Last week, the Caribbean Institute of Meteorology and Hydrology and The University of the West Indies Climate Studies Group Mona advised governments, businesses, farmers and households across the region to step up preparations for potentially severe climate extremes as El Niño conditions are and set to intensify the hot and dry conditions already affecting parts of the Caribbean.

Both entities warned that the region should remain particularly vigilant as August to October marks the peak of the Caribbean’s heat season.

This year’s El Niño is on track to be the strongest on record, threatening to unleash extreme weather across the globe and make 2027 the hottest recorded year by far.

Under such severe heat, tents would not be suitable to serve as classrooms for children.

On Monday, when asked how all her students would be accommodated, Principal Watson-Barrett said the National Education Trust (NET) had promised to deploy temporary wooden classrooms, but up to Monday afternoon there was no structure or even foundation to give assurance of the buildings.

“I am yet to see them. Between the Ministry of Education, NET, and the contractor, they promised that we would be getting two buildings each holding two classrooms, so that would be a total of four classrooms. Up to this morning (Monday) there was no updated information. The contractor said he is waiting on NET to give approval for the building of the [wooden] classrooms,” Watson-Barrett told the Observer.

She said the school is exploring two options to accommodate students if the temporary buildings are not erected in time.

“We will have to look at rotation and/or merging of classrooms into one room. For instance, last academic year I had a classroom with two grade two classes and they were placed in one room and then the teachers team-teach,” she said.

“Because of the heat, also, I am not considering a shift system. Imagine coming to school at 12 o’clock to start classes in this heat on a shift system,” added Watson-Barrett.

She said the school is expected to have seven accessible classrooms based on ongoing construction work.

“Currently, we have one block that is 85 per cent complete. That block can host two classrooms. The other two blocks that are available are currently being worked on and we are hopeful that by this Friday those two blocks will be completely cleaned and ready for the opening of school, September 7,” she said.

A deteriorating building had to be demolished last week at the school.

“That would leave me wanting five more classrooms to accommodate the other students, because as of last week I lost a building that had four classrooms, the guidance counselling room and the library on it,” said Watson-Barrett.

She said Middle Quarters Primary and Infant will be receiving students from the now shuttered Giddy Hall Primary School, three-and-a-half kilometres away.

“Even without the inclusion of the Giddy Hall Primary children I would be short of classrooms. I have 170 students expected to attend school in the primary department with an additional 29 from Giddy Hall Primary School, seeing that the school was consolidated and we are the receiving school,” she said while pointing out that five academic and two auxiliary staff were moved to her school from Giddy Hall.

“The ministry has made the decision to close down smaller schools based on the enrolment there… For the infant department we are expecting to have about 52 students,” she added.

When asked about the availability of potable water, Watson-Barrett said the school has been getting reliable water supply from the National Water Commission.

“Currently, I am seeing where improvement has been made on the water system; it is still being worked on, but whenever it is locked off we purchase water,” she said.

“During Hurricane Melissa [last October] the drums were blown off the building. However, we have a large metal tank that we store water in. Those drums that were blown down are yet to be replaced,” she added.

World.title: Tough guardrails
World.content:
Casino Gaming Commission (CGC) Chief Executive Officer Cleveland Allen (second left) gestures while speaking at this week’s Jamaica Observer Monday Exchange. Flanking him are CGC executives (from left) Caleigh Reid, legal officer; Damion McKenzie, senior director, investigations and enforcement; and Shainee Myles, director of human resource. (Photo: Joseph Wellington)

WITH Jamaica’s first licensed casino operator set to commence operations by March next year, once all outstanding conditions are met, the Casino Gaming Commission (CGC) is assuring that stringent guardrails are in place to keep criminal elements out, with operators required to verify players, monitor suspicious transactions, and protect vulnerable gamblers.

Speaking during this week’s Jamaica Observer Monday Exchange, both CGC Chief Executive Officer Cleveland Allen and Senior Director of Enforcement and Investigation Damion McKenzie outlined a multi-layered system of checks that will follow casino operations from the moment a player registers to the regulator’s ongoing monitoring of the business.

The safeguards include know-your-customer (KYC) checks, scrutiny of suspicious transactions and sources of wealth, anti-money laundering controls, surveillance systems, responsible-gaming interventions, and direct regulatory access to the casino’s operations.

The officials were speaking as Adamas Grand Casino Limited, Jamaica’s first licensed casino operator, moves towards opening at Princess Grand Jamaica Resort in Green Island, Hanover. The CGC granted the operator its licence on July 29, but the licence is conditional and does not yet authorise the casino to begin operations.

CGC Legal Officer Caleigh Reid said the operator must first satisfy all remaining requirements, with March 31, 2027 set as the deadline to commence operations.

“They have a specific time frame in which to open. There are certain deliverables that they have to satisfy us with, certain things that they have to provide us with before they get the go-ahead. Right now they have the licence, but they are not authorised to begin operations until all of those other deliverables are satisfied, which is all outlined in their conditions of licence,” she said.

The safeguards are intended to address several risks associated with casino gaming, particularly money laundering, organised crime, problem gambling, and the potential exploitation of vulnerable players.

At the heart of the CGC’s financial crime controls will be requirements for casinos to know who their customers are and to scrutinise the money moving through their operations.

According to McKenzie, the regulator will not simply assess an operator’s anti-money laundering system once and walk away.

“A part of our legislation requires us to do ongoing monitoring as it relates to money laundering and proceeds from illicit means. We will continue to monitor, but the training that we provided to our officers… allow them to understand the different typologies that are related to money laundering in the gaming sector, to understand the myriad things that happen that can be classified as money laundering,” McKenzie said.

The commission will also examine whether an operator has properly carried out those checks and whether the financial profile of a player makes sense.

“Our audit plan also allows us to go in and check on persons who have signed up, if you did the proper KYC and anti-money laundering check against this person: What does this person do? How did they come about the cash? The source of wealth? So all those checks continue throughout the lifecycle of the licence,” McKenzie added.

Furthermore, Allen noted that the commission is designated as the competent authority for casino gaming under the Proceeds of Crime Act, with responsibility for anti-money laundering, counter-financing of terrorism and counter-proliferation financing compliance in the casino sector.

He explained that casino gaming in Jamaica is restricted to approved Integrated Resort Developments, meaning a casino cannot operate as a stand-alone gambling establishment.

Therefore, this creates a two-stage screening process.

“At the first stage of the development of it, the Government wants to be satisfied that the operators, the financiers, their funding is from good sources, they have good standing in other jurisdictions, not just for the development but for the operations of the casino… and when you come to stage two, when you come to us, we then conduct our own due diligence, specifically in respect to the conduct and operations of a casino,” Allen said.

He also noted operators will be required to maintain surveillance systems capable of supporting regulatory monitoring, as well as provide space for commission officers at the premises.

“In Las Vegas, on any one casino property, there are about 5,000 cameras. These cameras can zoom in and read the serial number on a note at a table four miles down the road. We have similar surveillance and monitoring requirements for the casino. More than that, the operator is required to have facilities on its premises for the commission and our officers to be able to have access to and at any time go on site and monitor,” Allen said.

The CGC’s guardrails are not limited to criminal activity. Allen explained that the regulator’s responsible-gaming framework is designed to identify people who may be developing harmful gambling habits and provide avenues for intervention.

That framework includes staff training, player information, behaviour monitoring, exclusion and self-exclusion mechanisms, as well as controls on advertising. The commission has worked with the Responsible Gaming Council of Ontario and signed an MOU with RISE Life Management, which has experience in counselling and self-exclusion relating to gambling.

“The mechanism behind responsible gaming is that the staff will be trained to spot persons who have a problem, persons who sit all day and gamble. There’s some form of intervention from the staff to allow some kind of cooling-out period for this individual. Also, because Jamaica will be a cashless system, they’ll also be able to track the pattern of a player to see his betting patterns and some form of intervention can be implemented because of that pattern of constant gambling, constant topping up, constant chasing, constant losses,” he added.

Allen also assured that responsible-gaming controls will extend to how casinos advertise and promote their services.

He said s should not target children or young people and should not rely on influential figures who children might look up to.

He also noted that the CGC intends to leverage existing responsible-gambling programmes, including initiatives involving schools, while keeping casino-related promotion within the resort environment.

World.title: 60 years of Tastee: A celebration of food, music and Jamaican legacy
World.content:
Patrons enjoy the free concert hosted by Tastee Jamaica as part of their 60th anniversary celebrations.(Photo: Karl Mclarty)

FOR 60 years, Tastee Jamaica has commanded the support of Jamaicans, becoming as synonymous with the island as the patty itself. But the company’s legacy stretches far beyond food. Having established itself as a key contributor to the discovery of some of Jamaica’s most talented entertainers, Tastee has firmly cemented its place in the hearts of Jamaicans globally. On Friday night, the company showed its appreciation to its local fanbase, treating scores of Jamaicans to a free concert of the highest entertainment quality.

With Emancipation Park transformed into a sprawling celebration of music and memories, the event was far more than an anniversary concert. Hosted by veteran broadcaster Jennifer “Jenny Jenny” Small, it was as much a celebration of Jamaican music as it was a birthday party for the company. Agent Sasco, Tarrus Riley, King Yellowman, Nadine Sutherland and a host of others created an atmosphere that reflected both legacy and loyalty.

For some of the night’s performers, however, appearing on the Tastee stage carried even greater significance, having gained their break in the industry decades ago through the talent search spearheaded by the company.

“We a eat patty over 60 years. Big up Tastee. Tastee is the one that make people know me international,” said King Yellowman as he paused his set to remind the audience of his third-place finish in the inaugural Tastee Talent Contest in 1979.

Giving a commanding performance, Yellowman treated the crowd to a short yet energetic set, which included songs such as I’m Getting Married in the Morning and Zungguzungguguzungguzeng.

Also turning in a vibrant performance was the 1979 competition winner, Nadine Sutherland. She performed hits such as Action, Starvation — which she released a year after her win — and Babyface. In what she described as a full-circle moment, Sutherland recalled how Tastee changed her life when she was just 11 years old.

“I’m still in disbelief that it’s been 46 years since the 11-year-old me was brave enough to get on that stage. I was known as ‘the little girl from Above Rocks’ who was brimming with confidence. I had to draw back for that little girl tonight and just soak it all in. I’m grateful that I’m still here, and I still love this,” she said.

Tastee’s own story began in 1966 when Vincent and Valerie Chang opened the company’s first operation at Union Square in downtown Kingston. As demand grew, the business expanded, eventually establishing its headquarters in Cross Roads and developing a footprint across the island. Somewhere along that journey, Tastee’s relationship with Jamaica began extending beyond what it served across the counter.

Over its decades-long run, the Tastee Talent Contest — later known as the Tastee Talent Trail — became an important proving ground for emerging Jamaican performers, including Beenie Man, Papa San, Cobra, Mr Vegas, T.O.K., Glacia Robinson, Brian and Tony Gold, and several others.

It was therefore little surprise that the company received an abundance of praise from the night’s performers.

That spirit of giving was not confined to Tastee’s entertainment history. After the company awarded 13 students $60,000 each towards tuition through its back-to-school initiative, Agent Sasco extended the gesture from the stage, committing to cover the tuition of another high-school student.

Sasco’s giveback didn’t stop there, as he treated patrons to a delightful set, which included spirited performances of crowd favourites such as Winning Right Now, Hand To Mouth, Hand Inna Di Air, Idiot Thing Dat, Banks of the Hope, and others.

Alaine also turned in a quality set, performing songs such as Dreaming, Rise In Love, Bye Bye and Ordinary Love.

Abijah, Carey Sayles, Tony Rebel, Sista Pat, Tarrus Riley, Richie Stephens and saxophonist Dean Fraser were among the evening’s other performers, rounding out a musical package that traversed generations and genres.

Speaking with the Jamaica Observer following the concert, patrons sought to explain Tastee’s longevity. Noting that not many companies would think to give back to their supporters in such a tangible way, concertgoers said Tastee’s knack for recognising the support of its consumers has helped establish its 60-year legacy.

“Tastee is not just about the patties. They’ve always been about giving back in some way, shape or form. If it weren’t for Tastee, Jamaica and the world would not have discovered talent such as Beenie Man, Yellowman, Nadine Sutherland, and so many others,” said Suzette Morgan.

“Their dedication to the Jamaican people has always been evident and it was proven again tonight when they hosted this free concert. The fact that we didn’t have to pay anything didn’t take away from the quality of the show. We got solid performances while we nibbled away on patties. It was a perfect way to celebrate their anniversary.”

Marcia Stewart agreed.

“Tastee is big in Jamaica because it’s big on supporting Jamaicans. We love our patty and the company has proven over the years that they value the support of their consumers. Hosting a free concert showed exactly how much they appreciate Jamaicans, and I hope they last another 60 years,” she said.

Friday night proved that while patties built the Tastee name, the company’s legacy has also been shaped by the love of the Jamaican people.

For decades, Tastee fed Jamaicans more than simply food. Through its talent competition, it also helped feed an entertainment industry that would eventually send some of the artistes it discovered onto stages around the world.

Behind the songs, the memories and generations of performers sharing one stage was the story of a Jamaican institution that has managed to remain part of the country’s everyday rhythm for six decades.

At 60, that relationship remains as much a part of Tastee’s legacy as the patties themselves.

World.title: Jamaica secures Tottori training base
World.content:
(From left, front) Tottori Athletics Association President Shinichi Hamasaki, Jamaica Athletics Administrative Association President Garth Gayle and Tottori Prefecture Governor Shinji Hirai; (back) Local Government Minister Desmond McKenzie, Sports Minister Olivia Grange and Japan’s Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary to Jamaica Kohei Maruyama during yesterday’s ceremonial signing of a partnership agreement between Jamaica and Tottori Prefecture in Kingston.Garfield Robinson

JAMAICA’S preparations for the 2027 World Athletics Championships received a boost yesterday with the signing of a 2027 World Athletics Championships Training Camp Agreement between Jamaica and Tottori Prefecture in Japan.

The agreement represents the latest chapter in a sporting partnership that began in 2007 following the World Athletics Championships in Osaka and has since developed into a nearly two-decade relationship built around athletics, cultural exchange and friendship.

Garth Gayle, president of the Jamaica Athletics Administrative Association (JAAA), was pleased with the agreement, which he believes sets the tone for a successful campaign at the championships.

“We want to ensure the best facilities and all that is needed for a successful campaign in Beijing 2027,” Gayle said.

Gayle says the Japanese will provide additional technical support, while the camp will also allow Jamaica to stage trial meets for its athletes. He said the trial meets proved pivotal for Oblique Seville, who went on to strike gold at the 2025 World Athletics Championships in Tokyo.

“The camp also allows the athletes to acclimatise as there is not much difference between Japan and China, so this is a good opportunity for coaches, managers and athletes to get ready for a successful championship,” Gayle said.

Sports Minister Olivia Grange described the renewed agreement as an important step in strengthening Jamaica’s sporting diplomacy and international partnerships.

“Today’s signing represents another decisive step in strengthening Jamaica’s sporting diplomacy, international partnerships and preparations for continued success globally,” Grange said.

She said the relationship with Tottori had evolved beyond simply providing Jamaican athletes with a venue to train, becoming a lasting friendship between Jamaica and Japan.

“What began in 2007, in the wake of the World Athletics Championships in Osaka, has evolved into more than a training arrangement. It has become a lasting friendship between Jamaica and Tottori,” Grange said.

The partnership has already produced tangible benefits for Jamaica’s athletes, particularly through the 2025 training camp ahead of the World Championships in Tokyo.

Grange says Team Jamaica was provided with world-class facilities and comprehensive support services, allowing athletes and staff to concentrate fully on competition preparation.

She also highlighted the contribution of hundreds of volunteers, interpreters, medical personnel, officials, sponsors and community members who helped make the Jamaican delegation feel at home during its stay.

Grange also pointed to exchanges between Jamaican athletes and Japanese communities, including a visit by Assinie Wilson, Kelly-Ann Beckford and teammates to students at Hakuto Special Needs School. That interaction subsequently inspired the Buddy Art Project, through which artwork created by students with disabilities was incorporated into flags displayed to welcome the Jamaican delegation.

Other exchanges included Jamaican athletes interacting with kindergarten children in Sendai, where they played games and received handmade medals.

“These moments remind us that this relationship extends far beyond training and competition; it is a bond of friendship, community, and shared humanity,” Grange said.

The sporting ties between the two countries have also been strengthened through the Japan Exchange and Teaching Programme, which saw Jamaican Olympian Christine Day appointed Jamaica’s first sports exchange advisor.

Day is based in Tottori, where she shares her sprinting knowledge and mentors athletes, providing another avenue for the development of athletics and cultural links between Jamaica and Japan.

Tottori Governor Shinji Hirai and Chairman Shinichi Hamazaki attended the signing and greeted guests in Jamaican dialect with “What a gwaan” before reverting to Japanese, with their remarks translated by an interpreter.

Minister of Local Government and Community Development Desmond McKenzie was also on hand for the signing and highlighted the broader relationship between Jamaica and Japan, including the friendship and cooperation between Tottori Prefecture and Westmoreland.

McKenzie says Jamaica and Japan are celebrating 62 years of bilateral relations, with cooperation extending beyond sport into community development, emergency communications and economic revitalisation.

He also highlighted the impact of Japan’s Grant Assistance for Grassroots Human Projects programme on micro and small businesses and municipal corporations, while noting the Social Development Commission’s continued collaboration with Japan on community initiatives, including sport.

World.title: MESSI’S IMPACT
World.content:
Argentina Captain Lionel Messi poses with the FIFA World Cup Trophy after Argentina won the 2022 World Cup final football match against France at Lusail Stadium in Lusail, Qatar, on Sunday, December 18, 2022. (Photo: AFP)

FOLLOWING Lionel Messi’s decision to retire from international football, Jamaica Football Federation (JFF) President Michael Ricketts believes the Argentine legend has made a significant impact on Jamaican football through his exploits on the international stage.

Messi made the announcement in a statement on social media on Monday, bringing an end to his 21-year stint with the national team.

“This is one that hurts me a lot. I love, I loved, and I will always love being part of the national team. I gave everything I had, and I don’t have anything more to give,” he said.

“I leave with peace and pride, knowing that together with my teammates we gave you moments we once dreamed of. It was crazy to experience all of this with you. I love you! Thank you God for making me Argentine.”

The 39-year-old cemented his legacy in 2022 after guiding Argentina to the FIFA World Cup, ending a 36-year drought. He almost made it two World Cup title lifts in a row in this summer’s World Cup in the USA, Mexico and Canada but went down 1-0 to Spain in the final.

Eight-time Ballon d’Or winner Messi leaves as the country’s all-time leading goal scorer and most capped player with 125 goals in 207 appearances. He also led Argentina to the 2021 and 2024 Copa America titles and the gold medal at the 2008 Olympics in Beijing.

Ricketts says Messi’s contribution on football, particularly in Jamaica, cannot be ignored.

“Messi in contemporary football would be arguably the most talked about player and probably the most highly rated player right now. He would have impacted the lives of so many young boys and girls,” Ricketts told the Jamaica Observer. “If you walk around any township, you will always see somebody, some youngster wearing a shirt marked Messi and that just goes to show what sport generally, and what football in particular, can do to the psyche of a nation.”

“Every good thing must come to an end and it has been an era for Messi and even his impact on the just-concluded World Cup speaks volumes for his footballing skills and of course the impact that he would have made in global football. Truly, Messi has impacted not just Jamaica but the world.”
