One of Messi’s milestone international games came against the Reggae Boyz, when he made his 100th appearance for Argentina in a 1-0 win at the 2015 Copa America in Chile.

Former national midfielder Jobi McAnuff played the full 90 minutes and swapped shirts with Messi at full time, which he says is one of the greatest moments of his career.

McAnuff, though, says he developed an even greater respect for the Argentine maestro after his kind gesture towards the entire Jamaican team following the game.

“There was a queue of Jamaican players, staff, everything, waiting for him outside the changing room,” he said. “He just took his time, signed every autograph, shaking hands, pictures, like [he was] class. He did not have to do that. They’re the little things for me that just set him apart for me, yes he’s a great footballer, but we come back to people as people and just respect that you can show to people.”

The Reggae Boyz would face off with Messi again seven years later in an international friendly in New Jersey, just months before lifting his first-ever World Cup title. Messi came off the bench and scored twice to lead Argentina to a 3-0 win.

“Everybody wanted to get to the touching distance of Messi — not even so much to touch him, but to get close to him — and a number of our players tried to embrace him, tried to take pictures with him. Our coaching staff really wanted to be identified with arguably one of the best footballers of all time,” Ricketts recalled.

“I don’t know if it’s fair to say we have lost an icon but he has now gone into retirement, but the name Messi will probably live forever in the minds of those who have an interest in the sport of football.”

Many players over the years have been dubbed the “next Messi”, including former Reggae Boy Chevone Marsh, who earned the nickname during his days at Cavalier FC and Calabar High.

Ricketts says the chances of the world producing another Messi are slim but hasn’t ruled it out, especially with the possibility that talent could come from Jamaica.

“What has happened in recent times is that coaching education now has improved leaps and bounds, not just locally, but throughout the Caribbean, throughout Concacaf and throughout the world,” he said.

“We would have established probably the best coaching education programme, so it’s not far-fetched. It’s not impossible but certainly, based on the newness of our coaching skills and our coaching workshops, it’s not far-fetched. It’s certainly not impossible.”

World.title: Fashion Radar: House of Clay
World.content:
​An intimate behind-the-scenes moment dressing the bride on her wedding day in an off-white stretch-satin slip gown. (Photo courtesy of House of Clay)

Tuesday Style Fashion (TSF) spotlights Keisha Allen, creative director of luxury for bridal fashion brand House of Clay.

TSF: Please share your House of Clay story — how you started, and the reason behind the name.

House of Clay: My journey to House of Clay officially began when I studied garment production and fashion design for two years at Garmex HEART Academy between 2005 and 2007. Following my training, my first job was at a prominent bridal boutique here in Jamaica. That experience proved to be pivotal. I fell in love with the transformational power of a wedding gown — that exact moment when a woman saw herself in the right dress and her entire demeanour changed. I could physically see her confidence bloom and watch her realise just how beautiful she was. I knew then that I wanted to dedicate my life to creating that feeling for women of all shapes and sizes.

Working directly with gowns from international designers and doing minor alterations also exposed me to global standards. I had already resolved in my heart before that any brand I built would be of such high quality that it could stand beside any international designer brand and not feel out of place. Seeing those gowns up close simply confirmed that this was standard work I could definitely do and surpass.

The reason behind the name ties back to my faith. I remember reading a story in Jeremiah 18 about a potter working at his wheel, taking a vessel of clay that didn’t turn out as he wanted, squashing it, and starting over to reshape it. I thought about the significance of how a potter takes a lump of clay — which, to most people, and as we say in Jamaica, is really just “dirt” — and turns it into something meaningful. Clay seems insignificant to the untrained eye, yet in the hands of a skilled artisan, it becomes a masterpiece. That mirrors my process with textiles. Taking a flat, two-dimensional piece of fabric and sculpting it to perfectly contour or fit a three-dimensional woman’s body is an art form.

Initially, the brand was simply supposed to just be called Clay. However, when we went to register the business in 2011, we were told we couldn’t register the single word “Clay” on its own because it’s a common substance, so we had to add something to it and registered as “Clay Fashioned.” But that felt a bit too on-the-nose so I could not settle with it. Having always been a fan of global couture houses, I realised that many of them use “House of” before their brand name — like House of Chanel. I knew this was the kind of house and legacy I was building, so we decided on House of Clay in 2015. While our inner garment labels simply read “Clay,” the company name reflects our commitment to couture, uncompromising quality, and the legacy we are building in how we make women feel… like “The Most Beautiful Woman in the Room”.

TSF:When did you thread that first needle and know this was your destiny?

House of Clay: I don’t think I knew it was my destiny the exact moment I threaded my first needle. As a child, I was always making clothes for my dolls. My father was very perceptive and good at recognising those subtle traits and creative gifts, so he bought me my first sewing kit when I was about nine years old. Even then, I wasn’t dreaming of fashion yet — I actually wanted to be a paediatrician!

It wasn’t until high school, around third form, that I realised I had a bit of a love-hate relationship with the sciences. I started evaluating what I genuinely loved doing and what I was naturally good at. I loved working with my hands, creating, and engaging in meticulous tasks like hand-sewing and embroidery — even the most tedious parts. That was when the thought clearly hit me: I want to be a fashion designer. From that moment on, I set my mind to pursuing it.

I grew up with a very meticulous mother, so a detailed and deliberate approach to my work came naturally. Because of that, I was never drawn to “fast” fashion or quick, ready-to-wear pieces you could whip up in a few hours. In my early days, of course, I made those kinds of garments because I had to master every aspect of garment construction. But I found that I was always most at peace, happy, and in my element when doing intricate, labour-intensive work — like hand-beading an entire gown over several days. Where others might feel anxious or restless during such tedious processes, I enter a state of complete calm and focus. Looking back, I realise that inclination is rare; even among talented creators, not everyone gravitates toward the technical, painstaking side of couture. That affinity was the quiet signal that this was where I belonged.

TSF:Why wedding dresses?

House of Clay: There are two primary reasons why I chose bridal wear. First, from a purely technical standpoint, bridal is the pinnacle of couture. Virtually every major couture runway show concludes with a showstopping bridal gown because it represents the highest, most complex form of garment construction — and naturally, that level of craftsmanship is where I gravitated.

Second, and most importantly, a wedding dress is arguably the most significant garment a woman will ever wear in her lifetime. From my earliest days working with brides, I fell in love with being part of that sacred moment. It is a true privilege to create something that doesn’t just fit a woman, but honours her and helps her feel breathtakingly beautiful and confident on one of the most important days of her life.

TSF: Take us back to the completion of that first gown.

House of Clay: When that very first bride trusts you with her wedding gown, the feeling is almost overwhelming. It comes with an incredible sense of reverence, paired with a genuine fear of messing up — because you know this is not just an ordinary dress; it is monumentally important to her. Looking back, I felt the fear and did it anyway, pouring absolutely everything I had into it. As a naturally creative person, the design aspect is often the easy part. Designing simply takes deep compassion — listening intently to what the bride desires, understanding her fears, and being mindful of her insecurities. Once you have that connection, and hopefully taste, creativity naturally flows to create a beautiful design. What truly makes it a masterpiece — what sets the process apart, is the technical execution — the desire and discipline to operate at the absolute highest standard.

After weeks upon weeks of meticulous, painstaking labour, stepping back to look at that finished gown on the hanger and thinking, “Wow, I made that,” was incredible. But the most significant moment — the moment that still defines my work to this day — is when she puts it on. Seeing her posture shift, her expression change, and watching that same transformational confidence and joy wash over her is my ultimate reward. Experiencing that same feeling that first made me fall in love with bridal wear as a young consultant confirmed everything for me.

TSF: Who in the field of wedding gowns do you most admire and why?

House of Clay: When I was first starting out, the designer I admired most was Vera Wang. Back then, her name was completely synonymous with luxury bridal, but what fascinated me was that she wasn’t creating typical, traditional wedding dresses. She essentially turned the bridal industry on its head.

She stepped into the space without trying to conform to it, which I thought was brilliant, brave, and deeply admirable. Her approach proved that there are always brides who want to wear something that authentically represents who they are, rather than simply following traditional expectations. That willingness to innovate and stay true to a distinct artistic vision is something I have always respected.

The Core Ethos of House of Clay



At the heart of House of Clay are three fundamental brand pillars that define every single gown we create:

Transformation: We believe that every woman’s body is inherently beautiful, regardless of shape or size. Our philosophy is that a woman should never have to force herself to fit into a gown; rather, the gown must be engineered to honour and fit her unique structure and architecture. It is about accentuating who she is so she feels completely radiant and confident.

Craftsmanship: This is at the very soul of what we do — from technical pattern drafting to intricate hand-finishing. In today’s fashion climate, true pattern drafting has become somewhat of a lost art, with many relying on shortcuts like “freehand cutting”. We hold fast to the mastery of pattern drafting because it unlocks endless structural possibilities and ensures precision fit right from the initial foundation. Coupled with traditional couture finishing techniques and meticulous attention to internal details (down to the millimeter on every seam allowance), our garments are built to world-class standards.

Made in Jamaica: We take immense pride in our roots. Jamaica is world-renowned for its global impact in music and athletics — we have given the world reggae and the fastest athletes alive. We believe Jamaican fashion deserves that exact same global stage. Growing up, there was often a stigma attached to local dressmaking, where “Made in Jamaica” was associated with ill-fitting, homemade, or poor-quality garments. House of Clay is actively dismantling that narrative. Everything we produce is designed and crafted in-house right here in Jamaica, serving as a standard for couture, luxury, and excellence.

Photos: Terry-Ann Miller | Merrick Cousley Photography | Courtesy of Keisha Allen

World.title: Sheree Martin named first female CEO of NCBJ, effective Sept 1
World.content:
Sheree Martin appointed CEO of National Commercial Bank Jamaica

KINGSTON, Jamaica — After months of acting in the post, Sheree Martin has been appointed chief executive officer by the Board of National Commercial Bank Jamaica Limited (NCBJ), effective September 1, 2026.

She will be the first woman to hold the post.

Martin served as interim CEO since January 19, 2026, leading the bank’s strategic and operational priorities with a focus on efficiency, governance and the customer experience.

In a statement, the bank said her appointment provides continuity as it continues to work on the same priorities.

Group Chief Executive Officer of NCB Financial Group Limited and Chairman of NCBJ Robert Almeida said Martin’s leadership during the interim period reinforced the board’s confidence in her ability to lead the bank.

“Sheree brings deep institutional knowledge, a strong understanding of our customers and a clear appreciation of how the different parts of the Bank must work together to deliver,” Almeida said.

“She combines strategic judgement with practical, hands-on leadership and a strong focus on execution. These qualities will serve NCBJ well as it builds on the progress already underway.”

Martin said she was honoured by the appointment and energised by the opportunities ahead.

“NCBJ has an extraordinary legacy, talented people and a vital role in the lives of our customers and in Jamaica’s development,” she said. “I look forward to working with our board and teams to build on that foundation – accelerating our progress, strengthening the customer experience and bringing the full capabilities of the bank together more effectively.”

She added, “Our priorities are clear: empower our people within the right culture, improve the way we deliver and earn our customers’ confidence through the quality and consistency of the service, financial solutions and platforms they experience every day.”

Martin brings more than 20 years of executive leadership experience across the financial services and energy sectors. Before assuming the role of interim CEO at NCB, she had leadership responsibility for several functions including retail banking, operations, credit underwriting, marketing and enterprise information management.

World.title: Former gang member found guilty of murdering Tupac Shakur
World.content:
Rapper Tupac Shakur attends a voter registration event in South Central Los Angeles, August15, 1996. (AP Photo/Frank Wiese, File)

LAS VEGAS, United States (AFP) — Duane Davis, a former Los Angeles gang member, was found guilty on Monday by a Las Vegas court of the 1996 murder of rapper Tupac Shakur.

Thirty years after the rap legend’s death at a Las Vegas casino, the jury found Davis, 63, guilty of murder after just a few hours of deliberation.

World.title: Pressure mounts on Europe as Trump deals push pharma to the US
World.content:
Industry leaders in Europe warn that if the U.S. continues to sign more deals with companies — designed to drive down prices for American citizens while boosting U.S. investments — European patients will feel the effects.

Since the most-favored nation policy will see Washington copy some EU countries’ prices, companies are opting not to launch new drugs in Europe to maintain higher prices in the U.S. where they can make bigger profits. In addition, companies are increasingly choosing America for research and manufacturing.

“Companies may hesitate to launch in Europe or in Japan or Canada if they think that the price in Europe or Japan or Canada will be lower than the price they could obtain in the U.S.,” Adrian van den Hoven, director general of Medicines for Europe, told POLITICO. “That's the risk for Europe going forward.” Medicines for Europe represents the generics industry, which largely makes cheaper off-patent medicines. Two large generics firms that also make branded drugs were included in the nine new deals.

Meanwhile, Europe’s current biggest offering to entice industry to stay local — a proposed patent extension for certain biotech drugs — is too little too late, some argue. Industry says the patent extension comes with too many conditions and it won’t come into effect in time to stop the sector from pivoting more to America where market conditions are more favorable.

The patent extension and other industry perks in the proposed Biotech Act are a step in the right direction, said Alexander Natz, secretary general of the European Confederation of Pharmaceutical Entrepreneurs. But “it’s probably too late if we wait for the Biotech Act” to take effect, likely in a couple of years, he said.

Capturing more companies

The latest deals mark a shift away from the previous 17 deals with multi-billion dollar big pharmaceutical companies and include a mix from small specialist firms with only a handful of licensed drugs to vast generic drugmakers.

World.title: Germany blames Russia for drone incursion, announces retaliatory measures
World.content:
German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul announced a series of domestic countermeasures, including the closure of Russia’s Bonn consulate on September 18, stricter entry controls for Russian nationals and the termination of the agreement governing the Russian House in central Berlin—a cultural institution suspected of serving as a hub for espionage operations and whose Russian operator is under EU sanctions.

Germany will also propose new EU sanctions targeting Russian individuals connected to hybrid attacks, while pushing to increase measures targeting Russia’s shadow fleet, Wadephul said.

His comments come as EU foreign ministers are set to meet in Ireland on Tuesday night and Wednesday. “The matter, including additional sanctions, will be prepared by Foreign Ministers at their upcoming meeting,” European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen wrote on social media after the press conference.

“If the gravity of the events is confirmed”, French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot told reporters earlier on Tuesday morning, “there will inevitably be consequences, particularly regarding the sanctions that might be imposed on Russia.”

Berlin’s response marks a hardening in the German government’s approach to Russia under Chancellor Friedrich Merz. Merz has long maintained that Germany is neither at war nor at peace, but it is rare for Berlin to so definitively attribute a hybrid attack to Russia and take targeted countermeasures.

“NATO stands in full solidarity with Germany after the Russian hybrid attack in Leipzig,” the alliance’s secretary-general Mark Rutte said on X. “I welcome the measures announced by Germany in response,” he added.

This story is being updated.

World.title: Leuven mayor bans Europa League match against Israeli team
World.content:
Violence and hooliganism are not uncommon at European-level football matches, nor are occasional orders that games should take place in neutral venues, behind closed doors or with certain fans banned from attending for safety reasons.

The war in Gaza, though, has politicized such decisions as they relate to Israeli clubs, at the same time as exacerbating tensions around the visits of Israeli fans to some parts of Europe.

In Amsterdam in November 2024, supporters of Israeli club Maccabi Tel Aviv were involved in violence across the city before and after a match with Ajax, with dozens of arrests and several people hospitalized.

Keeping boisterous groups of opposing teams’ football fans away from each other and under control is already a challenge for police, and adding the potential for political, antisemitic and racist provocation into the mix stretches their ability to keep the peace.

“We have full confidence in the Belgian security authorities and their ability to ensure that a football match can take place safely and securely,” said the Israeli embassy in Brussels. “Should assistance be required, Israel would be happy to provide it.”

This is not the first time Belgian authorities have blocked a match involving an Israeli team on security grounds. In 2024, Brussels refused to host Belgium’s Nations League game against Israel, citing the risk of major demonstrations and counter-demonstrations. The game was eventually moved to Debrecen, Hungary, and played behind closed doors. Ridouani had also previously refused to allow both the Belgian women’s and men’s national teams to play Israel at Leuven’s Den Dreef stadium.

World.title: Les datacenters énergivores se développent en Europe, la résistance aussi
World.content:
Une résistance croissante pourrait toutefois venir contrecarrer les ambitions de l’entreprise. Un groupe d’opposants locaux — inquiets de la consommation énergétique vorace du centre de données et méfiants face à la mainmise d’un mastodonte américain de la tech — se bat pour empêcher son extension.

“Nous voulons vraiment leur donner du fil à retordre”, assume Harald Müllner, un expert en informatique originaire de Linz, une ville voisine, et qui a cofondé un collectif local regroupant des scientifiques, des artistes et des militants opposés au centre de données. “Ils doivent comprendre que ça ne convient pas à la population.”

Leurs manifestations et leurs pétitions contre les projets de Google reflètent une tendance observée de l’autre côté de l’Atlantique, où les démocrates surfent sur une vague croissante de rejet à l’égard des centres de données à l’approche des élections de mi-mandat américaines de cette année. Le président Donald Trump, quant à lui, a pris le parti des Big Tech, affirmant lundi dans un post sur son réseau social que les communautés s’opposant aux datacenters “finiront par être arriérées et pauvres”.

En Europe, des militants s’attaquent à des projets en France, tandis qu’en Italie, les habitants manifestent contre certains projets. En Irlande, où les centres de données consomment déjà un cinquième de l’électricité totale, les opposants ont tenté — sans succès — d’en faire bloquer la construction devant les tribunaux.

Mais jusqu’à présent, les inquiétudes suscitées par les centres de données en Europe se sont heurtées à la crainte des gouvernements de voir le continent prendre du retard par rapport aux Etats-Unis et à la Chine dans la course à l’intelligence artificielle.

“Nous ne pouvons pas réclamer une plus grande souveraineté européenne en matière d’IA, tout en dressant sans cesse de nouveaux obstacles qui entravent l’infrastructure même sur laquelle elle repose”, a déclaré Elisabeth Zehetner, secrétaire d’Etat autrichienne à l’Energie, à propos des demandes visant à renforcer la réglementation des centres de données de grande envergure, comme celui de Kronstorf.

World.title: What Iceland’s snub means for the EU’s place in the world
World.content:
“At a time when the international security environment has become far more uncertain than it was a decade ago, many expected support for reopening accession negotiations to grow,” said Nicola Procaccini, co-chair of the right-wing European Conservatives and Reformists group in the European Parliament. “The fact that the Icelandic people nevertheless chose not to take even that first step should give Brussels pause.”

Reykjavik’s narrow rejection of restarting EU accession talks in a referendum on Saturday is hardly a death blow to the 450 million-strong bloc. With fewer than 400,000 people and a smaller GDP than Estonia, Iceland was never the prize that would make or break Commission President Ursula von der Leyen’s European project.

But the result is still an uncomfortable reality check for a Brussels establishment that has spent the past four years betting that a hazardous world would make the EU more attractive — and had taken Iceland’s renewed interest as a flattering signal of its own relevance.

“A nation weighed what membership would add to what it already has,” center-right Finnish MEP Mika Aaltola said, “and answered: not enough.”

Vote of (no) confidence

Enlargement is about more than adding countries to the EU. It is also a branding exercise: a way for Brussels to show that its model of democracy, prosperity and predictability remains attractive in a world of hard power politics.

Every country that knocks on the EU’s door gives the bloc a chance to present itself as a desirable club, in contrast to Trump’s claims that the continent is “decaying.” Iceland was unusually useful in that regard: a wealthy democracy that paused its membership bid in 2015, but was coming back and asking to be let in.

World.title: Andy Burnham will attend COP31
World.content:
Expressing his “profound shock and horror” at the Himalayan flash floods, in which more than 1,000 people are now known to have died, Burnham said: “This is what the climate crisis looks like. We have just ourselves experienced what is likely to have been the hottest summer on record.

“This government will meet the climate challenge and I can confirm to the House that I will attend COP31 in Turkey in November.”

The U.K.’s Met Office confirmed Tuesday that the U.K. recorded an average mean temperature of 16.5C from June to August, the hottest summer on record, breaking a previous record of 16.1C set just last year.

World.title: Ed Miliband to attend EU foreign ministers meeting in Ireland
World.content:
“Working closely with our European neighbours will make Britain a wealthier, safer country- that is why I am putting the European relationship at the heart of my agenda as Foreign Secretary,” Miliband said ahead of the meeting, which will take place in Wicklow in Ireland.

The foreign secretary is set to hold a series of bilateral meetings, including with his EU counterpart Kaja Kallas and German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul.

He is also due to meet his Irish counterpart Helen McEntree, Canadian Foreign Minister Anita Anand and Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha — the latter two also attending the meeting as guests.

Ahead of the meeting the Foreign Office said the discussions would focus on deepening U.K. cooperation with European and international partners, as well as supporting Ukraine.

He is expected to announce new British funding to support reconstruction in the invasion-hit country, as well as measures to allow British companies to participate in rebuilding efforts there.

Ministers will also discuss wider challenges facing the continent such as climate pressures — following the hottest summer on record in the U.K.

The so-called “Gymnich” meeting is meant to be a more informal setting than most EU summits so leaders can speak candidly without officials.

The format is named after the German castle Schloss Gymnich which hosted the first such meeting in 1974.

World.title: Team up with EU on energy to combat China, Andy Burnham told
World.content:
These moves would help support investment in the North Sea, address price instability and protect companies on both sides of the channel from incoming carbon border taxes.

But it also suggests going further — with a view to establishing regional independence on green energy.

Competing with China

The authors argue that the U.K. rejoining the North Sea Energy Cooperation Group (NSEC) as a full member would make it easier to coordinate energy investments like carbon capture storage, energy interconnectors and offshore wind farms — crucial to the green transition.

Since Brexit, the U.K. has only been a partial member of the deliberative body via a memorandum of understanding, but full membership would make “technocratic planning challenges around grid build-out” a lot easier to navigate, the authors say.

The report also argues for another extension of the grace period on electric vehicle battery rules of origin, which has been plaguing car manufacturers on both sides of the channel since Britains’s exit.

It also warns that in the long term, battery production and the rest of the EV supply chain need to be moved as far as possible to Europe from China.

World.title: US military says it struck IRGC targets in Iran after attacks on shipping in Strait of Hormuz
World.content:
The US military said its forces struck Iranian Revolutionary Guards (IRGC) targets in Iran on Tuesday in response to attacks on shipping as well as American service personnel.

 

In a post on X, US Central Command (CENTCOM) said the strikes followed "recent attempted attacks by the IRGC against commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and against American service members deployed to the region."

Iran's Fars news agency reported that explosions had been heard in the areas of Bandar Abbas, Sirik, and Qeshm. The outlet said local authorities had also reported strikes in the districts of Chabahar and Konarak.

Hostilities sparked back into life on Sunday after the US carried out fresh strikes on what it said were IRGC minelaying forces in the Strait of Hormuz, its first military action in the waterway in a month.

The IRGC quickly confirmed strikes had hit Larak Island and warned of a "retaliatory response." It then said on Monday that its forces had carried out attacks on two US bases in Jordan and a base in the UAE. The UAE's Ministry of Defence later denied that its Al Menhad air base had been targeted.

CENTCOM has rejected Iran's claims that its Sunday strikes were an "act of aggression" and said its forces were responding to an "imminent threat in the Strait of Hormuz," a strategic waterway that usually carries around a quarter of the world’s seaborne oil trade.

"In essence, Iran created the threat and the U.S. military eliminated it to protect civilian mariners, commercial shipping, and the free flow of global commerce," it said.

Washington and Tehran have been locked in conflict since late February, when the US and Israel launched a first wave of strikes on Iran.

Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz following those strikes, and it has since become a key sticking point in peace talks with the US.

World.title: Ryanair Boeing 737 stairs: 85 falls in three years, ANSV study finds
World.content:
Ryanair's Boeing 737 hides a hazard just outside the cabin door: its retractable onboard stairs.

 

Passengers who have used them have faced a significantly higher risk of falling than those using stairs provided by airports. That is the conclusion of a study by the National Agency for Flight Safety (ANSV), published in August 2026.

The study analysed falls reported in Italy during boarding and disembarkation between 2023 and 2025. Of 104 incidents, 85 involved passengers who used the forward integrated stairs of Boeing 737s. That accounts for 82 per cent of cases, noted Corriere della Sera. (source in Italian)

The scale of the figures is even clearer when compared with total passenger numbers. Over the same period the Irish airline carried around 27 per cent of all passengers in Italy. The other carriers, which make up the remaining 73 per cent, recorded 19 falls.

The trend is not confined to Italy. Since 2021 Ryanair has registered 489 falls on stairs, 360 of them (73 per cent) on the Boeing 737's integrated stairway. According to ANSV, that is three times as many falls as those recorded on airport stairways.

To track and analyse the incidents, ANSV used the ECCAIRS system, the digital platform run by the European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA). The system collects and analyses aviation safety data from EU countries.

Why are Ryanair's Boeing 737 stairs linked to more falls?

For disembarkation, airlines often hire mobile stairs from airports. Ryanair's Boeing 737 instead has the option of an integrated system that can be deployed while parked, allowing passengers to disembark without requiring airport handlers. This cuts disembarkation times and ground-service costs.

The integrated stairway has 12 steps, about 61 centimetres wide and 20 high, with a tread depth of 25 centimetres and an inclination of 35 degrees.

According to ANSV's investigation, the dimensions "are at the limits for step height and steepness" compared with those used by airport operators, "who have lower steps and, usually, a less pronounced inclination, and platforms and treads that are considerably larger."

It also notes that "the first step" of the stairway "is asymmetrical" for passengers on the way down because of the shape of the fuselage in relation to the step.

According to Ireland's air accident investigation unit (AAIU), EU regulations do not impose requirements on the size of integrated stairs because they are not deemed critical to flight operations.

ANSV's study began with three incidents (source in Italian) in Genoa, Venice and Bologna, in which three people suffered "serious injuries".

In Genoa on 22 March 2025, one person was taken by ambulance to hospital after a fall that occurred "most likely due to the inattention of the passenger", according to ANSV's reports.

Two days later in Venice, another passenger suffered serious injuries after falling from the integrated stairs. According to staff, the passenger was carrying two suitcases and was not holding the handrail. In the Bologna incident, the passenger also fell while carrying two bags.

After these incidents, Ryanair updated its disembarkation protocol and since 23 July cabin crew have been repeating the warning to use the handrail also in the language of the country of origin and destination.

The problem with the integrated stairs on the Boeing 737 had already been examined by the aviation safety agencies of Ireland and Spain (CIAIAC), after falls in 2021 in Dublin and in 2024 in Alicante.

Following those incidents, the Spanish agency urged Boeing to redesign the stairway, reducing its steepness and increasing the surface area of the steps. CIAIAC also called on Ryanair to abandon use of the integrated system and rely solely on stairs provided by airport operators.

No investigation carried out so far has concluded that the system is defective. ANSV has endorsed the Spanish recommendations to Boeing and Ryanair, while attributing the falls to human factors such as inattention and failure to use the handrail.

World.title: SCO challenges West as diverse group of nations pursues multipolar future
World.content:
The Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO), a diverse group aiming to balance the West’s global influence, has called for a more representative and fairer multipolar world order as its summit in Kyrgyzstan ended on Tuesday with a run of headlines.

 

The 25th gathering of the 10 members — China, India, Iran, Pakistan, Russia, Belarus, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan and Uzbekistan — brought together regional leaders as “dialogue partners” from Central Asia, the Caspian region, the Middle East and wider Asia in a broad forum of meetings to address a rapidly changing multipolar world, even amid significant disagreements and often diverging interests.

The Iran war and Russia’s all-out invasion of Ukraine defined the summit’s focus, with disruptions in global supply lines and emerging alternatives through Central Asia and the Caspian, as well as the rapid geopolitical shockwaves and realignments they have generated.

In a surprise moment with global impact, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi told Russian President Vladimir Putin directly, on live television, to end his war against Ukraine.

"Every single day spent in war pushes humanity backwards, ” Modi said unexpectedly to a visibly tense Putin. “We need to move from endless war to the end of war, to the end of hostilities.”

“This is very important for all of humanity," Modi added.

"We have to move in that direction, which is also essential for the welfare of humanity. It is humanity’s call to resolve all issues peacefully as soon as possible," the Indian premier told the Russian president.

"This is India’s message — the message from the land of Gandhi, the land of Buddha: a message of peace, a message of humanity."

Putin did not reply to Modi, but in a speech later at the summit said that "today, 1 September, is the day World War II began."

"We must do everything to exclude from world practice any provocation of armed conflicts," Putin added. Russia’s war in Ukraine is now longer than World War II in duration.

Members of the SCO Plus meeting. Press service of Kyrgyzstan President

In another snub for the Kremlin, a bilateral meeting between Putin and his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping produced no progress on a Siberian natural gas pipeline that Moscow urgently needs as the country’s infrastructure and economy reel from continuous Ukrainian strikes on key energy targets across Russia.

The Russian president however received the public gratitude of his Iranian counterpart Masoud Pezeshkian, who thanked Putin "for your positions at every stage.”

Putin said that Russia is providing Iran with assistance and “supplying the needed goods,” and that “Russia stands in solidarity with the people of Iran, who are defending their interests. He further said he "admires their courage and steadfastness” in their fight against the US and Israel.

"Today we are experiencing an erosion of the foundations upon which international order is built," Pezeshkian said.

"If such actions are met with no effective response from the international community, what state can be certain that its sovereignty and security will be protected in the future against the use of force?"

The Iranian delegation pushed for maximum results at the SCO summit, with Pezeshkian also meeting his Azerbaijani, Indian and Pakistani counterparts, while Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi met his counterparts from China, Pakistan, Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Tajikistan and Russia.

China and Turkey laud multilateralism

China, which sees the SCO as an alternative to Western-aligned organisations like the G7, has recently shown it wants to expand the organisation's scope and influence, while Russia and Iran joined the summit to build relations with non-Western partners and seek support and recognition.

In his speech at the summit, China’s Xi said the SCO should “foster an environment of universal security,” while criticising “hegemony, unilateralism, and protectionism” which run “counter to the tide of history.”

Xi further urged the SCO leaders and partners to “shoulder the responsibility of the times,” as multipolarity is an “irreversible trend” and that “dominance by just one or several countries, or bloc politics are not true multilateralism.”

Turkey, which holds partner status within the SCO, also seeks to use the platform to strengthen its position in the region, viewing its partnership in the organisation as part of a balanced foreign policy that maintains its traditional ties with the West through NATO while strengthening its influence in Eurasia.

Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan told the summit that the SCO is “a rising star in every field” and that with its “3.5 billion people and $35 trillion in gross domestic product (it) is an indispensable element of a multipolar order."

Calling the SCO a “complement to the UN,” Erdoğan said the organisation “has a structure that aligns with our multidimensional foreign policy centred on regional ownership,” adding that “as Türkiye, we are taking responsibility for resolving conflicts around us through dialogue and diplomacy.”

Erdoğan highlighted one of the new thrusts of the SCO summit participants: alternative transport and energy corridors, as the war with Iran disrupted traditional avenues.

"We believe that the organisation can play a role not only in ensuring peace and stability, but also in establishing uninterrupted and secure transportation corridors, which are vital for the prosperity of our peoples, and in areas such as energy supply security," the Turkish president said.

Billions in Central Asia and Caucasus projects

The leaders of Central Asia and the South Caucasus pushed relentlessly during the summit to maximise the economic opportunities for their regions as the Iran war and wider Middle East disruptions place them at the forefront of new global trade and connectivity solutions.

Azerbaijan’s President Ilham Aliyev and Armenian Premier Nikol Pashinyan held a new round of their peace talks in Bishkek, with Aliyev saying “the South Caucasus is becoming a zone of peace.”

Pashinyan said transport corridors and regional connectivity are now developing toward the Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity (TRIPP).

Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev told the summit that trade among SCO countries has reached $1 trillion and that much more remains to unlock the full potential of cooperation and resource use.

Uzbekistan's President Shavkat Mirziyoyev proposed establishing a bank for inter-regional projects, natural resource management, digital services and healthcare.

Mirziyoyev agreed with his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping to raise bilateral trade from $18 billion in 2025 to $30 billion in the coming years through a portfolio of joint investment projects and industrial cooperation.

"The existence of multiple centres of political influence is an important condition for advancing a political pluralism on the international stage," Tajikistan's President Emomali Rahmon said.

New security centre approved

Away from the diplomacy, the summit closed Kyrgyzstan's year as chair with a package of institutional decisions. Leaders signed the Bishkek Declaration and a protocol amending the SCO's Founding Charter, which Kyrgyz Foreign Minister Jeenbek Kulubaev said would create the basis for a more flexible bloc.

On security, members approved the rules for a Universal Centre for Countering Security Challenges based in Tashkent and an anti-drug centre in Dushanbe.

A unit to fight transnational organised crime will open in Bishkek under that centre, the first permanent SCO body on Kyrgyz soil.

Members also agreed to complete consultations "in the shortest possible time" on a long-discussed SCO development bank, with a view to signing its founding document, although they concluded no deal in Bishkek.

Leaders adopted further documents on artificial intelligence, climate, energy and information security, a declaration on nuclear safety, and a decision to develop cooperation with the African Union.

Kyrgyzstan said it held around 200 events during its chairmanship, more than 50 of them in the country itself, and marked the anniversary by naming a 4,050-metre peak in the Ala-Archa range "SCO Peak".

Pakistan now takes the chairmanship and will host the next summit in Islamabad.

World.title: Von der Leyen pledges response to Russian hybrid attacks ahead of Rutte meeting
World.content:
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said she stands in "full solidarity" with Germany after officials in Berlin formally attributed a high-profile drone incident to Russia at a press conference on Monday.

 

Von der Leyen said she would use a meeting with NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte on Wednesday to discuss the matter, with additional sanctions to be prepared by foreign ministers at an upcoming meeting.

"We will keep the EU united despite these escalating and serious acts," she said in a statement posted on social media platform X on Monday.

"The German government has taken strong measures. And the message is clear: hybrid attacks will not go without a clear response."

The “short notice” bilateral was confirmed by European Commission Chief Spokesperson Paula Pinho on Tuesday, who said the meeting would also occur in the context of Europe and NATO strengthening defence cooperation.

A NATO official told Euronews the meeting would centre mostly on how to deepen coordination against hybrid threats.

In the wake of the news from Germany, Rutte posted a similar statement on X, stating that NATO stands in full solidarity with Berlin and "the evidence is clear" that Russia was to blame.

"NATO will continue to strengthen our ability to deter and defend all Allies against any threat — including malign actions like those seen in Leipzig and elsewhere across the Alliance," he said.

Von der Leyen's comments came after Germany's Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt announced on Monday that the "means to carry out the act" of a drone sabotage incident occurring in August is "known to use from other hybrid operations conducted by Russia and its war against Ukraine."

"The German government therefore concludes that Russia is responsible for the hybrid attack in Leipzig on 4 August," he said.

Germany has ordered the closure of the Russian consulate in Bonn, while the Russian House in Berlin will also be shut down. Foreign Affairs Minister Johann Wadephul said Russia’s actions form part of a “long series of attempts at destabilisation, disinformation, threats, sabotage and aggression directed at Europe."

On 4 August a drone was found in the security zone of the Leipzig/Halle Airport near a Ukrainian cargo aircraft used to transport military supplies. Later, a second unmanned aerial vehicle collided with an aircraft, with the plane unable to land.

Merz has previously vowed a response to the incidents, with action coordinated between EU and NATO allies.

The Russian Foreign Ministry released a statement late August condemning Europe’s blame, stating this occurred well before an investigation had been completed.

Meanwhile, the EU’s foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said Russia is hitting Europe with increasing kinetic hybrid incidents aiming to “scare us away” from supporting Ukraine.

“They will not succeed,” she said, following a defence ministerial meeting in Wicklow, Ireland. Kallas said it is obvious the risks from these incidents are rising, and “clearly we are not doing enough to stop this.”

Irish Foreign Minister Helen McEntee**,** delivering the press conference alongside Kallas, said “support for Ukraine and pressure on Russia” remains central to Ireland’s six-month EU council presidency.

“We are now starting to see threats materialise as recently as the last 24 hours, where our colleagues in Romania and Latvia and Estonia, and of course Germany, have spoken of incursions into their own airspace, but also into their own land domain,” she said.

Romania and Estonia both reported drone incursions occurring on Tuesday. Several improvised explosive devices were found near coal-fired power plant in Germany also on Tuesday.

On his way into the talks, Estonian Defence Minister Hanno Pevkur said Europe must prepare itself for more Russian hybrid warfare incidents.

"They are testing always this threshold — where is this red line," he said, adding that Europe must keep a “very clear” head.

World.title: Russia's Starlink copycat has failed so far, but still threatens Ukraine
World.content:
None of the 16 satellites Russia launched on 19 July as part of its Rassvet programme, Moscow's attempt to build its own version of Starlink to guide the drones and missiles it has used against Ukraine for more than four years, have reached their planned orbit, according to the Institute for the Study of War (ISW), citing data from live satellite tracker N2YO.

 

Most of the satellites are sitting at altitudes of 300 to 400 kilometres, "well short of the intended 870-kilometer operational altitude for the Rassvet satellites," the report said.

At least two satellites appear to be heading for reentry into Earth's atmosphere.

Those flying at lower altitudes face greater atmospheric drag, burn through fuel faster and have shorter operational lifespans than those flying higher, meaning the affected satellites are unlikely to last as long as Russia had planned, even if they stabilise.

Satellite internet has become central to how both sides fight this war.

Ukraine's access to Starlink has let its forces fly reconnaissance and strike drones, coordinate artillery and stay connected in areas where Russian strikes have destroyed ground infrastructure.

The stakes involved are not abstract. Since Russia's full-scale invasion began in February 2022, the UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine (HRMMU) has verified at least 16,874 civilians killed and 51,173 injured, as of the end of July.

HRMMU said in a report published on 13 August that July 2026 was the deadliest month for Ukrainian civilians since March 2022, with at least 437 killed and 2,610 injured, driven by a sharp rise in aerial bombardment and glide bomb attacks alongside continued long-range missile and drone strikes on cities far from the front line.

The mission's monthly reports also recorded successive records for short-range drone casualties near the front in April and May.

A functioning Rassvet constellation would extend Russia's ability to direct strikes over greater distances and with greater precision, which is why the programme's repeated failures matter well beyond the technical details.

A troubled launch record

Of the 16 Rassvet satellites launched on 24 March, 12 reached their intended altitude of 550 kilometres and remain there, according to the report.

Those satellites already give Russian forces two daily windows of connectivity with ground terminals, lasting up to 90 minutes in total over Ukraine.

Moscow appears to be rushing the programme to compensate for the loss of Starlink access. Ukraine's defence ministry said in early February that Starlink terminals being used illicitly by Russian forces had been deactivated after Kyiv and SpaceX moved to a "whitelist" system restricting the network to verified terminals.

"Russia may have been unprepared to accelerate constellation deployment at this pace and will likely face additional delays," the ISW report said.

But the threat has not gone away. ISW warned that the existing satellites "may allow Russian forces to conduct more precise strikes against Ukraine using remotely controlled unmanned systems" during the windows when connectivity does work — a reminder that Russia does not need a fully functioning constellation to keep inflicting harm, only a partially working one.

Falling short of scale

Bureau 1440, the Russian aerospace firm developing the satellites, has said it plans "dozens" more launches to deploy hundreds more satellites.

Serhii Beskrestnov, then an adviser to Ukraine's defence minister, said on 31 May that Russia would need at least 200 to 250 satellites in orbit to achieve continuous, stable connectivity, and that Moscow was unlikely to hit that target in the near term.

The report attributed Russia's bottleneck to its reliance on the Soyuz-2.1b, "a costly and scarce asset."

The country has carried out only six to eight Soyuz-2.1b launches across all space and commercial missions since 2022, a tempo that ISW said would allow for "a maximum of 128 Rassvet satellites per four years," and only if every launch succeeded and none were diverted elsewhere.

So far, only 37.5% of launched Rassvet satellites have reached a sustainable operational altitude.

Ukraine targets the supply chain

Ukrainian forces have also gone after the infrastructure behind the programme, in an apparent effort to slow a system that would extend Russia's ability to deliver deadly strikes in Ukraine.

Ukrainian forces struck the Progress Space Rocket Center, which produces Soyuz-type launch vehicles, overnight between 14 and 15 August.

A further strike was attempted against the Plesetsk Cosmodrome on 23 August, two days before Russia launched a Soyuz-2.1b vehicle reportedly carrying a GLONASS-K1 satellite, part of Russia's GPS alternative.

Both Rassvet batches were launched from Plesetsk, and the report concluded that Ukrainian strikes "threaten not only Russia's limited supply and production of launch vehicles but also the scarce launch infrastructure to place satellites into orbit" — infrastructure that, if it succeeds, will make Russia's war on Ukraine much more lethal.

World.title: Brussels says €90 billion loan for Ukraine is enough for now amid growing doubts
World.content:
The European Commission is reluctant to reopen the sensitive debate on financial support for Ukraine, despite growing doubts about whether the €90 billion loan agreed by leaders last year will last until the end of 2027, as originally conceived.

 

Brussels intends to disburse €45 billion this year and €45 billion next year. So far, €3.2 billion in budgetary aid and €8.35 billion in military aid have been paid out.

"In terms of longevity, that is what is foreseen: that this €90 billion loan should be disbursed (over) the two years," Paula Pinho, the Commission's chief spokesperson, said on Tuesday in response to a Euronews question.

"It's important to remember that these disbursements are also linked to the reforms that are being introduced in Ukraine, and this is, of course, a critical aspect," she added.

"We are focused now on what is already a very ambitious disbursement plan, and for the moment that's where our focus lies."

Russia's escalation, however, is rapidly adding to the bill.

Moscow has launched a new tactic of non-stop drone attacks aimed at disrupting daily economic activity and sowing terror among civilians. At the same time, it is ramping up strikes of ballistic missiles on critical infrastructure ahead of the winter season.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has asked allies to plug a €23 billion gap in the Ministry of Defence to pay for weapons and remain "competitive" in deep strikes.

"We need more money, much more," Zelenskyy said last week.

As a solution, Zelenskyy suggested the EU front-load a share of the €45 billion earmarked for next year, which would mean having less money available in 2027.

The Commission has not yet received a formal request from Kyiv in that regard.

Member states discussed the matter on Tuesday during an informal ministerial meeting in Ireland, where support for Ukraine topped the agenda.

At the end of the talks, Irish Foreign Minister Helen McEntee said there was "consensus across the room" to "bring forward funding" under the ongoing loan. But she admitted the question required further deliberations in Brussels.

Back to the assets?

In the meantime, Sweden, the Netherlands, Spain and Poland have revived the idea of tapping into the immbolised assets of the Russian Central Bank to provide additional support for Ukraine, warning the €90 billion loan "will not be enough".

The EU holds €210 billion of these assets, sanctioned since February 2022.

"What we see is that Ukraine needs more support and, to be honest, we're not providing enough support bilaterally and through the EU, and then what is left is the frozen assets," Swedish Foreign Minister Maria Malmer Stenergard told Euronews.

"This is what is fair to Ukraine, it's what is fair to taxpayers," she added.

The Commission is treading carefully on the divisive issue.

Last year, the executive threw its weight fully behind an inventive proposal to turn the Russian assets into a financial lifeline for Ukraine. But the plan soon met fierce opposition from Belgium, which holds the majority of the €210 billion.

It eventually fell apart at a make-or-break summit in December, when leaders opted instead for joint debt to finance a €90 billion loan.

Officials in the Commission have never abandoned the idea of tapping the Russian assets but are mindful of tabling a new proposal without a guarantee of success. Capitals are already ensnared in fraught negotiations over the next EU budget.

Instead, Brussels is turning up the pressure on Western allies, who are expected to complement the loan by covering one-third of Ukraine's needs.

"There is one-third which cannot be covered by the EU and where we have been urging our partners to come in and step in," Pinho, the spokesperson, said.

Last month, Norway, a major non-EU donor, pledged 85 billion krone (€7.86 billion) for Ukraine in 2027, matching the amount allocated this year.

World.title: Russia behind attempted drone 'attack' at Leipzig airport, Berlin says
World.content:
Berlin has blamed Russia for an attempted drone "attack" at Leipzig airport last month.

 

In a press conference on Tuesday, German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said an assessment of the incident "fits the known pattern of Russian hybrid operations in Europe."

NATO member Germany, which supports Ukraine in its fight against Russia, has long accused Moscow of targeting it with a campaign of hybrid attacks involving espionage and sabotage, claims the Kremlin has rejected.

Germany has for months reported suspicious drone sightings over military and industrial sites, but an incident at Leipzig/Halle Airport on the night of 4-5 August raised the alarm as a drone found there carried explosives.

Police used a robot to defuse the device found near a Ukrainian cargo plane. Another drone was reportedly discovered weeks later near the airport, also with traces of an explosive substance.

The airport in eastern Germany plays a key role in the transport of military goods, including by the German military and NATO allies, and also serves as a base for Ukraine's Antonov Airlines.

Germany's Foreign Minister, Johann Wadephul, announced on Tuesday that Berlin would be taking action against Russia "as the perpetrator of the hybrid attack in Leipzig."

Wadephul said Russia's consulate in Bonn and its Berlin cultural centre would be closed as part of the German government's response to the incident.

"The Russian general consulate in Bonn will be closed by 18 September," he said, adding that there would also be tighter border controls for Russian nationals going forward and increased pressure on Russia's shadow fleet.

Ukrainian Antonov aircrafts are parked behind a fence on the grounds of Leipzig/Halle Airport, 6 August, 2026 AP Photo

Chancellor Friedrich Merz previously said Germany had increasingly "found itself in the crosshairs of hybrid attackers."

But Berlin had initially refrained from blaming Russia for the incident while speaking only of the possible involvement of "foreign powers."

Merz had warned on 25 August that the perpetrators of hybrid attacks against Germany would "pay for them," without naming a target.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz at a press conference in Berlin, 27 August, 2026 AP Photo

The Russian House of Science and Culture in Berlin, a seven-story building opened in 1984 in what was then East Berlin, is located near the Russian embassy.

Conservative lawmaker and security policy expert Roderich Kiesewetter recently told Welt TV that the facility is assumed to be a hub for espionage.

He said more than 100 people lived there "with no one knowing who they are" and the building's power consumption is disproportionately high.

It was "presumably filled with technical surveillance equipment", he said, and used by "people who are not well-disposed toward Germany."

Europe reacts

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said in a post on X that she had spoken with Merz about the Leipzig incident on Tuesday morning.

"I assured him that the EU stands in full solidarity with Germany in the face of this attack by Russia," she wrote, adding that she would also discuss the issue with NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte on Wednesday.

Speaking after a meeting of European Union defence ministers in Ireland earlier in the day, Kaja Kallas, the bloc's top diplomat, said Moscow was hitting Europe with increasing "kinetic hybrid attacks."

"With this, Russia wants to scare us away from supporting Ukraine. They will not succeed," she said.

"We will increase our support to Ukraine and invest in our own defence," she continued, adding that the EU was "planning the most far-reaching sanctions against Russia yet."

This is a developing story. Check back here for further details.

World.title: EU’s green fashion rules face test as global emissions rise 6.3%
World.content:
The global apparel and fashion industry is moving in the wrong direction on climate emissions, with greenhouse gas emissions rising 6.3% in 2024 compared to the previous year, despite a growing number of companies investing in renewable energy, cleaner materials and coal phase-outs, according to the Apparel Impact Institute’s latest assessment.

 

The increase in emissions was driven largely by higher fibre consumption, particularly polyester, putting the European Union's fashion industry further away from its goal of cutting emissions 45% by 2030 from 2019 levels.

Since roughly 80% to 90% of the EU's fashion footprint lies outside of Europe, according to the European Environment Agency, the EU’s sustainability laws are specifically designed to penalise "outsourced" pollution through a few key mechanisms.

Nonetheless, end-of-life products remain in the EU, with roughly 12.6 million tonnes of textile waste generated in the EU per year.

According to the World Integrated Trade Solution, China is the top textile exporter to the EU, with over €26.5 billion in apparel and accounting for roughly one-third of all textile and clothing products sold in Europe. Bangladesh ranks second, followed by Turkey, India, Pakistan, Vietnam and Morocco.

For the EU, which is tightening rules around fashion to make the industry more circular, new data from the Apparel Impact Institute suggests that clothing production will keep rising even if the bloc's laws succeed in cutting emissions.

"Decarbonising apparel requires action on both sides of the equation: reducing the carbon intensity of material production and manufacturing, while also addressing the growth in material volumes that can outpace those gains," reads the report.

In a bid to end the growth in textile waste, Brussels has introduced a package of measures aimed at changing how clothes are designed, sold and eventually discarded. The EU has also moved to make fashion companies financially responsible for the waste they generate.

But the apparel industry's rising emissions suggest that waste policy alone will not solve the climate problem. The industry's biggest source of emissions is linked to the processing of materials.

Polluting non-EU factories

According to the Apparel Impact Institute's report, textile processing accounts for about 51% of apparel emissions, followed by raw-material production at 26%.

That puts the spotlight on the factories producing fabrics and fibres, many of which are outside the EU.

The bloc can regulate what is sold on its single market, but most of the emissions associated with European consumers' clothes occur in global supply chains, resulting in a clash between EU industrial and climate policy.

With this backdrop, European policymakers are under pressure to decarbonise supply chains while simultaneously responding to concerns from industry about regulation, costs and competitiveness.

The same tension arises from the industry's perspective, according to the report. Manufacturers frequently lack the financing to invest in energy efficiency and renewable power, while clean electricity and alternatives to coal can remain unavailable or too expensive in key production countries. In many cases, sustainable materials can also cost more than conventional alternatives.

The report argues that brands need to share the financial and operational burden with suppliers through longer-term purchasing commitments, project financing and closer partnerships.

It also calls for climate targets to be converted into actual factory-level investment, particularly in energy- and heat-intensive textile processing.

"This includes improving access to appropriate finance, sharing project costs and risks, providing stable and longer-term purchasing commitments and aligning commercial relationships with decarbonisation objectives,” reads the report.

More sustainable fashion

Swedish major international fashion retailer H&M reduced the number of supplier factories using on-site coal boilers from 118 in 2022 to just 10 by the end of 2025, the report reveals.

Industrial electrification is also emerging as an alternative. Heat pumps are being deployed for processes such as laundry, dyeing and drying, while Lenzing, a company that produces wood-based cellulosic fibers, and power generation company VERBUND have commissioned a 14 MW power-to-heat facility in Austria that uses renewable electricity to provide industrial heat.

However, under business-as-usual assumptions, apparel emissions could reach 1.277 gigatonnes in 2030, compared with the 489 million tonnes the sector would need to reach to remain on a 1.5°C-compatible trajectory under the UN Paris Agreement.

Even if factories become more efficient and switch to cleaner energy, the report warns, it will not be enough if the industry keeps producing more carbon-intensive materials like fiber.

World.title: What the SDF’s dissolution means for Syria’s Kurds and neighbouring Turkey
World.content:
Nearly a week after the Syrian Democratic Forces agreed to dissolve, the consequences are beginning to take shape for Syria's Kurds and neighbouring Turkey. As the former US-backed force is absorbed into the Syrian state, questions remain over what the country's Kurds have secured in return – from language and political rights to protections for women – and what the end of more than a decade of Kurdish-led autonomy means for Turkey's own conflict with Kurdish militants.

Advertising

SDF leader Mazloum Abdi announced the force's dissolution last Tuesday, saying its fighters would be integrated into the Syrian army.

At its height, the predominantly Kurdish force numbered around 100,000 fighters and controlled nearly a fifth of Syrian territory in the northeast, including major oil fields and fertile land. Under SDF rule, Kurds gained cultural and political rights denied to them under previous governments in Damascus.

“It means the end of Kurdish autonomy. After more than one decade of freedom, now they are under the control of Damascus,” said Syria expert Fabrice Balanche of Lyon University, who frequently visited the region.

Kurdish rights

“There are no guarantees for the Kurdish language because it's just a presidential decree: ‘let the Kurds use their language and teach Kurdish in schools,’ but there is nothing in the constitution,” Balanche said.

The decree, issued by President Ahmed al-Sharaa in January, recognised Kurdish as a national language and allowed it to be taught in schools in areas with significant Kurdish populations.

It also restored citizenship to Kurds who had been left stateless under measures stemming from a controversial 1962 census and made Nowruz, the Kurdish New Year festival, an official national holiday.

The Education Ministry followed up on 27 August with rules providing for three Kurdish-language classes a week in public and private schools in areas with significant Kurdish populations, with marks counting towards pupils' final grades.

‘Words and promises not enough’ as Syria’s Kurds face uncertain future

Abdi was also appointed as an adviser to al-Sharaa on Friday, days after announcing the SDF's dissolution. It remains unclear whether the role will be more than ceremonial.

But questions remain over what the end of the Kurdish-led administration will mean for women. The SDF and affiliated institutions used a system in which governing bodies were jointly headed by a man and a woman.

“During these 10 years of autonomy, men and women were equal,” Balanche said. “In the region’s administration. It was always a co-presidency. In Raqqah, for example, the mayor was Leyla Mustafa, a woman, and the co-president was a man. Now that is no longer the case.”

Balanche also said the change could threaten restrictions on polygamy introduced under the Kurdish-led administration. Another unresolved question is what will happen to female SDF fighters as the force is absorbed into Syria's armed forces, which currently have no female troops.

Shifting alliances

For years, the SDF was Washington's main partner on the ground in Syria in the fight against the Islamic State group. But its position weakened as the United States built closer relations with Syria's new rulers.

A Syrian government offensive in January seized large areas held by the SDF and pushed the Kurdish-led force back into negotiations over integration with Damascus.

Washington, meanwhile, has increasingly embraced al-Sharaa's government, dismantling broad sanctions against Syria in 2025 and last week removing the country from its list of state sponsors of terrorism.

Turkey has emerged as one of al-Sharaa's main foreign allies and has long pressed for the SDF to disarm and integrate into the Syrian state.

Ankara considers the SDF a terrorist organisation linked to the Kurdistan Workers' Party (PKK), which launched an insurgency against the Turkish state in 1984. The SDF has rejected Turkey's claim that it is an extension of the PKK.

A year after Assad's fall, Syrian hopes for transitional justice are fading

The United States and European Union designate the PKK as a terrorist organisation, but not the SDF.

Turkey has carried out several cross-border military operations against the SDF in northern Syria since 2016 and still has thousands of troops stationed in the country. Ankara says those forces will remain until the security threats it faces have been eliminated.

The SDF's dissolution therefore achieves a longstanding Turkish objective in Syria. Turkey's ruling AK Party welcomed the move last week as an important step towards strengthening Syria's unity.

“Stability in Syria means Turkey perhaps being able to divert some of the resources it's been spending on counterterrorism into other areas of its defense that are absolutely necessary at a time like this, a time of regional turmoil,” said Turkey expert Asli Aydintasbas of the Washington-based Brookings Institution.

Turkey's Kurdish conflict

The SDF's dissolution could also remove an obstacle to the fragile peace process between Ankara and the PKK.

The process is intended to end the PKK's decades-long armed campaign against the Turkish state through the group's disarmament and dissolution.

Jailed PKK leader Abdullah Ocalan called on the group to disarm and disband in February 2025, and the PKK announced three months later that it would do so. A group of militants symbolically burned their weapons at a ceremony in northern Iraq in July 2025.

Turkey's parliament passed a law in August establishing a legal framework for the PKK's disbandment. Kurdish politicians have said broader democratic and legal reforms will also be needed for lasting peace.

Macron to become first Western European leader to visit post-Assad Syria

For Ankara, however, the process does not stop at Turkey's borders. It has repeatedly insisted that the SDF must also dissolve, because it regards the Syrian force as part of the same militant movement as the PKK.

The SDF has disputed that characterisation, with Abdi saying in 2025 that the PKK's decision to disarm did not apply to his forces in Syria.

The dismantling of groups Ankara regards as PKK affiliates across the region is essential to the process, said Middle East expert Serhan Afacan of Istanbul's Marmara University.

“The PKK should not exist anywhere in the region. This is what Ankara has been saying for more than a year,” Afacan said.

“If there is going to be any kind of peace process or reconciliation, the PKK is not supposed to exist anywhere in this region, in Turkey, in Iran, in Iraq, Syria.”
