World.title: Poland is terrible at promoting itself – but has never had better press
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. By Daniel Tilles Two incidents this month have highlighted how state-led efforts to promote Poland abroad often disappoint. Yet, at the same time, the country has never had better international press. Politicians should let Poland’s successes speak for themselves, and support those already telling its story. Poles care a lot about what the world thinks of their country. Major Polish media outlets regularly devote entire articles to what Western journalists, commentators and influencers are saying about Poland. “A German showed what he saw on the streets of Poland,” read one typical recent headline by Onet, Poland’s biggest news website, which devoted an entire report to one video by a German-speaking TikToker with around 7,000 followers. One rarely sees such reports in more self-confident Western countries. Given Poland’s history, such sensitivity regarding the country’s status is not surprising. Poland was, up until the 18th century, a major European country. But, for most of the last 250 years, it has been under foreign subjugation. Only since 1989 has it been able to develop independently, and Poles are understandably keen for the world to take note of their return to the top table. Poland has emerged as Europe’s undisputed growth champion over the past 35 years. In the first part of a new series of articles and podcasts, @AlicjaPtak4 explores the reasons behind Poland's rapid economic development, and the dangers that may lie ahead https://t.co/bW3bnV7Ozn — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 7, 2025 Polish politicians are also inevitably eager to capitalise on such sentiment by showing voters that they are making an effort to promote Poland abroad. The problem is that such efforts are often poorly conceived and executed – as two examples this month have shown. In mid-August, the sport and tourism ministry launched a new advertising campaign intended to attract visitors from western Europe and the United States. However, the first advert – featuring Polish football star Robert Lewandowski, supermodel Anja Rubik, Hollywood filmmaker Jesse Eisenberg, and actor Nikodem Rozbicki playing Fryderyk Chopin – was widely panned in Poland. Res Futura, an organisation that monitors social media sentiment, found that 85% of comments about the advert were negative. The campaign’s slogan – “Poland. More than you expected” – is negative and lacking confidence. The Polish Tourism Organisation says it is based on research showing that visitors to Poland are often positively surprised by how nice it is. Yet, while that is undoubtedly true, it does not mean it is a good idea to try to attract potential tourists by focusing on their low expectations. Poland has launched a new advertising campaign to attract tourists from Europe and the US. The first video, under the slogan "Poland. More than you expected", features footballer Robert Lewandowski, Hollywood star Jesse Eisenberg and supermodel Anja Rubik https://t.co/3jtqyUWQyy — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 19, 2026 The video also has no narrative, with the creators seeming to think that showing famous faces will be enough. Rubik does not speak a single word, while Eisenberg says only “Poland” and Lewandowski “More than you expected”. The film itself does nothing to show that Poland is more than anyone expects. In fact, its depressingly colourless palette and focus on Warsaw’s Stalinist Palace of Science and Culture actually reinforce (false) stereotypes of Poland as grey, dull and post-communist. The country has so many interesting and colourful places that could have been showcased instead. The advert is also a wasted opportunity to tell a story about the film’s stars, especially Eisenberg, who has reconnected with his family’s Polish roots, produced a critically acclaimed movie set in Poland, and last year obtained citizenship. Instead, Chopin dominates the film, but his dialogue is incoherent. When he says, “Warsaw is where my heart is”, almost no potential visitors would understand that this is a reference to the real Chopin’s heart being transported from Paris, where he died, to Warsaw, where it is now entombed in a church. Not long after that advert launched, another controversy emerged around a state official, Barbara Mróz-Gorgoń, who had been appointed only weeks earlier by the government to lead the promotion of Poland. It quickly transpired that a report she had authored last year on creating a national brand – and which appeared to have played a big part in her getting the new job – contained significant errors, questionable methodology, and bizarre language. Many parts showed signs of being AI-generated. Mróz-Gorgoń, who has now resigned, insists that the report was the genuine product of work by her and her team at Marka Polska (Brand Poland), a think tank she leads. However, that is not particularly reassuring given the report’s content. Many parts are simply obvious: at the end of the 26-page text, the three recommendations for the government are to “develop a coherent, long-term national branding strategy”, “invest in promotional campaigns in key markets”, and “coordinate between ministries and other entities”. Other sections are very strange, such as noting that “Germany does not build its brand on the Holocaust”. But perhaps the most telling aspect is that, although the introduction claims it is “a comprehensive report on building…a coherent, long-term branding strategy in the international arena”, the document focuses entirely on how Poles themselves view their own country (its title is even A Self-Portrait of the Poles). It includes no research into what foreigners know or think about Poland and what could interest or attract them. While any national branding exercise should of course take account of the views of the native population, it is clearly incomplete without research into the target of such a campaign, the outside world. Yet that is sadly typical of many state-led efforts to promote Poland, which focus more on pleasing a domestic audience – the voters that politicians want to keep happy – than on being truly outward looking. A government official appointed last month to promote Poland's brand abroad has been hit by a wave of criticism after it emerged that she authored a report containing major errors, bizarre language, and signs of being generated by AI https://t.co/9fpfzFCFuI — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 21, 2026 It should be noted that such failings are nothing new. Successive governments have been responsible for botched efforts to promote Poland. The uninspiring slogan “Poland. More than you expected” has been used since 2021. A previous one, “Polska. Spring Into”, launched in 2014, was simply bizarre and quickly disappeared. In 2016, the former Law and Justice (PiS) government established the Polish National Foundation (PFN), which was pumped full of money from state-owned companies and tasked with promoting Poland abroad. Instead, it focused much of its efforts on domestic activity, often intended to support PiS’s political agenda. The work it did do internationally was often of questionable efficacy, such as spending millions on buying a yacht, naming it “I Love Poland”, then attempting to sail it around the world (before it ended up breaking down and getting stuck in port). A senior official under the former PiS government has been charged over alleged misspending of funds. The case relates to a campaign in 2017 that used money meant for promoting Poland abroad to instead advertise PiS's judicial reforms domestically https://t.co/tH64Bekhec — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 15, 2026 Yet, despite woeful state-led efforts to promote Poland abroad, the country has in recent times been enjoying a soaring international reputation. Western media have been full of articles about the country’s economic success; about how not only are Polish emigrants returning from the UK, but many Brits are moving to Poland too; about how Poles are becoming major buyers of property in Spain; about how companies with roots in Poland, such as InPost and ElevenLabs, are pioneering their industries. Social media feeds are full of influencers extolling Polish cities, with their safe, clean streets; the beauty of Polish nature, with its mountains, lakes and beaches; and the sense of dynamic development that you can feel as soon as you set foot in the country. Last weekend,@thetimes reported on how Brits are moving to Poland. This weekend, on how Poles are replacing Brits as property owners in Spain. pic.twitter.com/IDDdDlluTE — Daniel Tilles (@danieltilles1) June 21, 2026 This positive publicity is largely organic – it is the product of Poland’s own actual successes, not of artificial efforts to create an image of success. It is generated from the bottom up, not from the top down. While the state can play a role – for example, by arranging visits for foreign journalists and influencers and supporting media and institutions that are already telling Poland’s story – it would be better for politicians to focus on creating the conditions for those successes, rather than concocting cockeyed schemes to promote them. World.title: Polish government sets out draft 2027 budget with deficit remaining at 7.1% of GDP
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland’s government has approved a draft budget for 2027 that keeps defence, healthcare and the energy transition among its spending priorities, while projecting another year of heavy borrowing. The deficit is forecast at 7.1% of GDP, unchanged from 2026 but well above the level of 3.7% the government had committed to reach by 2027 after Poland was placed under the European Union’s excessive deficit procedure in 2024. Rada Ministrów przyjęła projekt ustawy budżetowej na 2027 rok. Projekt odpowiedzialnie łączy finansowanie bieżących potrzeb państwa i przedsięwzięć wzmacniających jego bezpieczeństwo oraz potencjał rozwojowy.#BudżetPolaków 🔗 https://t.co/SjWyBUwi8U pic.twitter.com/X9ue6cw5ns — Ministerstwo Finansów (@MF_GOV_PL) August 28, 2026 The budget – which must still be consulted with business and trade union representatives before being approved by parliament and then signed by opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki – sets total expenditure at 977.6 billion zloty (€225.4 billion), 58 billion zloty more than this year. Revenues are projected to rise by 68.4 billion zloty to 695 billion zloty, leaving a nominal budget deficit of 282.6 billion zloty, the highest on record and 10 billion zloty more than this year. Defence spending will remain high, at 198.1 billion zloty, equivalent to 4.5% of GDP, one of the highest levels in NATO. The healthcare budget will reach 274.1 billion zloty, up 26.3 billion zloty from 2026. Spending on energy security and transformation will rise 8.3% year-on-year to reach 19.7 billion zloty. The government expects GDP growth to remain strong, at 3% in 2027, while average inflation is forecast at 2.8%, within the central bank’s target of 2.5%, plus or minus one percentage point. Average wages are expected to rise by 5.9% next year in nominal terms, slightly slower than the 6.4% forecast for this year. The government expects that unemployment, measured according to the national methodology, will stand at 6% at the end of 2027, broadly unchanged from its current level. Poland’s gross borrowing needs are projected at 565 billion zloty in 2027, below the 688 billion zloty budgeted for this year. Debt-servicing costs, however, are expected to rise to 107 billion zloty, up 17 billion zloty from this year. Finance minister Andrzej Domański said that the rise in debt-servicing costs is driven by an increase in the overall volume of debt and the need to refinance bonds issued in 2020 and 2021 at very low interest rates. Poland's debt has been growing at the second-fastest rate in the EU this year, and is set to continue rising. What is behind this trend – and should we be worried – asks Alicja Ptak in the latest of her series of articles and podcasts on Poland’s economy https://t.co/1pvnb2ZxoY — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 30, 2025 The projected deficit leaves Poland under continued pressure to bring its public finances into line with EU fiscal rules. In 2024, the country was placed under the EU’s excessive deficit procedure after its deficit exceeded the bloc’s limit of 3%. Warsaw pledged at the time to bring the deficit below 3% by 2028. However, last year the deficit actually rose, from 6.4% of GDP in 2024 to 7.3% in 2025, which was the second-highest level among all EU member states. This year, Poland’s public debt passed the EU’s limit of 60% of GDP for the first time on record. “The 2027 budget represents a continuation of expansionary fiscal policy, and Poland is making no progress in correcting its excessive deficit and is taking no action to bring it below 3% of GDP,” wrote analysts at ING Bank Śląski today. “The result is a further increase in public debt.” Poland’s public debt has passed 60% of GDP for the first time, thereby exceeding the limit enshrined in EU law. The country is already under the EU's excessive deficit procedure, requiring it to take steps to bring public finances under greater control https://t.co/LNJ0YrP2Ge — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 12, 2026 Efforts to reduce the deficit have also been complicated by political stalemate between the government and opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki, who has vetoed several fiscal measures, including tax increases. Nawrocki did, however, approve a new levy on banks that came into force this year. The situation has led two of the big three rating agencies, Fitch and Moody’s, to shift Poland’s credit outlook to negative. This year, Fitch warned that the political gridlock between Nawrocki and the government was making tackling the deficit and debt more difficult. However, speaking today, Prime Minister Donald Tusk said that the 2027 budget reflects Poland’s position at a time when war is being waged across its eastern border and other conflicts are weighing on the country’s finances. Meanwhile, 2027 will also see pivotal parliamentary elections, at which Tusk’s ruling coalition, which ranges from left to centre right, will seek a second term while the right-wing opposition, supported by Nawrocki, will attempt to win power. Ratings agency Fitch has again warned that the "political gridlock" between Poland's government president – such as the current clash over EU defence loans – is hindering efforts to tackle "large fiscal deficits and rapidly rising debt" https://t.co/JSqwwayTdm — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 18, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Polish “vampire” burial sheds light on 17th-century efforts to keep the dead in their graves
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Researchers investigating an unusual 17th-century burial in northern Poland, in which the remains of a teenage girl were found with a padlock fastened to her toe and a sickle placed across her neck, believe the measures may have been intended to stop her returning from the dead. The burial, discovered in 2022 at an unmarked cemetery in the village of Pień, is an example of what archaeologists describe as “anti-vampiric” or “anti-demonic” burial, in which precautions were taken to protect the living from a deceased person believed to pose a danger. In a newly published academic paper, a team of researchers led by Dariusz Poliński, an archaeologist at Nicolaus Copernicus University in Toruń, say that the girl, whom they have named “Zosia”, may have been blamed by her contemporaries for misfortunes such as disease and famine. The unusual combination of objects that Zosia was buried with – a triangular padlock attached to her left big toe and an iron sickle laid across her throat, with the blade facing towards her neck – immediately attracted archaeologists’ attention when they were discovered. Poliński and his colleagues have used radiocarbon dating, DNA sequencing, isotope analysis and X-ray and microscopic imaging to investigate the burial. Their findings have now been published in the Journal of Archaeological Science: Reports. The researchers have established that Zosia, who was aged between 17 and 19, died around the mid-17th century, most likely between 1620 and 1674. Her grave appears to have been secured in two stages, with analysis of soil layers showing that it was reopened after the initial burial and the sickle added later. “It was unusual that there were two precautions, two methods of showing that this skeleton should be kept in the grave – so the fear of the body coming back to life was greater,” Poliński told CNN. The researchers say the padlock had several possible meanings in funerary symbolism. It could mark the end of earthly life and the transition to the world of the dead, prevent contact between the living and the dead, break a run of bad luck, or protect the community from the deceased returning. “In some interpretations, it was also believed to help halt the spread of epidemics,” Poliński told the Polish Press Agency (PAP). The sickle had a more direct purpose: if the deceased tried to rise from the grave, it was positioned to sever the head or slit the throat, preventing her from returning to the world of the living. However, the latest findings suggest there may have been a third protective element. Researchers found “a distinct green discolouration” in the oral cavity, suggesting that an object containing a high proportion of copper had been placed in the girl’s mouth. Given the extent of the discolouration, they have largely ruled out the possibility that it was simply a coin. “The protective measures taken at the time of the original burial and subsequently after the grave was opened clearly demonstrate the immense fear of Zosia,” said Poliński, quoted by news website Wirtualna Polska. The grave of a "vampire child" – who was turned face down and secured with a padlock to ensure he could not rise from the grave – has been discovered in Poland Researchers believe the site was a cemetery for those excluded or feared by the local community https://t.co/Ez2QgvMnuX — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 11, 2023 Poliński believes that the woman may have been ill or had a physical or mental disability, leading her neighbours to treat her badly while she was alive and fear that she would haunt them after her death. However, the researchers found no skeletal evidence of trauma, violence or disease that might explain her treatment, and her cause of death remains unknown. The Pień cemetery, which has not been marked on maps, contains several other unusual burials, including a child buried face down with a padlock beneath the foot and skeletons weighed down with rocks. This has led researchers to suggest that the cemetery may have been located on unconsecrated ground, away from a church or chapel, and used for people who were poor, disgraced, feared, or otherwise excluded from the community. Zosia’s burial, however, appears to have been unusual in another respect. Analysis suggests she was of relatively high social status. Traces of silk and gold-and-silver thread near her skull suggest she wore an expensive cap, a luxury item generally associated with nobility or wealth. Two years ago, sculptor and artist Oscar D. Nilsson unveiled a 3D facial reconstruction of Zosia, based on measurements of her skull and skeletal clues about her age, weight and health. The reconstruction shows a young woman with blue eyes, light brown hair and a broad nose. “It’s really ironic, in a way,” Nilsson told Reuters at the time. “These people burying her, they did everything they could in order to prevent her from coming back from the dead…We have done everything we can in order to bring her back to life.” A team of scientists has reconstructed the face of a 400-year-old woman, once believed by her neighbors to be a vampire, revealing the human story buried by supernatural beliefs https://t.co/Q6sipo7h4O pic.twitter.com/0gLVIEfaZi — Reuters (@Reuters) October 30, 2024 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Dozens of Hot Air Balloons to Fill Czech Skies During September Festival
World.content:
Dozens of hot air balloons are expected to take to the skies over eastern Bohemia this week as the Balonové Nebe festival returns to Hradec Králové, Jaroměř and nearby areas.

The five-day event will run from Wednesday, September 2, through Sunday, September 6, with a program combining competitive balloon flights, mass launches and evening shows. All public events are free to attend.

Weather will play a major role in the festival schedule. Balloon flights can only take place under suitable conditions, meaning launch sites and departure times may change at short notice.



Organizers say the exact location of each flight will depend mainly on wind direction and other weather conditions. Planned flights may also be postponed or cancelled if conditions are unsuitable.

The festival has established itself as one of the country’s major hot air balloon gatherings. Last year’s event set a Czech record when 81 balloons flew into the sky at the same time.

The 2026 edition will once again feature morning competitions, during which pilots will complete a series of tasks while large groups of balloons rise over the region.

Evening programs will offer a different spectacle, with balloon shows planned for spectators. The precise locations of these events will be announced according to the weather forecast and flying conditions.

Visitors planning to attend are advised to check the festival’s official website before setting out. The organizers will publish the latest information about launch locations, times and any changes to the schedule there.

World.title: VIDEO: Golden STARLUX Lands in Prague for the First Time
World.content:
A golden Airbus A350-1000 operated by Taiwan’s STARLUX Airlines landed at Václav Havel Airport Prague for the first time on Tuesday, September 1.

The aircraft, registered as B-58554, carries the special AIRSORAYAMA Gold livery created in collaboration with Japanese artist Hajime Sorayama.

Prague is one of only three destinations where STARLUX plans to operate the specially designed aircraft on a regular basis, alongside Tokyo and Phoenix.



The arrival marks another step in the expansion of STARLUX’s new direct connection between Prague and Taipei.

The airline launched the route on August 1, initially using the smaller Airbus A350-900. From September, the carrier has switched to the larger A350-1000, which can carry up to 350 passengers in four travel classes.

STARLUX, Airbus and paint manufacturer Mankiewicz developed a multilayer coating using mica particles to create the metallic effect while meeting aviation safety requirements.

Increasing capacity on Prague route

STARLUX launched Prague as its first European destination on August 1, connecting the Czech capital directly with Taipei three times a week. The service currently operates on Tuesdays, Thursdays and Saturdays.

Flight JX101 leaves Taipei at 12:10 a.m. and arrives in Prague at 8:35 a.m. The return flight, JX102, departs Prague at 10:35 a.m. and arrives in Taipei at 7:55 a.m. the following day.

The switch to the A350-1000 increases the available capacity on the route. The aircraft has four travel classes, including First Class, Business Class, Premium Economy and Economy.

An additional Monday flight is scheduled to operate from October through November, bringing the route to four flights per week during that period.

World.title: September 19: Celebrate South Africa’s Heritage Braai Day in Prague
World.content:
On Saturday, 19 September, Prague’s Rohan Beer Garden will host Heritage Braai Day, bringing the flavors and traditions of South Africa to the city.

The event is organized by Saffa Maso.



From noon, visitors can enjoy a relaxed day of grilling, music and socializing outdoors.

Heritage Day in South Africa is a public holiday celebrating the country’s cultural diversity. It has also become closely associated with the tradition of braai, or South African-style barbecuing, with friends and family gathering around the grill to share food.

In Prague, the event is open to everyone and will feature multiple grills, allowing visitors to prepare their own food. Those who prefer to leave the cooking to someone else can use the on-site grill master service, available for an additional fee.

Standard tickets include grills, coals and all braai equipment. Visitors can also choose a braai package, which includes 500g of traditional boerewors sausage and 150g of biltong.

On-site, guests will also be able to purchase Nando’s sauces, chutney, braai spices and other South African products.

Visitors should not bring their own drinks, as a selection of alcoholic and non-alcoholic beverages will be available at the venue. Guests should bring their own plates and cutlery, although disposable options are also allowed.

Tickets are available via SMSTicket at this link. Children under 12 enter free.

World.title: Prague Philharmonic Could Begin Construction in 2028. New Visuals Reveal Design
World.content:
Prague has taken another step toward building the long-planned Vltava Philharmonic.

The Prague Development Company (PDS) submitting an application for planning permission and new visualizations revealing the project in greater detail.

The application covers not only the Philharmonic building but also the surrounding public spaces, transport infrastructure and connections to the existing metro, tram, road, cycling and pedestrian networks.



If the permitting process stays on schedule, the city expects to receive the necessary approval in the first quarter of 2027. A tender for the construction company would then follow, with building work potentially starting in the first quarter of 2028.

The project is planned for the Bubny-Zátory district, near the existing Vltavská metro station. The new cultural complex is expected to be completed in 2033, when trial operations could begin.

The building was designed by Danish architecture studio BIG – Bjarke Ingels Group, which won an international competition in May 2022. Preparation of the detailed permit documentation began in 2025.

The complex will have three underground levels and six floors above ground. It will contain five music halls, creative spaces, restaurants and other facilities.

The project is also intended to provide new premises for the Prague Symphony Orchestra FOK and music collections belonging to the Municipal Library of Prague. The Czech Philharmonic is also expected to gain additional facilities, addressing the limitations of its current premises.

Construction could start in early 2028

The current estimated cost of the Philharmonic building is around CZK 12.33 billion, including equipment but excluding VAT. The surrounding infrastructure and public spaces are expected to cost an additional CZK 5 billion, also excluding VAT.

World.title: Tiny Steps, Big Milestones: What Really Matters When Toddlers Start Preschool
World.content:
For a one-year-old, starting preschool is not about learning letters or sitting through lessons.

It is about feeling safe without Mum or Dad nearby, discovering the joy of playing alongside other children, and slowly gaining the confidence to explore the world independently. At Tiny Tots in Prague, these small everyday moments are at the heart of the programme.

A favourite toy clutched tightly in one hand. A cautious look back at Mum or Dad from the classroom door. Perhaps a few tears (from either side).

For families with children aged one or two, the first experience of leaving a little one in someone else’s care can feel like a very big step.

And for the child, it is one too.



At this age, development happens through moments that can look almost insignificant to adults: reaching for a spoon without help, joining another child in play, recognising a familiar song, saying a new word, or feeling comfortable enough to wander a little further away from a trusted adult.

These are precisely the moments that Tiny Tots, a programme for children aged 1–2 at Nessie English Preschool, part of Park Lane International School, is designed to encourage.

Before learning comes feeling safe

For very young children, a good first preschool experience begins with something much more fundamental than an academic curriculum: trust.

“Parents often want to know how their child will cope with separation, whether we can follow the rhythm they are used to at home and, above all, whether their child will really be seen as an individual,” says Catalina Gonzalez-Got, who leads the Tiny Tots programme.

Catalina knows the feeling from both sides. An early-years educator with international experience, she is also a mother herself. Becoming a parent, she says, gave her a much deeper understanding of how emotional it can be to entrust a young child to somebody else for the first time.

That is why settling in is treated as a process rather than a test that a toddler is expected to pass on day one.

Some children may quickly become curious about their new surroundings. Others need more time, reassurance and proximity to a familiar adult before they are ready to explore.

Both are perfectly normal. The goal is to allow each child to find that confidence at their own pace.

For toddlers, play is serious business

Adults sometimes separate “playing” and “learning”. Toddlers do not.

When a child squishes playdough between their fingers, listens to a story, sings along to a familiar song, explores the garden or watches another toddler build something, they are constantly learning.

They are practising movement and coordination. They are discovering cause and effect. They are learning how to communicate, negotiate space with other children, manage emotions and make choices.

Tiny Tots therefore follows a play-based approach inspired by the English Early Years Foundation Stage framework, with activities designed around the developmental needs of one- and two-year-olds.

There are no miniature school desks or pressure to perform.

Instead, children encounter language, movement, music, creative activities, sensory experiences, stories and outdoor play as a natural part of their day.

The programme keeps the class to a maximum of eight children, allowing teachers to pay close attention to individual personalities, routines and developmental stages.

English without the flashcards

The same philosophy applies to language.

At one or two years old, learning English does not mean memorising vocabulary lists. Children absorb language through relationships and repetition: hearing the same words during snack time, listening to songs, following simple instructions, sharing a picture book or hearing an adult describe what is happening during play.

Tiny Tots provides an English-language environment, giving children regular, natural exposure to the language throughout their day.

Catalina, who raises her own child in a multilingual family, sees communication as something that should grow out of connection rather than performance.

Toddlers often understand far more than they can say, she explains. What matters is creating a positive environment in which language is associated with people, experiences and emotions that make sense to the child.

Learning to do things “all by myself”

Anyone who lives with a toddler knows how powerful those words can be.

Between one and two, children increasingly want to try things independently — even when the result is a spoon on the floor, mismatched shoes or a task that takes considerably longer than if an adult simply did it for them.

Tiny Tots gives children safe opportunities to practise that emerging independence while knowing that an adult is close by when they need help.

The milestone may be eating more independently, choosing an activity, joining a group song, approaching another child or simply becoming comfortable enough to explore a new corner of the room.

For a toddler, these are significant achievements.

And independence does not mean pushing children away from adults. In fact, the opposite is often true: children are more willing to explore when they know they have a trusted person to return to.

A small community for Prague’s smallest residents

For international families in particular, early-years programmes can provide something else that is easy to overlook: a sense of community.

Many parents raising children in Prague live far from grandparents, siblings and the wider family network that might otherwise form part of everyday life.

A nurturing preschool environment can therefore become more than somewhere a child spends part of the day. Familiar teachers, other children and their families can gradually become part of the support network that makes a new city feel more like home.

Tiny Tots is based at Nessie English Preschool in Prague 5, in a quiet residential setting with its own garden. The programme combines experienced early-years teachers, personalised attention and structured routines with plenty of room for children simply to play, discover and be little.

Because at one or two years old, success does not need to look impressive.

Sometimes it is a child who cried at the door last week walking in happily today.

Sometimes it is making a first little friend.

Sometimes it is a new word, a messy painting, a favourite song or the confidence to let go of a teacher’s hand and go exploring alone.

Those tiny steps are exactly where the big journey begins.

Tiny Tots at Nessie English Preschool is designed for children aged 1–2 years. Families interested in the programme can arrange a visit to the Prague 5 campus to see the environment and meet the team.

Enrolment for the 2026/27 school year is now open.

World.title: Wine Harvest Festivals in Prague in September: The Full Guide
World.content:
Every September, Prague celebrates vinobraní, the traditional wine harvest festival marking the end of the grape season.

Visitors can look forward to concerts, dance and theatre performances, food stalls, and tastings of young wine and the seasonal favorite burčák (partially fermented grape juice). The festivals are family-friendly, offering children’s theatre, horse rides, folk craft demonstrations, competitions, and workshops.



Here is an overview of the main wine festivals in Prague in 2026:

Vinohrady Wine Harvest Festival

September 11–12, 2026, 10:00–21:00

náměstí Jiřího z Poděbrad

Facebook

Winemakers from across Europe — Austria, Slovakia, Hungary, Italy, Slovenia, Croatia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Romania, Serbia, Ukraine, and Poland — will join Czech and Moravian producers.

Alongside wine, expect a wide range of food: sausages, cheeses, potato spirals, langoše (fried dough with toppings), and traditional Wallachian cakes (frgály). The festival also offers live music and a children’s zone with a playground, carousel, and creative workshops. Admission is free.

Wine Harvest at Prague Castle

September 5–6, 2026, 11:00–18:00

Royal Garden & Ball Game Hall, Prague Castle, Hradčany

hrad.cz

Set in the historic Royal Garden of Prague Castle, this festival features tastings of Czech and Moravian wines, sparkling wines, fresh grape juice, burčák, and high-quality local produce. The program includes folk ensembles, historical fencing, and family activities.

Entry to the garden is free; a tasting glass costs 120 CZK.

Grébovka Wine Festival

September 18, 2026 (14:00–20:00) at náměstí Míru

September 19, 2026 (13:00–20:00) at Havlíčkovy sady (Grébovka Park)

Facebook

Organized by Prague 2, the Grébovka Festival is one of the city’s largest and most popular wine events. Set in Havlíčkovy sady (often described as a hidden gem of Vinohrady), the festival offers wine tastings, culinary specialties, live music, dance performances, and a cultural program celebrating wine traditions. Families can enjoy workshops, theatre, competitions, and children’s activities.

St. Clare’s Vineyard Harvest Festival

September 12–13, 2026

Prague Botanical Garden, Fata Morgana greenhouse, Troja

botanicka.cz

Hosted at the St. Clare’s Vineyard in the Prague Botanical Garden, this festival is renowned for its carefully made burčák, produced from handpicked grapes. Guests can sample varietal wines, cuvées, and brandies from this rare Prague vineyard, along with wines from leading Czech and Moravian producers. Guided cellar tours, food stalls, live music, and terrace dancing complete the program.

Troja Wine Harvest Festival

September 13, 2026, 11:00–20:00

Gardens of Troja Chateau, Prague 7

Facebook

Held in the baroque Troja Chateau, this festival combines wine tastings from Czech, Moravian, and international producers with burčák, traditional food, and live music. Children’s activities include games, workshops, and a kids’ zone. Admission is free.

St. Wenceslas Wine Festival

September 28, 2026, 12:00–18:00

Villa Richter & St. Wenceslas Vineyard, Prague Castle

Facebook

Taking place in the historic St. Wenceslas Vineyard, the oldest in Bohemia, this festival is steeped in legend — St. Wenceslas is said to have planted and harvested vines here for sacramental wine. Visitors can enjoy wines from leading Czech and Moravian wineries, sample burčák, and take in panoramic views of Prague’s Old Town.

17th Malá Strana Wine Festival

September 19, 2026, 13:00–22:00

Kampa Park, Malá Strana

Set along the Vltava River in Kampa Park, this festival celebrates the traditions of the Horňácko region in South Moravia. Expect cimbalom music, folk dancing, local wines, burčák, homemade sausages, and slivovice (plum brandy). Craft stalls and lively performances bring a taste of Moravian countryside to the heart of Prague. Free entry.

Vinobraní na Náplavce

Tents selling wine and burčák from Czech producers will be located on the Rašínovo nábřeží embankment (between the railway bridge and the Vyšehrad rock). The festival will also offer snacks that pair perfectly with wine. Organizers have prepared live music and several different wine competitions for guests, including a corkscrew competition, blind tasting, flavor identification, and more.

September 25 and 26, 2026, from 1:00 PM to 9:30 PM;

Price: 100 CZK (includes a glass tasting glass)

World.title: Czechia Spent CZK 19 Billion on COVID Vaccines and Used Less Than Half
World.content:
The Czech Republic has spent roughly CZK 19 billion on COVID-19 vaccines since 2020, but fewer than half of the 41 million doses supplied under its pandemic-era procurement agreement were ultimately used in the country.

More than 18 million doses expired and had to be destroyed, representing a value of about CZK 8 billion.

A further four million doses were donated to other countries, according to information provided by the Czech Ministry of Health in response to a request from the Czech Technical Committee.



For the 2026-27 vaccination season, around 900,000 doses will be available in the country. By comparison, fewer than one-third of that number was administered during the previous season. The vaccination season runs from September through the end of August the following year.

Demand for COVID-19 vaccination has fallen sharply since the initial rollout. More than 15 million doses were administered during the first year vaccines were widely available. A year later, demand had fallen to roughly one-fifth of that level. Between 2022 and 2023, interest dropped by more than 80 percent, followed by further declines of about one-third in subsequent years.

Only about 1,500 doses had been administered by July 26 this year. Most vaccinations, however, take place during the autumn months.

The low demand has contributed to substantial vaccine waste. When the original purchases were made, authorities faced considerable uncertainty over how the pandemic would develop, how many booster doses would be required and how many people would seek vaccination.

Maintaining sufficient supplies was considered necessary in case the epidemiological situation deteriorated.

The Czech Republic is now considering a different approach to future procurement. The Ministry of Health is negotiating with vaccine manufacturers, health insurance companies and medical organisations over supplies and financing for the 2027-28 season. The talks are taking into account both the expected demand and the cost-effectiveness of vaccination.

World.title: Foreign Pupils on the Rise in Czech Schools — Nearly One in Five in Prague
World.content:
Of the nearly one million pupils attending Czech primary schools last academic year, almost 8% were foreign nationals, most commonly from Ukraine.

According to the Czech Statistical Office (CSO), Prague recorded the highest proportion, with foreign pupils making up 18% of all children in its primary schools.

Compulsory education is mandatory for Czech citizens as well as citizens of other European Union member states who reside in the Czech Republic for more than 90 days. The requirement also applies to foreign nationals with long-term residence permits.

Their children therefore have the same rights as Czech children, including access to free education, school meals and extracurricular activities.



The number of foreign pupils increased significantly after Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022, nearly doubling that year. Their numbers have continued to rise ever since. Today, children from Ukraine account for 5% of all pupils in the Czech Republic.

The trend is similar in secondary schools, where the proportion of foreign pupils reached its highest level in the past 10 years, at almost 5% of the total.

Although the number of children in primary schools has remained relatively stable at just over one million in recent years, a sharp decline is expected in the coming years due to the falling birth rate, according to Vendula Kašparová of the CSO’s Social Development Statistics Department. The office said the birth rate has been falling continuously for the fifth consecutive year.

The decline is already visible at the kindergarten level. The number of children enrolled in kindergartens fell below 350,000 in the 2025/2026 academic year, the first time this has happened since 2013. Over the past three years, enrolment has dropped by more than 21,000 children, or around 5.8%.

Fewer Children Receiving Deferrals From Starting School

Kašparová identifies another clear trend: fewer children are being granted deferrals from starting compulsory school. Since the 2021/2022 academic year, the proportion of six-year-olds whose school entry was deferred has fallen from 24.1% in September 2021 to 17.7% in September 2025, representing just under 21,000 pupils.

Furthermore, an amendment to the Education Act is expected to reduce the number of deferrals even further. Under the new rules, deferrals will only be granted when justified by a medical condition that prevents a child from attending school.

This could include a serious medical condition following surgery, cancer treatment or a moderate intellectual disability.

World.title: Cash refund for recycling bottles could soon disappear in Budapest
World.content:
Hungary’s bottle-recycling system could be facing a major change, with cash payments for returned bottles and cans potentially abolished at REpont collection points.

Cash could soon disappear from Hungary’s bottle recycling scheme

MOHU, the company responsible for Hungary’s deposit-return system (DRS), is proposing that the government remove the option of receiving the 50-forint deposit in cash. Instead, consumers would be able to use a voucher for shopping or have the money transferred to their bank account through the REpont app. Donations to charity would also remain available.

The proposal comes amid growing concerns in Budapest about people collecting returnable bottles from bins and the associated problems of litter, damaged rubbish bins and public safety. Also, several claims have arised that many of those spend the money from collecting and recycling these bottles on drugs.

MOHU proposes ending cash payments

Csaba Bozóki, MOHU’s director responsible for the deposit-return system, announced the proposal in a Facebook video, arguing that cash is not necessary for the system. Under the current rules, a voucher issued by a reverse vending machine can be redeemed for cash at the relevant shop. Changing this would require an amendment to the government regulation governing the scheme.

According to reports, MOHU has already discussed the proposal with representatives of Budapest and its districts. A joint proposal from MOHU, the capital and district municipalities could eventually be submitted to the government.

Bottle collecting and recycling has become a problem in Budapest

Since the HUF 50 deposit was introduced in 2024, the system has dramatically increased the collection and recycling of drinks packaging. However, it has also created a new phenomenon in Budapest, where people search through rubbish bins for returnable bottles and cans. Several district mayors say this has contributed to litter being left around bins, containers being damaged or overturned, and additional pressure on local cleaning services.

Terézváros (District VI of Budapest) Mayor Tamás Soproni previously called for the recycling system to be temporarily suspended until the problems could be addressed. The government rejected that idea, while MOHU has stressed that the deposit-return system is required by EU rules and cannot simply be abolished, as HVG.hu reported.

Stay up-to-date with our Hungary Weekly Briefing: subscribe on Substack!

MOHU: The system did not create the underlying problems

Bozóki has argued that homelessness, drug addiction and deep poverty in central Budapest are not new problems caused by bottle returns.

“These are very important social problems that we need to talk about,” he said, while stressing that a solution should involve local authorities, social organisations and the authorities. Supporters of removing cash payments nevertheless believe the measure could reduce the incentive to collect bottles from bins for immediate cash.

In case you missed it: Another Budapest city centre district may ban Airbnb – referendum on the horizon

Who could be affected?

Critics warn that eliminating cash would make the system less accessible for some people. Those without a bank account or smartphone, or those who simply want their HUF 50 deposit returned in cash, could face additional difficulties. The proposal would therefore change how people receive their own deposits without addressing the wider issues of homelessness, poverty or drug use.

The government now faces a choice over whether to amend the rules. If the proposal goes ahead, cash could soon disappear from Hungary’s REpont system, leaving shoppers with vouchers, bank transfers or charitable donations as the main alternatives.

World.title: The Tisza’s message reaches Tiszalök: What the PET Cup found beneath the trees – PHOTOS
World.content:
When the PET Cup fleet reached Tiszalök on 22 August, the boats had already spent eight days travelling along the Bodrog and Tisza. The finish line marked the end of a demanding competition, but the final stretch revealed a more troubling reality: tonnes of waste remain hidden in floodplains even when no recent flood has carried it there. The expedition therefore raised a question that reaches beyond the event itself. How much of the pollution comes from upstream, and how much is created or abandoned locally? I spoke with Viktória Doró from the PET Kupa press office for this article.

Author: Zoltán Rokonál

A record with an uncomfortable meaning

The VII Bodrog–XIV Tisza PET Cup took participants from Olaszliszka to Tiszalök between 15 and 23 August. Twelve teams worked along the riverbanks and floodplains, collecting and sorting 18.9 tonnes of waste. That result exceeded the previous record of 17.5 tonnes, set on the same route in 2024 with 15 teams. Eleven of the participating teams had already taken part in earlier editions, giving them valuable experience in locating waste deposits that are difficult to see from the water.

Such a result is not easy to interpret. A larger amount of collected rubbish does not automatically prove that the river has become more polluted. It may also indicate that volunteers have become more efficient at finding material that has accumulated over a long period.

This distinction was especially relevant in 2026. Neither the Bodrog nor the Tisza experienced a major flood wave capable of transporting large quantities of new waste into the area. Much of what the teams discovered was already lying in the floodplain. Organisers said some deposits may have remained there for years or even decades.

The finding adds another layer to the familiar story of Tisza pollution. Waste arriving from the upper reaches of the river, including from the direction of Ukraine, remains a serious regional issue. Earlier clean-up campaigns have also shown the scale of the challenge. In a previous Daily News Hungary report, volunteers removed more than six tonnes of waste from the River Tisza.

At the same time, the latest route showed that not every discarded object can be blamed on the current. Some rubbish had never needed the river to carry it.

What was found near Tiszalök

The final section between Tiszaladány and Tiszalök covered approximately nine river kilometres. During that part of the journey, the teams collected 2,120 kilograms of waste, including 522 bags, eight tyres and numerous larger objects.

Behind those figures lies a considerable amount of manual labour. Volunteers had to enter dense vegetation, search difficult sections of the floodplain, remove objects from bushes and transport everything back to collection points. A bag of plastic bottles may appear insignificant on its own, but hundreds of such bags represent many hours of work.

Compared with other parts of the route, the Tiszalök section was not the most heavily polluted. Nearly seven tonnes were collected between Tokaj and Tiszaladány in just two days. The Bodrog section between Olaszliszka, Szegi, Bodrogkeresztúr and Tokaj produced almost 9.9 tonnes, while the Tisza section accounted for a further nine tonnes overall.

The uneven distribution illustrates why a single total cannot fully describe the condition of a river. Waste gathers in particular locations where vegetation, currents, earlier floods and human activity create natural traps.

If you missed it: Tiszalök’s hydropower plant stops operating as drought pushes River Tisza to a critical point

When the river is not responsible

One of the most troubling discoveries was an illegal waste deposit along the Bodrog. According to the organisers, the arrangement of the rubbish made it clear that people had taken it to the riverbank rather than the water carrying it there. The same area had been visited during the 2024 expedition, yet some sections appeared to contain even more waste this time.

The list of objects found elsewhere was equally revealing: tyres, parts of car bodies, refrigerators and other bulky items. These discoveries challenge the idea that the Tisza is merely a conveyor belt transporting waste from distant places into Hungary.

The reality is more complicated. Pollution can cross national borders, but it can also originate beside a local road, fishing spot or riverside shelter. Abandoned rubbish may remain hidden for years until a clean-up team exposes it.

That difference has practical consequences. International cooperation is necessary to address pollution entering Hungary from upstream countries. Local enforcement and waste-management systems are just as important when the source is illegal dumping within the country.

A competition built around environmental work

The PET Cup differs from a conventional clean-up campaign because its participants do not simply walk along the bank with bags. They build boats from recovered waste and use them to travel the river. Navigation, team challenges, quizzes and other activities form part of the programme, creating a structure that combines physical work with education and community-building.

The 2026 competition was won by Siemens Energy, followed by TOMRA and PETardáltak. A separate “Hero” award recognises the team collecting the largest amount of waste per participant.

Competition may seem unusual in an environmental programme, yet it helps maintain motivation during long and exhausting days. Teams return to the river year after year, become familiar with the terrain and develop practical knowledge about where waste tends to accumulate.

Young volunteers and participants involved in community-service programmes also encounter the problem directly. Seeing plastic trapped beneath vegetation can leave a stronger impression than learning about river pollution only through statistics or classroom discussions.

Stay up-to-date with our Hungary Weekly Briefing: subscribe on Substack!

Collection cannot replace prevention

The event’s success also exposes its central contradiction. The more effectively the PET Cup finds and removes waste, the more clearly it demonstrates how much rubbish has entered the natural environment.

That cannot be the final measure of progress. A future in which larger teams collect larger quantities every year would not represent a solution.

Prevention must therefore accompany clean-up work. Better waste management, stronger action against illegal dumping, cooperation among countries in the Tisza basin and systems that intercept waste before it reaches the floodplain are all necessary.

Recovery and recycling can extend the value of the work. At the Kisköre River Rescue Centre, collected material is sorted and prepared for further use. Earlier PET Cup projects also transformed recovered plastic into prototypes such as kayaks.

Still, recycling has limits. A bottle that is eventually processed after spending years in a floodplain has already caused unnecessary environmental damage. The most effective waste is the waste that never reaches the river.

What the arrival means for Tiszalök

Tiszalök was more than the endpoint of a sporting event. The town’s position along the route makes it a place where the consequences of upstream pollution, local dumping and floodplain accumulation become visible at the same time.

Repeated PET Cup arrivals can also influence how nearby communities relate to the river. A bottle floating past a bridge may be easy to overlook. Hundreds of bottles pulled from bushes create a different impression. So do abandoned tyres, refrigerators and illegal dumps.

Physical contact with the problem can change behaviour. Someone who has spent hours removing plastic from a floodplain may think differently the next time they hold a disposable bottle. That personal experience is one of the event’s most lasting effects.

Daily News Hungary has also previously reported on PET Cup clean-up expeditions, including an earlier campaign in which the Plastic Cup removed 8.2 tonnes of waste from the Tisza. Together, these reports show that the issue is not limited to dramatic waves of floating rubbish. It also involves hidden floodplain deposits, local responsibility and the long-term challenge of preventing waste from entering the river system.

The finish line is not the end

At Tiszalök, the boats arrived, the waste was weighed and sorted, and the results were announced. The competition had its winners, and the eight-day journey was complete. The environmental problem, however, remained.

The 18.9 tonnes collected during the expedition represent a significant achievement. So do the 2.12 tonnes removed from the final nine-kilometre section. Yet the most important figure may be the amount that volunteers did not reach.

The latest PET Cup showed that two explanations can exist at once. Some waste travels from far away, carried by the river across borders. Other rubbish is left much closer to home by people who treat the floodplain as a place where unwanted objects can disappear.

Volunteers can continue to remove what they find. Lasting progress will depend on reducing what reaches the river in the first place.

World.title: Police: Five men beaten and kept as modern-day slaves in Hungary for years
World.content:
They were promised work and accommodation, but allegedly ended up working 10–12 hours a day without pay, rest days or regular financial support, and were reportedly beaten and threatened if their performance was deemed inadequate, according to the police.

Men allegedly forced to work without pay

Hungarian police have arrested a 55-year-old man suspected of human trafficking and forced labour after five men were allegedly exploited at a property in Vecsés, near Budapest, for around two years.

According to the Pest County Police Headquarters, the victims were initially promised employment and accommodation. Instead, investigators say they were forced to work long hours under threats and physical abuse.

The men were reportedly accommodated at a property in Vecsés. On weekdays, they were taken to Budapest to carry out construction and electrical work, while in Vecsés they were made to perform tasks related to animal husbandry.

They allegedly worked 10 to 12 hours a day without proper rest periods or days off. Despite carrying out the work for around two years, they reportedly received no wages or regular financial support.

If you missed it: Hungarian man beats and tortures partner, forcing her to dig her own grave

Victims allegedly lived in fear

Police say the investigation revealed increasingly serious details after one of the alleged victims filed a report at the Budapest Police Headquarters’ 18th District Police Station late on 26 August.

Officers from Monor arrived at the Vecsés property shortly after midnight and began gathering information. The subsequent questioning of the alleged victims reportedly shed further light on the conditions in which they had been living and working.

According to investigators, the men were kept in a state of fear and were allegedly assaulted when their performance did not meet expectations.

One man was reportedly forced to continue working despite a musculoskeletal injury. Another was allegedly punched several times and was so frightened that he did not dare seek medical attention for his injuries.

Suspect denies the allegations

Police arrested the 55-year-old Lajos T. shortly after the report was made. He was taken into custody and prosecutors sought his pre-trial detention, which was subsequently ordered by the court. The suspect denies committing the offences and has lodged a complaint against the allegations.

Police are still searching for his alleged accomplice. The Pest County Police Headquarters is investigating the case on suspicion of human trafficking and forced labour committed against multiple victims. The investigation is ongoing.

World.title: Hungary’s new 2026 budget reveals a massive multi-billion-euro hole
World.content:
The Tisza government has submitted a revised 2026 budget that dramatically increases both state revenues and expenditure, while the projected deficit rises to HUF 7,110 billion (approx. EUR 19 billion), which is far above the figure originally approved under the previous government.

New government unveils dramatically revised budget

Hungary’s Ministry of Finance submitted the revised 2026 budget to Parliament on 31 August, just before the deadline. The overhaul was deemed necessary after the new government reviewed the country’s finances following the April change of government, 444.hu writes.

The previous administration had approved the 2026 budget last summer, based on assumptions that have since proved unrealistic, including economic growth of more than 4% and a significantly lower deficit.

According to the revised figures, the state is now expected to collect HUF 41,915 billion in revenue this year, compared with HUF 39,562 billion in the original budget.

At the same time, expenditure is projected to reach HUF 49,025 billion, up from HUF 43,781 billion. This leaves a projected deficit of HUF 7,110 billion, compared with the HUF 4,218 billion originally budgeted.

The government plans to reduce the deficit-to-GDP ratio to around 7.5% by the end of the year, compared with the 8.3% figure identified during its review of the inherited budget.

EU funds expected to boost revenue

One of the biggest changes on the revenue side is the amount expected to come from EU programmes. The revised budget forecasts HUF 3,708 billion in revenue from EU programmes, more than double the HUF 1,800 billion originally planned.

However, several other revenue streams are now expected to perform worse than initially forecast. Corporate tax revenue is projected to be almost HUF 250 billion lower than originally planned, while excise duty revenue is expected to fall by around HUF 220 billion. VAT revenue is forecast to come in nearly HUF 400 billion below the original estimate.

If you missed it: PM Magyar: Hungary has met all conditions to access frozen EU funds

State assets and other spending drive expenditure higher

Expenditure has increased much more sharply than revenue. The largest increase concerns spending related to state assets, which is now expected to exceed HUF 1,770 billion, more than HUF 1,400 billion above the original allocation.

This is particularly notable because only around HUF 120 billion had actually been spent from this budget line during the first half of the year, suggesting significantly higher spending could take place during the second half.

Other expenditure is also expected to rise by almost HUF 1,000 billion to around HUF 1,540 billion, while interest payments are also projected to be somewhat higher. Spending connected to EU programmes is expected to reach HUF 3,467 billion, also above the amount originally budgeted.

Government increases emergency reserves

The revised budget also strengthens the state’s reserves by a total of HUF 756 billion. Around HUF 500 billion will go towards a newly established Havaria Fund, designed to help deal with challenges including drought and the energy crisis.

A further roughly HUF 250 billion will increase contingency reserves, which had previously stood at less than HUF 750 billion. At the same time, the government plans to save around HUF 120 billion on spending by central budgetary institutions and centrally managed appropriations, reducing the planned amount from HUF 13,550 billion to HUF 13,427 billion.

Stay up-to-date with our Hungary Weekly Briefing: subscribe on Substack!

What about the promised extra money for healthcare?

The revised budget also provides a clearer picture of one of the Tisza government’s major election promises: increasing state healthcare funding by HUF 500 billion a year. The answer is more complicated than the headline figure might suggest.

According to Portfolio, the revised budget increases the Health Insurance Fund’s expenditure allocation from around HUF 4,945 billion to more than HUF 5,112 billion, representing an increase of approximately HUF 167 billion. Compared with the actual HUF 4,902 billion spent by the fund in 2025, the new allocation represents an increase of around HUF 210 billion.

The healthcare treatment and prevention budget rises from HUF 2,886 billion in the original 2026 budget to HUF 3,004 billion in the revised version — an increase of only around HUF 50 billion compared with the previous government’s original plan. The figures therefore depend heavily on what is being compared.

For example, spending on combined specialist healthcare services is projected at HUF 1,409 billion in the revised 2026 budget. Compared with the HUF 909 billion originally allocated for 2025, this represents an increase of exactly HUF 500 billion.

However, the previous government had already increased this spending allocation significantly for 2026, meaning the entire HUF 500 billion increase cannot be attributed to the new government.

The revised budget therefore does not provide a straightforward HUF 500 billion increase in healthcare spending attributable to the Tisza government. The promised 20–25% pay rise for healthcare professionals also cannot yet be clearly identified in the revised 2026 budget.

World.title: Industrial climber dies after falling from Hungarian government office roof
World.content:
A worker died after falling from the roof of a government office in Szeged on Tuesday. Police have launched an investigation into the fatal workplace accident.

Worker fell from Szeged government office

A fatal workplace accident occurred in Szeged on Tuesday around midday, when an industrial climber fell from the roof of the Csongrád-Csanád County Government Office, Szegeder reported.

The worker fell onto the roof of the Vármegye Restaurant next to the government office and died at the scene, according to local reports.

The man is believed to have fallen from a height of at least 15 metres. Local reports said he suffered a serious head injury, which may have contributed to his death, although the exact cause of death has not yet been officially established.

Photographs from the scene show ropes hanging from the government office building, apparently used by the worker during his work. Workers were also seen setting up a protective covering at the site following the accident.

Police investigate circumstances of fatal fall

The circumstances that led to the industrial climber falling from the roof remain unclear. Police told local media that the worker fell for reasons that are currently unknown.

The Csongrád-Csanád County Police Headquarters has launched an investigation into endangering safety in connection with employment. Experts have been involved in the investigation to establish what happened and whether any safety rules may have been breached. The investigation is ongoing.

World.title: Hungarian police seize thousands of documents in investigation into state Eximbank deals
World.content:
Police have seized thousands of pages of documents from Hungary’s Ministry of Economy and Energy as part of a criminal investigation launched following an audit of the state-owned Eximbank. The probe concerns suspected abuse of office and mismanagement of funds.

Thousands of pages seized from ministry

Hungarian police have seized thousands of pages of documents from the Ministry of Economy and Energy as part of an investigation into alleged irregularities at the Hungarian Export-Import Bank (Eximbank).

The National Bureau of Investigation (NNI) of the Rapid Response Police launched criminal proceedings after the ministry filed complaints based on information uncovered during an examination of Eximbank’s operations.

Police said on Tuesday that investigators seized the documents from the ministry on 31 August. The material had been collected during the ministry’s internal review and could provide further evidence concerning the alleged offences under investigation.

The case involves suspected abuse of office and mismanagement of funds.

If you missed it: Hungarian government seeks Eximbank investigations over EUR 2.74 billion in deals

Four controversial deals under investigation

Prime Minister Péter Magyar announced in July that the Ministry of Economy and Energy had filed criminal complaints concerning four deals dating from the previous government.

One concerns a HUF 59 billion (approximately EUR 161 million) financing deal connected to the Sofitel hotel and a company close to the business interests of István Tiborcz, the son-in-law of former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán.

According to Magyar, Eximbank made the relevant decision within just two days, allegedly failing to comply even with its own internal rules. The ministry filed a complaint over suspected mismanagement and other potential criminal offences.

A second case involves HUF 126 billion (around EUR 344 million) and an African project linked to Hungarian construction company Duna Aszfalt. The project involved plans to build an expressway between Zambia and the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Magyar also said the company had obtained financing from the state-owned Hungarian Development Bank in connection with the project.

The third case concerns the Dunakeszi Vehicle Repair Company’s Egyptian project, for which the Egyptian state railway was reportedly granted a HUF 176 billion (approximately EUR 480 million) loan from the Hungarian state.

The fourth investigation centres on a EUR 1 billion general-purpose loan granted to North Macedonia.

Stay up-to-date with our Hungary Weekly Briefing: subscribe on Substack!

Investigation launched after Eximbank review

The complaints were filed in July after the ministry reviewed the activities of Eximbank and identified information it considered potentially relevant to criminal proceedings. Police investigators are now examining the evidence gathered in the case, including the thousands of pages seized from the ministry.

The investigation is ongoing, and the seizure of the documents does not in itself establish that any criminal offence was committed. Further decisions will depend on the findings of the investigation.

World.title: Extraditing Hungarian MOL’s head to Croatia? Péter Magyar gives cryptic answer at Bled forum
World.content:
Hungary and Croatia could be preparing for a new round of high-level talks over the long-running dispute surrounding Croatian oil company INA and Hungary’s MOL Group.

Péter Magyar was asked about oil giant MOL’s chief

Speaking at the Bled Strategic Forum in Slovenia, Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar said Hungary was ready to negotiate with Croatia and that a “new chapter” could begin in relations between the two countries.

Magyar said he had held a brief meeting with Croatian Prime Minister Andrej Plenković in Bled. The two leaders agreed that their foreign and economic ministers should begin talks on the relationship between INA and MOL. Magyar also suggested that a meeting between the two prime ministers could take place in the foreseeable future.

“We are ready to negotiate. Naturally, everyone will defend their own national interests, but that is normal. At the same time, we all see that there is an opportunity to open a new chapter in relations between the two countries,” Magyar said, according to Croatian outlet Jutarni List.

What about Zsolt Hernádi ?

The issue of MOL chairman and chief executive Zsolt Hernádi remains one of the most sensitive aspects of the dispute. Magyar was asked directly whether Hungary would be prepared to extradite Hernádi to Croatia, where a European arrest warrant has been issued against him. However, the Hungarian prime minister did not give a straightforward yes or no answer.

Instead, he referred back to his comments about opening a “new chapter” in Hungarian-Croatian relations. “I have already answered the question by saying that there is an opportunity to open a new chapter between Croatia and Hungary. Both countries have their own obligations that need to be settled. That is my answer,” Magyar said. His response leaves unclear whether Budapest’s position on Hernádi could change. For now, there is no explicit confirmation that Hungary intends to extradite the MOL chief.

Stay up-to-date with our Hungary Weekly Briefing: subscribe on Substack!

INA dispute has strained relations for years

The relationship between MOL and INA has been a major source of tension between Hungary and Croatia for more than a decade. MOL acquired 25 per cent plus one share of INA in 2003 and subsequently increased its stake. It now holds 49.08 per cent of the Croatian oil company, while the Croatian state owns 44.84 per cent.

The dispute has centred on control of INA, corporate governance and the possibility of Croatia buying back MOL’s stake. The two sides have also been involved in arbitration proceedings. Plenković said the unresolved INA-MOL issues had held back wider Hungarian-Croatian relations, despite strong economic, tourism and energy links between the two countries. “I think we are now in a position where we can try to resolve this issue, and afterwards move on,” the Croatian prime minister said.

Stay up-to-date: Péter Magyar in Bled about crisis management, budget deficit, EU affairs, illegal migration, regional cooperation

Hernádi case remains unresolved

Croatian authorities have accused Hernádi of bribery in connection with MOL’s acquisition of management rights at INA. He has rejected the allegations. His legal case has become closely linked to the wider political and corporate dispute between Budapest and Zagreb.

The latest statements from both prime ministers could signal a renewed attempt to resolve the INA conflict. Whether the proposed talks can deliver a lasting settlement — and whether Hernádi’s case will form part of any broader agreement — remains uncertain.

World.title: Police aircraft spot wanted man hiding in woodland and suicidal missing man in cornfield in Hungary
World.content:
A police helicopter and a thermal-imaging drone helped officers locate two men in separate incidents in northeastern Hungary last week: one a wanted man attempting to hide from police, the other a missing 28-year-old who had reportedly threatened suicide.

Helicopter tracks down wanted man

The two incidents took place on 25 August during a policing operation carried out by the Rapid Response Police in Szabolcs-Szatmár-Bereg County.

In the first case, officers were searching for wanted individuals in Tiszavasvári with support from a helicopter operated by the Rapid Response Police’s Air Policing Service. The helicopter crew spotted something suspicious as officers approached a house. A man was seen moving towards a wooded area at the back of the property, apparently attempting to escape.

The helicopter operator immediately directed the camera towards the man and continuously relayed his location to officers on the ground. The 55-year-old suspect attempted to hide beneath the trees, but the aerial surveillance allowed officers to locate him within minutes.

Stay up-to-date with our Hungary Weekly Briefing: subscribe on Substack!

Police subsequently established that two warrants had been issued against the man by Tiszavasvári Police Station. One was issued in March after he failed to pay a HUF 65,000 (EUR 178) fine, while the other followed an unpaid HUF 52,000 (EUR 142) fine issued in August.

Both fines had been converted into custodial sentences of 10 and eight days respectively. The man told officers that he was still unable to pay the fines, and he was taken to Tiszavasvári Police Station.

If you missed it: Hungarian man beats and tortures partner, forcing her to dig her own grave

Thermal drone finds missing man in cornfield

Later that same day, the Rapid Response Police’s Nyírbátor unit received a report about a different man who had left his home after allegedly threatening to take his own life.

The man’s father, from Besenyőd, told police that his 28-year-old son, who was receiving medical treatment, had run into a cornfield behind their home. He said he could no longer find him and was concerned because his son had threatened suicide.

Officers deployed a drone equipped with a thermal-imaging camera to search the area.

The technology quickly revealed the man’s location, allowing patrol officers to reach him without difficulty. Given his confused state, officers called an ambulance to provide him with medical assistance.

The two cases show the important role of aerial technology in police operations, from tracking suspects attempting to evade arrest to locating vulnerable people who may be difficult to find from the ground.

World.title: Bucharest association launches app for people caring for stray cats
World.content:
Last week, the Părinți de Cireșari Association announced the launch of CatChat, an app dedicated to stray cats in Bucharest. Through the app, people can find out whether a cat on the street is already being cared for by someone.

The idea came about when an abandoned cat from a Bucharest neighborhood was treated with antibiotics by members of the association, who later found out that the feline was already being treated for the same condition. After the cat was treated by members of the association, it returned to the yard some time later, wearing a collar around its neck. They put a note on the collar to find out whether the feline had an owner or was being cared for by someone, and the answer came from a neighbor.

“That was when we realized we had a problem: cats roam around the neighborhood, but we, the people, don't really know who takes care of them, or whether anyone takes care of them. That's how CatChat came about,” representatives of the Părinți de Cireșari Association said, cited by Buletin de București.

The app has two functions. The basic one is the PisID function, through which users can register cats in the community and see whether they are already being cared for by someone. Users can also see how many unsterilized cats there are in the community.

The app includes an “identity card” for each cat, containing its identifying features (fur, eyes, age, sterilization status, etc.), while the map shows the cats nearby, with their photos. A missing cat appears with a red alert on the map, and those who see it can report its appearance so that the people searching for it can be contacted. According to association representatives, the project's purpose is to encourage communities to pay more attention to the animals around them and, at the same time, to facilitate communication between the people who care for them.

According to the Părinți de Cireșari Association, the app also has a “less serious” function. More specifically, based on the descriptions entered in PisID, cats have their own “chat,” which operates at night, when people are sleeping. The cats' conversations are fictional, written with AI only from the cats' public profiles, without using users' personal data.

For now, CatChat is available on the App Store for iPhone users. The app is free, without ads and without subscriptions. Moreover, it can be used across the country.
