BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 1. U.S. President Donald Trump said the United States is currently carrying out strikes against Iranian targets near the Strait of Hormuz.

US President Donald Trump wrote about this in Truth Social.

According to Trump, the strikes are “large and powerful” and were launched in retaliation for Iran’s alleged attempt to place sea mines in the Strait of Hormuz. He claimed that the waterway is currently free of mines, saying they had either been completely removed or detonated.

Trump also said Iran had fired eight missiles at a U.S. military base in Jordan, but that all of them had been successfully intercepted.

The U.S. president warned Tehran of further military action if Iran retaliates against the latest strikes.

He added that the potential response would not be the largest attack, saying an even bigger operation was “waiting in the wings.”

“When it is over, there will be very little left of the Islamic Republic of Iran,” Trump said.

World.title: Azerbaijan's Central Bank announces new banknote auctions
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 1. An auction for the placement of banknotes issued by the Central Bank of the Republic of Azerbaijan (CBA) will take place on September 2 and 3 at the Baku Stock Exchange (BSE).

According to the BSE, bids will be accepted during the auctions from 11:00 a.m. to 11:30 a.m.

On September 2, two types of banknotes with a total face value of 125 million manat ($73.5 million) will be offered at the auction. Of these, 75 million manat ($44.1 million) will be in 28-day banknotes, and 50 million manat ($29.4 million) will be in 168-day banknotes.

World.title: Azerbaijan’s Parliament Speaker joins NAM anniversary event in Serbia (PHOTO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 1. Sahiba Gafarova, Speaker of the Azerbaijani Parliament, is on a working visit to Serbia to participate in a high-level ceremony marking the 65th anniversary of the First Conference of Heads of State and Government of the Non-Aligned Movement.

According to information released by the Parliament’s press service, the Speaker delivered a speech at the event as part of her visit.

At the beginning of her speech, the Speaker conveyed greetings from the President of the Republic of Azerbaijan, Ilham Aliyev, on the occasion of this significant event.

The Speaker then noted that 65 years ago, the Non-Aligned Movement brought together several states around common goals, such as the protection of their independence, sovereignty, and the right to determine their own future. Since the organization’s inception, the system of international relations has undergone significant changes. However, the principles of respect for the sovereignty, territorial integrity, and equality of states; non-interference in internal affairs; justice; peaceful coexistence; and fulfillment of international obligations, which form the foundation of the Movement, remain of great importance for ensuring stability and a just world order in the system of international relations.

The Speaker of Parliament noted that over the past 65 years, the Non-Aligned Movement has become an important platform for advancing the common interests and goals of its member states, as well as for making a collective contribution to addressing global challenges.

She noted that the fundamental principles of the Non-Aligned Movement are fully consistent with the guiding principles of Azerbaijan’s foreign policy, and these principles also guided Azerbaijan’s chairmanship of the Movement from 2019 to 2024.

The Speaker of Parliament noted that at the 18th Summit of the Non-Aligned Movement, held in Baku in 2019, President Ilham Aliyev reaffirmed Azerbaijan’s commitment to the Bandung Principles, international law, and justice, as well as its commitment to strengthening the unity, solidarity, and international standing of the Movement.

Gafarova noted that during Azerbaijan’s chairmanship, special attention was paid to strengthening solidarity and cooperation among the Movement’s member states; an initiative was put forward to hold high-level meetings between the Non-Aligned Movement and the United Nations, and a contribution was made to shaping a coordinated international response to the COVID-19 pandemic and its consequences. It was noted that Azerbaijan provided financial and humanitarian assistance to more than 80 countries, as well as technical support and educational grants. The speaker also noted that special attention was paid to the institutional development of the Movement and to broadening its participation across different generations and institutions.

She also highlighted the establishment in 2022 of the Non-Aligned Movement Youth Organization, headquartered in Baku. It was noted that the expansion of the Organization’s activities enables young people to play a more active role in promoting the Movement’s values and goals.

The Speaker of the Azerbaijani Parliament also highlighted the activities of the Non-Aligned Movement Parliamentary Network. She noted that the activities of the Parliamentary Network, established in 2021, have significantly expanded over the past period: five conferences have been held, important institutional decisions have been adopted, and the Network’s headquarters has been established in Baku.

The speaker stated that today the Network brings together the parliaments of 71 countries that are members of the Non-Aligned Movement. This reflects the determination of our parliaments to promote the implementation of the Bandung Principles and to advance dialogue, peace, justice, and sustainable development through parliamentary diplomacy.

In closing her remarks, Parliament Speaker Sahiba Gafarova stated that the main tasks facing the Non-Aligned Movement are to preserve its unity and solidarity, strengthen its international voice, and increase its contribution to peace, sustainable development, and a more just and equitable world order.

World.title: Iran confirms fulfillment of obligations under NPT
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 1. Iran, as a signatory to the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons (NPT), is fulfilling its obligations under the treaty.

This was announced in a statement published by the Iranian MFA, citing spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei's remarks at a press conference in Tehran.

“Iran, as a member of the NPT, considers it its duty to fulfill the obligations outlined in the treaty. Iran’s position on nuclear weapons remains unchanged and principled,” he noted.

Baghaei added that Iran considers nuclear weapons, as the most destructive weapons of mass destruction, to be contrary to humanity and civilization.

“However, the United States, as a party to this agreement and a nuclear-weapon state, must bear responsibility. This is because attacks were carried out against Iran even though it was fulfilling its obligations under the NPT,” he noted.

Meanwhile, on July 8, U.S. President Donald Trump announced a breach of the ceasefire and ordered new strikes against Iran. In response, Iran launched missile and drone strikes against U.S. military targets in the Persian Gulf region. Although Washington has not ruled out the possibility of Iran returning to the negotiating table, disagreements over security in the Strait of Hormuz, Iran’s nuclear program, and other issues leave the future of the peace process uncertain. At present, commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz has once again come to a virtual standstill.

World.title: European News Agencies Alliance joins SPUR Coalition on AI standards
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 1. The European Alliance of News Agencies (EANA), representing 33 news agencies across Europe, has joined the SPUR Coalition as an affiliate member, according to EANA.

The SPUR Coalition brings together organizations from the news industry seeking to establish technical standards and commercial frameworks governing the use of publishers’ content by generative artificial intelligence platforms.

The initiative was launched by organizations including the BBC, Financial Times, Sky News, Guardian Media Group, Telegraph Media Group and Associated Press. Its work focuses on enabling content owners to monitor how their intellectual property is used by AI applications and creating conditions for transparent licensing.

According to EANA, the affiliation will allow its member agencies to access SPUR resources and participate in discussions on content licensing, usage transparency and the development of standards for cooperation between news organizations and AI companies.

“EANA's affiliation with the SPUR Coalition is a natural extension of our mission to defend the interests of news agencies and the journalism they produce. For seventy years now, our alliance has stood for cooperation, news accuracy and trustworthiness, and the public value of that trusted information,” EANA Secretary General Alexandru Giboi said.

He added that joining the coalition would allow EANA to contribute the perspective of European news agencies to discussions over the role and value of journalism in the era of generative AI.

SPUR co-founder David Buttle said that news agencies represented by EANA produce journalism that is valuable to companies developing and deploying AI systems.

“The SPUR Coalition was founded to change that. We are building open technical standards that give publishers visibility and control over how their content is used within AI applications, and that make a functioning licensing market possible,” he said.

EANA was founded in 1956 and currently has 33 member agencies across Europe. It is headquartered in Bern, Switzerland.

The SPUR Coalition is a non-profit industry initiative focused on developing standards for reporting content usage and establishing technical and commercial infrastructure for transparent transactions between publishers and AI platforms.

World.title: Venezuela highlights significant impact of oil agreement with U.S.
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 1. Venezuela’s Acting President Delcy Rodríguez stated that the oil deal with the U.S. will have a significant impact on Venezuela’s future.

This was stated in her remarks on the oil agreement with the U.S.:

“Yesterday we announced a historic agreement with the U.S. government that will have a significant impact on the lives of all Venezuelans in the medium and long term.

We are committed to a prosperous Venezuela so that we, the Venezuelan people, can look to the future in one year, five years, ten years, fifty years; we are thinking about the Venezuela of the future.”

As everyone knows, our country possesses the world’s largest oil reserves, but having underground reserves is not enough. We need investment, technology, infrastructure, and production capacity to turn this wealth into prosperity for our people. There is no point in keeping our oil reserves underground so that they appear only in statistics or accounting records; even if we cannot transform them into Venezuela’s development, we will still be able to say, “We are the country with the world’s largest reserves.” Our reserves must be transformed into well-being, prosperity, and happiness for this country, which will allow us to restore our production capacity and strengthen our position as an energy and manufacturing powerhouse.

Rodríguez emphasized that the use of Venezuela’s oil reserves must serve the country’s development and the strengthening of its energy potential:

“It makes no sense for our underground oil reserves to appear only in statistics or accounting records, just so we can say that we are the country with the world’s largest oil reserves, when we cannot transform and use them for Venezuela’s development. Our resources must bring prosperity, well-being, and happiness to this country, as well as enable us to restore our productive capacity in order to strengthen our position as an energy and industrial power.”

“In this way, we are not only providing our people with better incomes, public services, healthcare, education, and transportation infrastructure, but we are also contributing to the hemisphere’s energy security and helping to create a more balanced and stable international energy market.”

Delcy Rodríguez noted that the agreement reached by her country with the United States is based on combining the parties’ strengths:

“This agreement is based on a very simple principle: each party contributes what it does best. Venezuela offers its oil, its industry, and the more than a century of experience of its workers. The United States provides the capital and technology needed to restore and develop these assets. In return, Venezuela gains production, jobs, infrastructure investments, higher government revenues, and supply chains for local businesses.”

The benefits go beyond mere numbers. This bilateral project, signed for a term of 25 years, calls for the development of 17 strategic oil fields with a target daily production of more than 1.5 million barrels. This was made possible solely by the bilateral agreement between Venezuela and the US. But our goal is even higher: we want to become an energy powerhouse, a major oil producer, a key gas exporter, and develop a world-class domestic petrochemical industry by entering into major agreements with other large companies, including Chevron, Repsol, Eni, Shell, bp, and others.”

Rodríguez also addressed the issue of the revenue the agreement will generate for Venezuela and disclosed specific figures:

“And here a legitimate question arises, one that every Venezuelan citizen has every right to ask: How much does Venezuela earn? If we take a price of $65 per barrel (this price may go up or down), our country’s revenues will total $209 billion 335 million for the Venezuelan state.” Specifically, this means that approximately $19 from every barrel of oil produced and sold goes directly to our country.

In conclusion, I would like to remind you that thirty years ago, as part of the privatization of the oil industry, a major project was implemented to develop four new fields in the Orinoco Oil Belt based on a strategic partnership with a 1% royalty (mineral extraction tax) and a 34% income tax. This bilateral project provides for the development of eight new fields in the Faja area with a minimum royalty of 16% and a 34% income tax.

World.title: Social media algorithm opt-in would curb 'manosphere', says advocate
World.content:
Consent advocate Chanel Contos is urging the federal government to pursue an opt-in for algorithmic social media feeds, as it will be "too easy" for tech giants to design their way around weaker reforms.

Ms Contos will make the case for reining in harmful algorithms, which she says are exposing young people to misogynistic "manosphere" content and fuelling the prevalence of sexual violence in Australia, during a speech to the National Press Club in Canberra on Wednesday.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has backed giving Australians more control over the content they are served online but has stopped short of backing the algorithm opt-in model proposed by Ms Contos.

"In response to community concern about the impact of algorithms, we are considering options to ensure people have greater control over what they receive on their devices," Mr Albanese said.

Anthony Albanese says Australians should have more control over what they see on their devices but has not backed an opt-in model. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

In an excerpt of her speech, seen by the ABC, Ms Contos will argue an opt-out system for algorithms would be a "first step" and congratulate the government for seeking to address the issue.

"However, opt-in algorithms would fundamentally make the transition onto social media for 16-year-olds and other children safer, and it would bring the principle of affirmative consent to our screens," she will say.

"This is crucial, and the detail in any reform will determine its success."

Algorithms are the automated systems used by social media platforms to decide which posts, videos and other content a user sees and in what order, based on factors such as their behaviour and apparent interests.

Ms Contos, who is the founder and chief executive of advocacy group Teach Us Consent, launched the "fix our feeds" campaign calling for the government to mandate an "opt-in" for algorithms in December last year.

Labor has since indicated an interest in addressing the broader issue to further complement its laws banning Australians aged under 16 from holding any social media account.

Communications Minister Anika Wells said "deliberately opaque" algorithmic recommender systems had allowed social media companies to influence Australian culture "for better or worse".

"Online harm has real-world consequences," she said.

"If we want to prevent harm, we must fix platforms that reward it."

Anika Wells says social media companies are influencing Australian culture via algorithm-driven recommendations. (ABC News: Ian Cutmore)

Digital duty of care next on Labor's agenda

Ms Wells has been developing a Digital Duty of Care, which would be a legal obligation on online platforms to proactively identify and reduce foreseeable risks of harm to their users.

It reverses the current situation that relies mainly on users reporting harmful content after something has gone wrong.

An exposure draft of the legislation is due to be released later this month, with Ms Contos describing the "overall strength" of those reforms as "critical" to their success.

Loading...

"It is too easy for big tech to design schemes that appear as structural reform but actually suit them just fine," she will say at the National Press Club.

In her speech, Ms Contos will link algorithm-driven harm to the "uphill battle" schools are facing in their attempts to teach consent to young students.

Ms Contos will say a yearly class had "little hope" of changing the attitudes responsible for the current culture of sexual violence in schools while an "addictive content producing machine" simultaneously targeted teens with a "contradictory message".

How algorithms fuel the 'manosphere'

She will outline how the "manosphere" is not simply a broad term describing online communities that hold male supremacy ideologies, but a money-making venture facilitated by algorithms.

Ms Contos will say young men online seeking community, belonging or self-improvement advice were "targeted" with content that blamed women for their "misfortune".

This content also reinstates "harmful and outdated" gender roles, like the idea women should not leave the house without their male partner, hold jobs or earn their own money.

"Boys and men have valid concerns about the economy, and their relationships with partners and friends," she will say.

"From these concerns, an industry has jumped onto a market opportunity, and unfortunately, misogyny is at the heart of its business model."

Ms Contos will describe how young men engaging in "harmless" workout or motivational videos are "very quickly" served content promoting the idea that emotional control, material wealth and dominance "especially over women" are "markers of male wealth".

She will point to research that men who subscribed to those sorts of beliefs are twice as likely to binge drink, six times as likely to problem gamble and eight times as likely to have suicidal thoughts.

They are also 17 times more likely to have hit their partner, according to the Man Box study.

World.title: How Coles and NSW Police busted an Apple gift card tampering scam
World.content:
It is a movement of the hands barely visible on the grainy CCTV.

A man standing in front of a rack of colourful gift cards reaches into his pockets, and in several reaching motions, places cards back on the supermarket racks.

It is one of the moments Coles's fraud team captured as they were building a case against the man last year, alleging he was tampering with Apple gift cards in its supermarkets.

US regulators are investigating gift card fraud in their country. (Supplied: Homeland Security)

The ABC can confirm the man was later convicted for the incident, after Coles worked with police to monitor the man originally from Taiwan and eventually bust him with a haul of tampered cards.

"Gift card tampering and fraud is an evolving challenge affecting retailers and customers both in Australia and internationally," the supermarket said to ABC News in a statement.

"Coles takes the issue extremely seriously."

Loading...

What is gift card tampering?

An ABC investigation this week revealed supermarket customers nationwide were reporting gift card tampering, with the issue possibly linked to a wider global scam.

Homeland Security in the US has been investigating this issue for several years, with Project Red Hook linking it to money laundering in China, human trafficking and even murder.

Adam Parks says gift cards are being targeted in the US. (Supplied: Adam Parks)

"All of America's top 20 retailers were being affected," lead investigator Adam Parks said.

"Young Chinese nationals were being interdicted and arrested while taking cards off the rack, blank cards off the rack, taking them away from the store."

Mr Parks said the organised crime they found had a network of people dedicated to taking apart the cards, stealing their codes, and then returning them packaged back in store.

"Once they were put on the rack, then an unwitting consumer would go and would purchase those cards, and put funds on the cards," he said.

"And then [the] Chinese organised crime syndicates were able to spend the card before the unwitting consumer was [able to]."

As well as the CCTV vision supplied to ABC News, Coles captured the man on numerous other occasions at supermarkets around Sydney in March and April 2025, court documents show.

In some security video, the man was seen taking gift cards from the supermarket's aisles, while in others like the one ABC has witnessed, he was seen returning them.

Security staff then went down the supermarket aisle and noticed numerous Apple cards worth hundreds of dollars had been tampered with, and some stock had gone missing from the shelves.

After an internal investigation, Coles contacted the police.

Loading...

How the arrest unfolded

In April, officers attached to Campsie Police Area Command started covertly tracking their suspect.

Phone mapping records show the man regularly travelled to regional New South Wales, Goulburn and the Southern Highlands, with police suspecting he was also tampering with cards there.

The gift card scam hidden on Australian supermarket shelves An ABC investigation discovers gift cards that have been tampered with are being sold by Australia's biggest supermarkets, with charges even being laid over the issue.

Police obtained a warrant and searched the 32-year-old man's home in Eastwood, in Sydney's western suburbs, on May 9, 2025.

They found a bag containing 47 iTunes gift cards in bundles of five labelled with Post-it Notes.

The cards ranged between $100 and $500 in value, and there were nine more of them in his car.

Police said he told them outside of the interview that he was hired by an unnamed criminal syndicate, according to the court documents.

After arresting him, police alleged that he handled 61 Apple and iTunes gift cards worth more than $10,000.

He was charged with five counts of dishonestly obtaining financial advantage, and with two counts of dealing with property proceeds of crime less than $100,000 and less than $5,000.

He was then refused bail after police said there was a risk of "interfering with witnesses and tampering with or fabricating evidence".

The man was eventually convicted on July 22, 2025, and received a 15-month suspended prison sentence and a two-year community corrections order.

The ABC has been unable to reach the man for comment.

Ken Gamble says gift card fraud could become prolific in Australia. (ABC News: Michael Lloyd)

Trouble 'joining all the dots'

While the case highlights that gift card tampering is happening in Australia, private investigator Ken Gamble said "joining the dots" nationally might take more work.

The Australian Federal Police and the financial crimes regulator AUSTRAC both said this was not their domain.

"This is not a matter for the AFP," a spokesperson said.

And the authority that handles complaints about financial products, the Australian Financial Complaints Authority (AFCA), said it had limited scope over gift cards.

"It's definitely theft, but it would be one law enforcement would give a very low priority to because of the monetary value," Mr Gamble said.

"Unless they join all the dots here and they can see that this is done in great volume, [then] you're not going to get law enforcement to put the resources in.

"And that's the problem. That's why this type of crime is potentially something that could become very prolific in Australia."

Illustration of old and new Apple gift card design. (ABC News: Eric Hao Zheng)

Apple changed its gift card packaging in early 2025 to make it harder to open. The tech giant defended its measures to prevent tampering and declined multiple requests for direct comment.

Coles said stopping the crime took more than just the supermarkets and police.

"Coles works in conjunction with other retailers, gift card and brand partners, and law enforcement agencies to share relevant information and support investigations into suspected gift card fraud," the company said.

"We know that there is no single measure that will eliminate gift card fraud, and this isn't an issue that can be solved by retailers alone. It requires cooperation across retailers, gift card providers and law enforcement."

World.title: Blak & Bright Writers Festival rare public safe space for conversation
World.content:
In the early days of what was then Twitter, the social media platform was a place where First Nations people could feel seen, share their thoughts and feelings with each other, and meet people from their communities, says Goorie and Koori poet Evelyn Araluen.

Araluen, who won the 2022 Stella Prize for her debut poetry collection Dropbear and the 2026 Victorian Prize for Literature for The Rot, says social media used to provide a space for people to come together.

"X, for example, Twitter, that used to be a really wonderful space for mob to come together and have yarns and share their identities, their cultures, their history, their thoughts, their reflections," Araluen says.

"And we had amazing conversations across so many different cultural divides.

"And in the years that I was really active on Twitter, I met so many Blackfellas through those spaces, and it felt like there was a really strong sense of collectivity there."

Then things changed.

In 2022, the richest man in the world Elon Musk completed his takeover of Twitter, later re-naming it and implementing a number of changes including sacking outsourced content moderators.

Araluen says the renamed X is no longer a safe space for marginalised peoples.

"Anytime anything related to Indigeneity, First Nations context, Aboriginal context is mentioned, the flood of comments are so violent and heinous and disgusting that it really just isn't safe for mob to be in those spaces whatsoever anymore," she says.

Araluen says while discrimination and nasty comments have always been there, there used to be better systems in place to block, delete and remove that kind of commentary from individual feeds.

She thinks things have got much worse since the 2023 Australian Indigenous Voice to Parliament referendum, not just online, but in schools, universities and workplaces, and research backs this up.

"Now the gloves are off and racists feel like they have permission to say things that they might have otherwise been cautious about saying in public, because now they know that they've got enough people to back them up in order to make those comments without really strong fear of reproach," Araluen says.

Blak & Bright a space for these conversations

Araluen says this is why Australia's only gathering of First Nations writers and storytellers Blak & Bright Writers Festival matters.

It will take place in Naarm (Melbourne) from September 3-6.

It's a space where people can engage with the richness, complexity and power of First Nations storytelling.

Featured speakers include Araluen, Melissa Lucashenko, Chelsea Watego, Tony Armstrong, Bruce Pascoe, Tasma Walton, Brooke Blurton, Anita Heiss, Claire G Coleman and many others.

Araluen is a big believer in building broad coalitions and is encouraging people from all walks of life to attend.

"While the speakers are First Nations, this is not a festival that closes doors for the broader public to come and attend and to join in on these yarns," Araluen says.

" We want a sense of community and collectivity to come out of this, which goes beyond race, colour, creed. "

Ten years of Blak & Bright

Blak & Bright artistic director and CEO Bebe Oliver, who is an award-winning Bardi Jawi author, poet and illustrator, echoes these sentiments.

Bebe Oliver is encouraging all people to read and listen to more First Nations stories. (Supplied)

"Our underlying belief is that Blak stories are for everyone," Oliver says.

"And so, you don't need to be an Aboriginal, Torres Strait Islander, First Nations or person of colour to attend our festival or any of our events.

"We simply ask that you come with an open mind and with an open heart and a commitment to learning and to changing as well."

He's also urging people to seek out First Nations storytellers.

"People need to not just attend the festival but need to be reading and listening to more Blak stories than we already do," Oliver says.

With Blak & Bright taking place every two years since 2016, Oliver celebrates the milestone while acknowledging that writers' festivals more broadly have come up against many challenges of late.

"It's deeply concerning to see the constant flux and changes that are happening within the broader national literary industry," he says.

"Funding cuts, left, right, and centre, constant ongoing censorship regarding what can be spoken and written about.

"Pressures, from publishing houses, from agents and publicists to say these are the hot topics that really sell right now, perhaps you could write more about this, we push against all of that.

"And we focus solely on the need to see the broader Australian community understand and acknowledge that First Nations storytelling is the absolute heart of our entire industry.

"We've made such huge progress over the last 10 years … and to see that our festival has been able to continue, it's been able to grow despite all of those challenges and setbacks, it's a testament to the resilience and strength of Blak stories."

World.title: US launches fresh strikes on Iran around Strait of Hormuz
World.content:
The US has launched new air strikes on Iranian targets, quashing hopes that an exchange of fire last weekend might not presage a wider renewal of hostilities.

Oil prices had already risen after that first exchange of direct attacks since July and after reports of two tankers being hit leaving the Strait, the global oil supply waterway that Iran has effectively closed to shipping.

US President Donald Trump confirmed on his social media site Truth Social that strikes were underway on Tuesday, local time.

"The United States is, as we speak, striking Iranian Targets near the Strait of Hormuz," he said.

"The strikes are large and powerful, and in retaliation for the Iranians’ failed attempt at adding sea mines to the Strait, which currently has no mines (They have been completely removed or detonated!), and the Iranians shooting eight missiles, all successfully knocked down, at our Military Base in Jordan."

He went on to say that if Iran retaliated it would be "hit again at a much harder and higher level".

Tehran remained defiant, warning that it would prevent oil being exported from the Gulf, despite the president's threat and a warning from US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent that Washington was about to impose new sanctions.

US President Donald Trump had threatened to hit Iran "hard" in response to renewed Iranian strikes. (Reuters: Kylie Cooper)

Iran's state broadcaster said there had been reports of explosions on Iran's Qeshm Island, on the northern side of the strait.

The state-linked news agency Nour News said there had been reports of explosions in the port city of Bandar Abbas and in Chabahar, a port on the southern coast.

Scale of fresh US-Iran hostilities unclear

The six-month-old conflict had shifted into an economic standoff before the weekend strikes, in which US forces attacked Iran's Larak Island on Sunday and Iran responded by launching missiles at two US air bases in Jordan.

Although he warned of a US response to the Iranian strikes, Mr Trump also told reporters on Monday that they did not signal a return to full-scale war, and a senior Iranian source told Reuters they were a "limited and contained confrontation".

But pledges by both sides to respond to further attacks have highlighted how quickly a conflict that has increasingly been fought through sanctions, blockades and economic pressure could spill back into military action.

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian had said early on Tuesday that Tehran would reciprocate immediately if Washington honoured its commitments under a June Memorandum of Understanding that was intended to halt the conflict.

The MOU declared an end to fighting that has now killed thousands in Iran and Lebanon since US and Israeli strikes began on February 28. But it also deferred many of the most difficult issues and paved the way for a broader 60-day negotiation period — which passed without further agreement.

Trump says Kharg 'blown to smithereens' Donald Trump says Iran's Kharg Island is "being blown to smithereens".

"I am stating clearly that if the U.S. returns to its commitments under the Memorandum of Understanding, the Islamic Republic of Iran will immediately reciprocate," Mr Pezeshkian said in the Kyrgyz capital Bishkek at a summit of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation, which includes Russia and China.

But Iranian officials have shown no public sign of bowing to pressure.

"If the enemy wants us not to export oil from the Persian Gulf, no one will be able to export oil," Iranian parliament speaker Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf was quoted as saying by Iranian media. If the US intensified its "siege", he said Tehran would respond militarily.

Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei told a press conference in Tehran that Washington was "addicted to making excessive demands and has mistaken negotiations for dictating terms".

"As long as they act in this manner, they will certainly get no result other than what they have achieved so far," he added, warning that Tehran would "use all our capabilities, whether on the battlefield or through our diplomatic apparatus".

World.title: Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor 'committed sex crimes in US', congressman says
World.content:
Breakaway Republican Thomas Massie used congressional privilege on Monday to accuse Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor, the former Duke of York, of committing sex crimes in the United States.

Mr Massey, from the same party as US President Donald Trump, made the comment during a speech in the House of Representatives about the late paedophile Jeffrey Epstein.

"We want perpetrators of these crimes to be investigated and prosecuted," Massie said. "And Prince Andrew, who committed sex crimes in the United States."

"Perhaps hearing these names will shame the Department of Justice into delivering justice."

Mr Mountbatten-Windsor, who is King Charles III's brother, was stripped of his royal titles last year, and has always denied committing sexual offences and has never been charged with any crime relating to the allegations.

Under US law, members of Congress cannot be prosecuted over statements they make in the House of Representatives or Senate, meaning they can speak without fear of court action. Similar protections exist in Australia.

Mr Trump has criticised Mr Massie, a long-time campaigner for survivors sexually abused by Epstein or his friends, who has been among those leading bipartisan efforts to hold perpetrators to account.

The president earlier this year described his political colleague as a "bum" and "the worst Republican Congressman in history".

Thomas Massie has a reputation for standing up to the US President. (Reuters: Kent Nishimura)

A congressional panel investigating Epstein's crimes summoned Mr Mountbatten-Windsor in November last year to give evidence. However, it does not have the power to compel the former royal, who lives in England, to testify.

"Rich and powerful men have evaded justice for far too long. Now, former prince Andrew has the opportunity to come clean and provide justice for the survivors," Congressman Robert Garcia said at the time.

Mr Mountbatten-Windsor, 66, has been described as a close friend of Epstein's between 1999 and 2008.

Virginia Giuffre, who died by suicide in Western Australia in 2025, had alleged she was trafficked by Epstein to Mr Mountbatten-Windsor as a teenager, and that the then-Duke of York had sexually abused her.

He denies any wrongdoing.

Mr Mountbatten-Windsor stepped back from royal duties in 2019 amid a deluge of public pressure, after a disastrous interview with the BBC's Newsnight program, in which he maintained his innocence in the face of those allegations.

Last year, Ms Giuffre's posthumously released memoir went on sale. In it, she alleged Mountbatten Windsor "believed having sex with me was his birthright". She claimed she met the former prince on multiple occasions, including at an orgy on Epstein's private island.

Epstein died by suicide in a US prison in 2019.

British police investigating Mr Mountbatten-Windsor in May asked witnesses who believe they have information about alleged sexual misconduct to contact them.

The former royal is also being investigated over alleged misconduct in public office, which relates to his time as a UK trade commissioner.

Mr Mountbatten-Windsor has been accused of sharing confidential government information with Epstein, something he also denies.

World.title: Germany says Russia responsible for Leipzig airport drone attack
World.content:
The German government has directly blamed Russia for an incident last month involving an explosive-laden drone at a strategic airport in the eastern city of Leipzig.

Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said that after assessing the technology used and other intelligence information "the government concludes that Russia is responsible for the hybrid attack in Leipzig on August 4".

In response, Berlin has announced it will close Russia's consulate in the former capital Bonn later this month, and cancel the lease for the Russian House, a cultural centre in the capital city, according to Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul.

He said Germany would also recommend more Russian individuals be targeted for European Union sanctions.

The announcement marks the latest accusation levelled at Moscow of alleged hybrid attacks across the continent.

EU chief Ursula von der Leyen said the bloc stands in "full solidarity" with Germany.

"We are united in our resolve to stand against Russian aggression. We will deter anyone who seeks to undermine our freedom and security," von der Leyen wrote on X, adding the European Union was preparing additional sanctions against Russia.

Mark Rutte, who heads up the NATO military alliance, said he had held talks with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz about the revelations.

Suspicion follows discovery of drone at German airport German prosecutors say the incident marked a "serious attack", with local media reporting that a technical issue prevented the drone from detonating.

"NATO will continue to strengthen our ability to deter and defend all Allies against any threat — including malign actions like those seen in Leipzig and elsewhere across the Alliance," he wrote on X.

" Russia's attempts to intimidate us, to undermine our unity and our willingness to support Ukraine are futile and will fail. "

Russia has been repeatedly accused of being behind hybrid attacks on logistics centres, transport hubs and undersea cables across Europe.

Security experts say such attacks are an attempt to weaken support for Ukraine among allies.

The Kremlin has repeatedly denied any involvement.

Last month's alleged attack saw a drone packed with explosives discovered at Leipzig/Halle Airport, a major logistics hub for military equipment and for German freight company DHL.

The drone was uncovered not far from a parked Ukrainian jet.

A bomb disposal robot was used on the drone and flights to and from the airport were temporarily disrupted.

Russian President Vladimir Putin is accused of directing a campaign of sabotage across Europe to weaken support for Ukraine. (Sputnik: Gavriil Grigorov via Reuters)

Another drone was reportedly found weeks later near the airport, also with traces of an explosive substance.

Germany's accusation came on that European defence leaders met to discuss beefing up their defences in the face of a more aggressive Russia.

"Europe is investing more in defence than ever, but spending alone is not automatically a guarantee for success," the European Union's top diplomat, Kaja Kallas, told journalists in Ireland.

" We have not been fast enough to cover the gaps in Europe's conventional power within NATO. "

European countries started ramping up military budgets after Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine.

US President Donald Trump has also piled pressure on Europe to spend more on defence as Washington signals it wants to step back from the continent to focus on other challenges such as China.

World.title: Twelve killed as Russia steps up aerial assault on Ukraine
World.content:
Russia has bombarded the Ukrainian capital for more than 12 hours overnight and into Tuesday, local time, killing at least a dozen people in another aerial onslaught that authorities said was aimed at menacing civilians.

The strikes marked an unprecedented sixth straight day of heavy Russian attacks on Kyiv since Russia launched the full-scale invasion of its neighbour more than 4.5 years ago.

The consecutive aerial assaults are designed to grind down civilians by disrupting daily life, Ukrainian officials have said.

The cruise and ballistic missiles, jet-powered drones, glide bombs and artillery salvos targeted Kyiv as well as eight other regions.

The strikes wounded more than a dozen people, including three children, just as millions of Ukrainian schoolchildren returned to classes Tuesday for the new school year.

The attacks appear to be an effort to intimidate and grind down Ukraine's population. (Reuters: Gleb Garanich)

The European Union's top diplomat said Russia's army is struggling to make progress on the front line and wants to scare off Ukraine's Western backers with its air campaign.

"Russia's war is becoming more ruthless and destructive, but it's unfortunately not closer to ending," EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said at a meeting of the bloc's defence ministers in Ireland.

" Russia's army is bogged down on the ground, and that is why they are killing civilians from the skies. "

The latest attack struck civilian infrastructure and residential buildings in several districts of Kyiv, authorities said, with eight people killed in the city itself and four others in the surrounding region.

Six employees of state-owned railway company Ukrzaliznytsia were among those killed in Kyiv when a ballistic missile hit a depot and other property, company Chairman Oleksandr Pertsovskyi said in a social media post.

Ukraine accuses Russia of targeting civilian targets with drones and missiles. (Reuters)

Residential building among targets

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the dead included an Indian citizen.

Nearly 350 emergency workers were deployed in Kyiv and the surrounding region, Mr Zelenskyy said.

The Russian Defense Ministry said its forces carried out a "massive strike" on Ukraine with "precision-guided weapons" and long-range drones. The assault targeted facilities that manufacture and store weapons, as well as military-related infrastructure, it said.

Ukraine's drones could crash Russian banks On the outskirts of Russian cities, warehouses belonging to the country's largest online retailer are being struck by Kyiv's drones, with some analysts saying it could lead to a financial crisis.

Ukraine's air force said the attack began at 6pm Monday, local time, using ballistic, cruise and anti-radar missiles, as well as 218 drones and decoys.

About a third of the drones were jet-powered, making them much harder to intercept than propeller-driven versions.

The main Russian targets were in the Kyiv and southern Odesa regions, the air force said in a statement.

The attack on the Odesa region on the Black Sea damaged civilian infrastructure and wounded one person, regional head Oleh Kiper said.

Two residential buildings were damaged, while a fire broke out at a textile factory. Russian forces also struck the Orlivka international ferry crossing on the border with Romania, he said.

Russia also shelled the northern Zhytomyr region, starting fires at an industrial facility and a warehouse, Ukraine's Emergency Service said.

In the capital, first responders worked to clear rubble from damaged apartment buildings and free trapped residents.

Ukraine hits Russian port

Meanwhile, the Russian Defense Ministry said Tuesday that its air defences overnight intercepted 516 Ukrainian drones over 18 Russian regions, as well as the illegally annexed Crimean Peninsula and the Black Sea.

In the Leningrad region, the drone attack sparked a fire in the port of Ust-Luga, Governor Alexander Drozdenko said, as Ukraine extended its campaign to hurt Russia's oil sector, which is a mainstay of the economy.

Ust-Luga is one of Russia's largest oil and gas export terminals, more than 800 kilometres away from Ukraine.

It has been repeatedly targeted by Ukrainian drone attacks this year.

Elsewhere, the war in Ukraine was discussed Monday at a summit involving the leaders of China, Russia and India.

Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi told Russian President Vladimir Putin through a translator that India supports efforts to end the fighting.

"We need to move from endless war to the end of war, to the end of hostilities," Mr Modi said, adding that "this is very important for all of humanity."

AP

World.title: The unnoticed rule change that has Penny Wong earning the PM’s salary
World.content:
Exclusive PoliticsFederalPolitical leadership The unnoticed rule change that has Penny Wong earning the PM’s salary Rob Harris September 2, 2026 — 4:45am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Penny Wong will pocket the same salary as the prime minister for the first time while filling in as leader of the country after a sudden rule change by the independent body that handles the pay rates of key Commonwealth offices, including politicians and judges. The foreign minister has been elevated to the top salary this week by the Remuneration Tribunal’s ruling while Anthony Albanese is in Palau for the Pacific Islands Forum and deputy Prime Minister Richard Marles is in the United States and Britain on defence business. Penny Wong is on the big bucks after taking the big chair - temporarily. Alex Ellinghausen The new rule was buried in the tribunal’s latest report on ministerial salaries, published on the tribunal’s website as coming into effect on August 25 this year. It ruled any minister who serves as acting prime minister should now be paid at the same annual rate as the prime minister. Previously, only the deputy prime minister was paid a higher wage while acting in the role. As the nation’s highest-paid politician, Albanese’s annual salary is $622,102, made up of the $239,270 parliamentary base salary plus a $382,832 loading (160 per cent of the base salary) for serving as prime minister. The additional salary is separate from parliamentary allowances, entitlements and expenses.



Wong, as leader of the government in the Senate, normally earns $448,631, including a $209,361 loading on top of the parliamentary base salary. Related Article Pacific diplomacy ‘The Pacific determines what happens’: Albanese pushes back against China over Taiwan warning The new ruling means she would receive the prime minister’s higher loading for the four days she is acting in the role – from Monday to Thursday. The difference between the two loadings is $173,471 a year, translating into about $1900 extra before tax. A spokeswoman for the tribunal was at pains to reject any suggestion the rule had been written for Wong while she was on higher duties. In a statement, it said the recommendation was “not related to, or timed to coincide with, Senator Wong’s appointment as acting prime minister”.



The tribunal said it had considered the issue as part of its annual review and that the recommendation “was not made in response to a request from the Prime Minister’s Office or the government”. She said the tribunal provided its 2026 report to Finance Minister Katy Gallagher on July 1 before it was tabled in parliament and published on August 25. The tribunal is required to report on ministerial salaries at least once a year. The three-member tribunal is chaired by corporate director Holly Kramer, whose board portfolio includes ANZ, Fonterra and Telstra. Veteran investment adviser Heather Zampatti and property executive Stephen Conry are the other members. Wong’s temporary promotion comes under arrangements signed by Albanese after the federal election last May for the exercise of his powers when he is absent from Australia or unable to perform his duties. Those arrangements put Marles, as deputy prime minister, first in line, followed by Wong if he is unavailable, then Treasurer Jim Chalmers, Gallagher as finance minister and Trade Minister Don Farrell.



The need for an acting prime minister when the leader is overseas has become less critical now that the RAAF jets they travel on have internet connection and secure communication systems. The role was traditionally vital when prime ministers were at sea to travel to Europe last century and often uncontactable for weeks. Related Article Exclusive

National security Labor declares AI biggest sovereignty moment ‘since World War II’ Both the prime minister’s and Wong’s offices were contacted for comment. In 2017, amid a Coalition fight over who should be acting prime minister when Malcolm Turnbull was overseas and his deputy, Barnaby Joyce, was ruled ineligible to sit in parliament over his citizenship status, Turnbull said he was still making the decisions while away. “The acting prime minister is a role that is really designed to cover circumstances where, for example, it was urgent for a document to be signed with my consent … but I’m not in the country to sign it.” Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. Subscribers can sign up to our weekly Inside Politics newsletter.

World.title: US launches major strikes against Iran for first time since late July
World.content:
Breaking WorldNorth AmericaMiddle East at war US launches major strikes against Iran for first time since late July Michael Koziol Updated September 2, 2026 — 3:35am ,first published 2:55am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Washington: The United States military announced its first major strikes against Iran in more than a month, in what it said was an operation targeting the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) following recent aggression. The strikes began at 7.30pm Tehran time on Tuesday (2am Wednesday AEST), US Central Command said. “The strikes follow recent attempted attacks by the IRGC against commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and against American service members deployed to the region.” The Strait of Hormuz near Bandar Abbas on Monday. AP Photo/Razieh Poudat Iranian state media reported explosions near the port city of Bandar Abbas, and other locations. The last time the US military confirmed strikes against Iran was on July 29, although it conducted “limited, precise actions” against Iranian rocket launchers near the Strait of Hormuz on Sunday.



US President Donald Trump confirmed the “large and powerful” strikes in a social media post. He said they were in retaliation for Iran’s failed attempt to add mines to the strait and its firing of eight missiles towards a US base in Jordan – which were intercepted. “If the failed Nation of Iran retaliates for this very justified attack, they will be hit again at a much harder and higher level, but it will not be the biggest attack of them all, that is waiting in the wings and, when it is over, there will be very little left of the Islamic Republic of Iran!” Trump wrote on Truth Social. President Donald Trump, pictured in the Oval Office on Monday, has warned Iran a bigger attack is “waiting in the wings”. AP Photo/Jacquelyn Martin The renewed strikes followed Iranian attacks on two large tankers carrying oil out of the Strait of Hormuz on Monday night, local time, after a period of relative calm. Projectiles hit the Saudi Arabian-flagged crude carrier Sidr, followed minutes later by a Liberian-flagged vessel, Senegal Prosperity, which is owned by a South Korean company.



The tankers each loaded 2 million barrels of ​Saudi crude at the Juaymah terminal last week, Kpler data showed. Saudi ⁠Aramco resumed oil loadings and sales from inside the strait in August. Related Article Updated

Middle East at war US strikes Iranian targets in first attacks in weeks, Tehran retaliates Monday marked six months since the US and Israel launched their first strikes against Iran, assassinating the supreme leader Ali Khamenei and destroying the country’s navy and other military assets. However, despite a memorandum of understanding between the US and Iran signed in June, there has been no permanent deal to end the war and re-establish safe passage for global shipping through the strait.



More to come With Reuters Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: Australia’s tiniest wallabies spotted in the north-west in a tale of survival against the odds
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Few people may have heard about Australia’s tiniest wallabies, the Monjon and the Nabarlek, since they live in the remote rocky plateaus of the Kimberley. Smaller than a domestic cat, they weigh little more than a bag of sugar. Like most of Australia’s small marsupials, they are endangered species and rarely sighted in remote northern Australia. And they’re fiendishly hard to tell apart. A Nabarlek on Augustus Island, off the Kimberley coast. Ian Bool But the Australian Wildlife Conservancy has recently confirmed the presence of the Nabarlek, Australia’s second-smallest wallaby, at two new locations in the Kimberley – in one location for the first time in 50 years. It hints at their survival against the odds – feral cats and fire – in pockets across the north. What makes the discovery compelling is the work required to confirm the Nabarlek’s identity. At just 1.7 kilograms and 36 centimetres long, the nocturnal wallaby is not only hard to spot in the wild, but can be easily confused with the near-identical Monjon and the larger short-eared rock-wallaby.



The AWC team, working closely with local Dambimangari rangers, first sets out camera traps in rocky terrain to capture images of these hopping marvels. “You’ve got to be out at night if you want to spot them in person,” says Larissa Potter, AWC’s senior field ecologist. Related Article Marine life WA hit by worst coral bleaching on record across 2000km of coastline “Mainly we use five camera traps each night that are triggered by passing animals.” But pictures aren’t enough – to conclusively distinguish a tiny Narbalek from a tinier Monjon requires climbing up rock platforms and gathering fresh animal droppings containing DNA that genetically confirms one species from another. The team has spent years linking camera images and genetic analysis of faeces in order to correctly identify the species. The new Nabarlek locations are welcome news in the leadup to next week’s Threatened Species Day on September 7, which commemorates the death of the last thylacine in Hobart Zoo in 1936.



“This is very exciting and great news for the species,” says Potter. “Confirming the Nabarlek’s presence at two new sites is a major step forward for our understanding of where the species occurs. “It’s also reassuring as it indicates that this threatened wallaby is persisting on the Kimberley mainland in places we didn’t previously know about.” Pilot Ritchie Stephenson, Rihanna Bangmorra (Dambimangari Aboriginal Corporation), Amelia Hurrell (DAC/Australian Wildlife Conservancy) and Naomi Blondel (Australian Wildlife Conservancy). Naomi Blondel The job of finding Nabarlek was the ecological equivalent of finding a needle in a haystack, she says. They were located at Yampi Sound Training Area, a vast Kimberley wilderness area identified as one of 20 priority places in the federal government’s Threatened Species Action Plan. Owned by the Commonwealth defence department, the training area can only be accessed by sea, air, or by making a rugged 130-kilometre drive from the port town of Derby.



A second Nabarlek population was confirmed around 170 kilometres away, an area also contained within the traditional country of the Dambimangari Aboriginal Corporation. Until the recent discoveries, the Nabarlek has only been recorded from a handful of mainland Kimberley sites and from five offshore islands. Potter says small populations appear to have withstood extensive wildfires on Augustus and Jungulu, two large uninhabited offshore islands at the southern end of the Bonaparte Archipelago. “You’ve got to be out at night if you want to spot them in person.” Australian Wildlife Conservancy Potter says the mainland Nabarlek DNA will be compared to the island populations. “We think that feral cats and fire might be getting them on the mainland, so it’d be great to have more funding to learn more about this animal.” The species was once thought to have lived widely across mainland northern Australia but in recent years has been rarely seen in the Northern Territory. The Nabarlek’s total population is uncertain, but according to the International Union for Conservation of Nature Red List of Threatened Species, mature individuals are estimated at just 5000 to 10,000 animals.

World.title: The greatest scientific mystery of our time may have just flashed in a gold mine
World.content:
NationalScience The greatest scientific mystery of our time may have just flashed in a gold mine Angus Dalton September 2, 2026 — 12:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Examine, a free newsletter covering science, is sent every Tuesday. You’re reading an excerpt – sign up to get the whole newsletter in your inbox. Sometimes it feels as if all the fundamental questions about existence have been solved. Then you remember dark matter. This unknowable substance constitutes as much as 85 per cent of all mass in the universe, and yet we cannot see or directly measure it, and we don’t know what it’s made of. Scientists believe dark matter underpins the structure of the universe. KIPAC/SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory But the structure of spiralling galaxies, the make-up of the cosmos, and indeed our very existence only make sense if the universe is woven with an undiscovered, invisible essence, holding it all together like a secret skeleton.



Needless to say, dark matter is the greatest scientific mystery of our time. That’s why physicists are intensely excited about a tiny spark of light detected in a pool of liquid xenon in the depths of an abandoned goldmine. The data is limited and fresh, and scientists are duly cautious. But there is a possibility this newly reported signal could be the first-ever detection of dark matter. How do we know dark matter exists? Fritz Zwicky was an unconventional and at times unpopular scientist who once said of his more orthodox colleagues: “Astronomers are spherical bastards. No matter how you look at them, they are just bastards.”



The Swiss stargazer was investigating the Coma galaxy cluster in 1933 when he realised the galaxies were rocketing around each other at 2000 kilometres per second – so fast they should have violently flung away from each other. The structure and speed of galaxies don’t make sense unless they contain far more mass and gravity than they appear to. AP He calculated the galaxies, to summon enough gravity to stay together, must have 400 times more mass than they appeared to have. What was providing this invisible gravitational glue? He proposed the existence of dark matter. Zwicky’s theory was treated as zany. Then American astronomer Vera Rubin spied another anomaly in the 1970s. Stars on the outer edge of a galaxy should orbit much slower than those at the centre. But Rubin discovered the outer stars of a galaxy travelled just as fast as those closer to the centre.



The visible matter in the galaxies didn’t have enough gravity to hold on to these distant, fast-spinning stars. Something else was holding on to them. Rubin concluded: “What you see in a spiral galaxy is not what you get”, and that dark matter must be real. Now astronomers can see how light is warped in space by gravity emanating from dense, invisible regions of suspected dark matter. The image below shows galactic gas highlighted in pink, while the blue areas show regions of intense gravity scientists believe can only be explained by dark matter. The Bullet Cluster, a pair of galaxy clusters that collided. Normal matter is shown in pink, suspected dark matter in the cluster shown in blue. This observation has provided one of the clearest direct examples of dark matter. NASA But that’s a shadow of a shadow. In the race to truly detect dark matter, instead of looking up through telescopes, we’re burrowing deep into the Earth.



The deep detector

Dark matter doesn’t emit or reflect light, and it barely interacts with normal matter. We also don’t know what it’s made of. So how do we find it? Dr Theresa Fruth, a dark matter hunter from the University of Sydney, helped design and construct one of the best dark matter detectors on Earth, called the LUX-ZEPLIN (LZ) experiment. About 250 scientists and engineers are participating in the project. Dr Theresa Fruth, from the University of Sydney, preparing to descend to the LZ detector in South Dakota. Theresa Fruth “It’s basically a big bucket of liquid xenon,” Fruth says. “Xenon is a trace element in the air around us, and it’s a noble gas. But if you cool it down enough, about minus 100 degrees, it’s a really dense liquid.”



Any skerrick of radiation might mimic dark matter and must be banished. “Xenon is good because you don’t have any long-lived radioactivity naturally in the xenon. It decays away and you can have this very clean, very quiet liquid.” The LZ detector was moved 1.5 kilometres underground into a gold mine to shield it from cosmic rays. Matthew Kapust/Sanford Underground Research Facility Researchers assess LZ’s central detector while it is wrapped in foil. Matthew Kapust/Sanford Underground Research Laboratory Looking up into the LZ outer detector, used to veto radioactivity that can mimic a dark matter signal. Matthew Kapust/Sanford Underground Research Laboratory



The ultrapure liquid xenon is contained in two tanks of medical-grade titanium and teflon, in turn encased by more than 250,000 litres of water for extra shielding. The entire thing is entombed in an abandoned goldmine in South Dakota, 1.5 kilometres underground, to protect the detector from cosmic radiation lashing Earth from space. In theory, if a skerrick of dark matter hits this pool of xenon – one of the stillest, quietest, most stable places on Earth – at the right angle, it would spark a tiny flash of light. On Wednesday, at midnight, scientists reported a flash. Finding WIMPs



The LZ experiment is designed to detect weakly interacting massive particles, or WIMPs, one of the leading theories for what dark matter could be made of. WIMPs are thought to be heavy, slow-moving subatomic particles between 10 and 1000 times heavier than a proton. Scientists think they might be constantly passing through Earth like ghosts. When a WIMP collides with a xenon atom, the xenon atom emits a flash of light and electrons. Greg Stewart, SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory If one of these WIMPS struck the nucleus of a xenon atom in the LZ detector, theoretically, this would unleash a tiny flash of light. Five hundred photomultiplier tubes in the tank set-up are tuned to pick up any flashes.



Scientists pore over the resulting data to see whether flashes might be explained by stray radiation given off by the material of the detector itself, or some other rogue background ray. Now they have reported a flash that, as yet, cannot be explained by a background signal: a possible hint of dark matter. “We don’t really know what to do with that, because we’re so used to not seeing anything,” Fruth says. “We usually make these jokes about how we’re not seeing anything better than anyone else. “The moment you see something and you don’t quite know yet what it is, it’s very exciting, but also a little bit scary.” Aussie detector in the hunt



The finding is below “5-sigma” significance, which in physics lingo is the level of statistical confidence needed to report an actual discovery. The LZ flash sits at 2.6 sigma, which means there’s a 0.5 per cent chance the flash could be due to a known background signal rather than a WIMP. The dark matter lab under construction a kilometre underground at the Stawell Gold Mine in 2021. Joe Armao The scientists are releasing their data so that other dark matter hunters can analyse and try to explain it, so we’ll know more about this detection in coming months. Meanwhile, the LZ detector team is waiting patiently for another event, which could help refine that sigma number. Should further data push the statistical firepower higher, we could be at the start of a historic moment in science.

World.title: Australia’s ‘shameful’ cocaine habit prompts $600m Pacific package
World.content:
PoliticsFederalDrugs Australia’s ‘shameful’ cocaine habit prompts $600m Pacific package Matthew Knott September 1, 2026 — 10:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Koror City, Palau: Prime Minister Anthony Albanese will pledge $600 million for a new Pacific-wide initiative to combat the surge of illicit drug smuggling in the region, especially cocaine bound for Australia. The major funding commitment came as Albanese pushed back against China’s Pacific envoy for threatening retaliation and lodging complaints over Taiwan’s presence at the Pacific Islands Forum in Palau, declaring it was up to Pacific nations to determine their own affairs. US Coast Guard members board a self-propelled semi-submersible in international waters in 2019. US Coast Guard/AP Tensions between Taiwan and China escalated as officials traded barbs, with Taiwan accusing Beijing of bullying smaller nations and China accusing the self-governing territory of humiliating itself. As they struggle to cope with a dramatic rise in transnational crime fuelling the illegal drug trade, Pacific leaders are preparing to endorse a new regional initiative known as Waqa Moana to beef up maritime patrols and intelligence sharing.



The $600 million package Albanese will announce on Wednesday would fund enhanced aerial surveillance to help track suspected drug vessels and provide extra support to police in Fiji, among the nations hardest hit by the rise in drug smuggling. The Waqa Moana initiative – named after a large, sturdy canoe – would include greater co-ordination of existing resources to combat transnational crime, including the 23 Guardian-class patrol boats Australia has given to Pacific countries. Federal police would also increase their co-operation with South and Central American countries to target the drug trade at its source. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese was welcomed at Palau Airport on Monday night. AAPIMAGE “The Pacific is our home and our family. That’s why it’s in Australia’s interests to work with our Pacific partners to combat organised crime,” Albanese said.



“For the good of every country in the region, including our own – we need to work together to stamp out the illicit drug trade.” Related Article Analysis

Pacific diplomacy Narco-subs and ballistic missiles: PM’s Pacific trip a swirl of geopolitical turmoil Pacific leaders are expected to officially endorse the initiative at the end of the week. Australian Federal Police Commissioner Krissy Barrett declared in May that “it is our nation’s shame that Australians consume too many illicit drugs and pay high prices for them”. At the same time, Barrett revealed that 17 tonnes of illicit drugs, mostly cocaine, had been seized by authorities in the Pacific since January, up from less than five tonnes in all of 2025.



Barrett warned that “greedy and ruthless narco-gangs are trying to make more money by identifying new ways to traffic illicit drugs”, including by sending semi-submersible vehicles (widely known as narco-submarines) to cross the Pacific. “The magnitude and endless maritime trafficking of illicit drugs to, and through the Pacific, has become a serious national security threat for the Pacific and Australia,” she said. A multinational police investigation implicating 11 Fijian police officers in collusion with drug traffickers was also handed over to prosecutors in May. A month later, Fijian police confirmed that 76 parcels that washed up in the country had been found to contain cocaine. Pacific Minister Pat Conroy said: “Drug trafficking is having a devastating impact on Pacific communities.



“This initiative responds to the calls of regional leaders to do more, and to step up regional coordination to address this scourge.” Related Article Pacific diplomacy ‘The Pacific determines what happens’: Albanese pushes back against China over Taiwan warning Speaking after the forum’s opening ceremony, China’s special envoy for the Pacific Qian Bo said he had “serious concerns” about the level of access being granted to Taiwan, a self-governing island that China claims as an integral part of its territory. “We have made our position very clear to the government of Palau and the secretariat,” he told reporters. Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun doubled down on Tuesday, telling reporters in Beijing that Taiwan “has no standing whatsoever” to participate in PIF activities.



“By sending ‘Taiwan independence’ separatists like [Taiwan Foreign Minister] Lin Chia-lung around to scheme for attention and clout, the Taiwan authorities will only end up bringing humiliation upon themselves,” Guo said. He also rejected New Zealand Foreign Minister Winston Peters’ claim that the non-attendance of several leaders was “highly suspicious”, insisting it was “completely groundless” to blame China for the no-shows. Lin urged Pacific leaders to hold firm against Beijing’s demands as he accused Qian of practicing an aggressive form of “wolf warrior diplomacy”. “We should not be making concessions just because of China’s bullying,” he said. He told reporters Taiwan had been a PIF development partner since 1993, and he had “every confidence” it would participate in next year’s conference in New Zealand. Blocking Taiwan from participating would “violate the spirit of the Pacific way”, he said.



China, the United States and other countries serve as official dialogue partners of the PIF, while Taiwan attends as a development partner. Palau is one of a handful of remaining countries in the world that still recognise Taiwan, rather than Beijing, as the legitimate government of China. China’s special envoy for the Pacific Qian Bo made it clear how unhappy Beijing was that Taiwan was invited to the forum. AAPIMAGE Saying he believed China had the support of most Pacific nations over the issue, Qian said that “there will always be consequences” when China is unhappy about a decision. Asked about Qian’s comments on Tuesday, Albanese told reporters: “The Pacific Islands Forum determines what happens here, not any other country.”



Albanese, who has previously holidayed in Palau, rejected the Chinese tourism ministry’s warnings of robberies, describing the Micronesian nation as a “paradise”. Asked about China’s warning of consequences, Foreign Minister Penny Wong said: “I think the Pacific should be able to determine its own relationships.” Opposition foreign affairs spokesman Ted O’Brien called Beijing’s behaviour “intimidating” and called for Albanese to be more outspoken about China’s attempted coercion. “The prime minister’s continued reluctance to confront increasingly concerning behaviour by Beijing risks projecting weakness and undermining Australia’s national interests,” he said.
