Tech.title: Roku Pro TV Now One of Cheapest OLEDs Starting at $999
Tech.content:
Roku has launched a significant upgrade to its Pro television lineup, the first Roku Pro OLEDs. The best bit? They’re some of the most affordable OLED TVs on the market with prices starting at $999.

Also read: Best Roku TV for 2026

The Roku Pro Series OLED TV and step-up Roku Pro Series LX OLED TV replace the existing Pro TV and are available exclusively on Amazon. Unlike the existing Pro, which uses LCD, the new OLED should boost picture quality with infinite contrast and better off-angle viewing.

The standard 4K Roku Pro Series TV features a 120Hz panel with Dolby Vision and Roku’s Smart Picture Max. The TV also includes an Automatic Game Mode with FreeSync Premium and VRR (Variable Refresh Rate) .

Meanwhile, the Roku Pro Series LX OLED TV upgrades include a brighter picture, a wider range of colors, a 144Hz variable refresh rate and an anti-reflective filter.

Both TVs include a ultra-thin metal bezel but, as a result, can no longer include the great Soundstage audio port from the old Pro. Roku’s Chris Larson told CNET the feature would make the TV too thick, which is a blow to people who want better sound quality built in.

Like the existing Roku TVs, the Pro includes usability features like an adjustable tool-free stand and velcro cable straps. The TVs come with a push-to-talk voice remote with backlit buttons and you can pair your Bluetooth headphones directly with the TV.

The Roku Pro (2025) was the company’s best TV yet, and the promise of OLED should make the new TVs better than ever. The price is also ultra-competitive, and these could be the late 2026 TVs to beat for their combination of price and picture performance. Given the upgrades of the LX — brighter panel and anti-reflective coating — it appears to be the one to choose of the two.

The Roku Pro Series OLED is now available in 55-inch and 65-inch sizes starting at $999. The Roku Pro Series LX OLED TV will be available starting in October 2026 for $1,299.

Tech.title: Sony’s New ULT Tower Max Wireless Party Speaker Delivered Massive Sound I Felt in My Chest
Tech.content:
Last year, Sony introduced new wireless Bluetooth speakers and an ULT Wear headphone as part of its new ULT Power Sound series of audio products. The floor-standing ULT Tower 9 speaker was part of the launch, but now Sony has expanded its party speaker offerings with three new ULT Tower models: the ULT Tower Max ($1,500), ULT Tower 7 ($650) and ULT Tower 5 ($650), with the two larger models featuring integrated wheels.

Ahead of the speakers’ launch, I had a chance to listen to all three speakers and came away impressed. They play loud and really pound out the bass while still offering good clarity and detail. Needless to say, the Tower Max, which weighs in at a massive 121 pounds, offers the most visceral listening experience, with bass that will shake you. That new flagship model has three woofers (two front-facing and one rear-facing) and four tweeters, along with midrange drivers. The drivers across the new speakers have been redesigned to take advantage of the new, larger speaker cabinets to push more air and sound, so the speakers live up to their ULT Power Sound billing.



All three new speakers have built-in handles (ULT Tower 5 shown here), though only the larger Tower ULT Max and Tower ULT 7 have wheels. David Carnoy/CNET

Amateur or professional DJs can mix and match the speakers, linking them together using a Party Chain mode to augment the sound, or create a stereo pair with two of the same model. They can also be used for karaoke or as a PA system (Sony’s ULT MIC two-pack is available for $118), and have XLR, RCA and USB-C connectivity. Sadly, the new models aren’t backward compatible with the ULT Tower 9 and ULT Tower 10 via Party Connect, which seems a little weird.

Sony has gone with a more industrial design that’s somewhat reminiscent of professional DJ speakers (but with rounded corners). The company says the lighting element has been improved with new lighting modes that make it “easier to switch the mood for different settings.” I also liked how when you raise or lower the volume, the lighting trail around the edge of the speaker retracts or extends to reflect the volume level as you adjust it.

The speakers have four sound modes that can be toggled on using the ULT button on the front of the speaker or the Sony Sound Connect app for iOS or Android. The modes include ULT1 (enhances deep bass), ULT2 (greater power boost), Flat (a neutral “true-to-source” setting) and Live (“spacious feel” of a live performance while preserving vocal clarity). Additionally, there are EQ settings to fiddle around with.

The speakers can be stood up vertically or laid down horizontally and have a sound calibration mode that automatically adjusts the sound to the room or environment the speaker is in. And in a first for Sony party speakers, the smaller ULT Tower 7 (50 pounds) and ULT Tower 5 (29 pounds) are IPX4 splash-proof (when stood up vertically). All three speakers have built-in handles.

The speakers have strong connectivity options. David Carnoy/CNET

While the ULT Tower Max is portable, it has to be plugged in and doesn’t have a built-in rechargeable battery. However, the ULT Tower 7 and ULT Tower 5 can be used untethered, with up to 30 hours of battery life for the Tower 7 and 20 hours for the Tower 5 at moderate volume levels. If you really crank the sound, the battery life ratings drop considerably.

After hearing all three speakers in action, I’d say the ULT Tower 7 will hit the sweet spot for a lot of folks looking for a party speaker that can deliver big, powerful sound while not breaking the bank with its $650 list price. That said, if you can afford two ULT Tower 7 speakers, they produce impressive sound as a stereo pair.

The ULT Tower Max is certainly more powerful and is a beast of a speaker, but it may be overkill unless you’re trying to power a pretty big party. Meanwhile, the more compact Tower ULT 5 would be a good speaker for a high school sports team looking to belt out music during its pregame warmups. It plays pretty loud but is more manageable to carry around at just under 30 pounds.

Tech.title: Google Is Showing Your Home to Anyone Who Looks. Here’s the Free Way to Remove It
Tech.content:
Google Street View photography is detailed enough to show house numbers, parked vehicles and the layout of a front yard, all publicly accessible to anyone who knows the address. Google Maps

Typing your home address into Google Maps and switching to Street View surfaces a level of visual detail most people have never paused to think about: the exact placement of windows and doors, the vehicles in the driveway, the security camera on the porch, the gap in the hedge that leads to the backyard. All of it is publicly accessible to anyone with an internet connection and 30 seconds to spare. Google has offered a way to remove that imagery through a blur request since Street View launched, but the option is buried far enough in the interface that most homeowners have never found it. Here’s where it is and how to use it.

Here’s exactly where it is and how the process works. It’s a simple way to take back control of your home’s online footprint and ensure that your driveway and windows aren’t part of a global database.

Here’s how to reduce how much of your home is visible online.

For more, check out essential Google Maps tips for travel.

Don’t miss any of our unbiased tech content and lab-based reviews. Add CNET as a preferred Google source.

How to blur your home on Google Maps

You’ll need to do this on your computer since the blurring feature isn’t available in the Google Maps application on iOS or Android. It is accessible through the web browser on your mobile device, but it’s rather difficult to use, so your best option is a trusted web browser on your Mac or PC.

At maps.google.com, enter your home address in the search bar at the top-right, hit return, then click the photo of your home that appears.

Click on the photo of your home, right above your address, on the top-left part of the page. Screenshot by Nelson Aguilar/CNET

Next, you’ll see the Street View of your location. Click Report a Problem at the bottom-right. The text is super tiny, but it’s there.

This is the Street View of your location. Screenshot by Nelson Aguilar/CNET

Now, it’s up to you to choose what you want Google to blur. Using your mouse, adjust the view of the image so that your home and anything else you want to blur are all contained within the red and black box. Use your cursor to move around and the plus and minus buttons to zoom in and out, respectively.

If you want to blur more than what’s in the red and black box, use the plus button to zoom in. Screenshot by Nelson Aguilar/CNET

Once you’re finished adjusting the image, choose what you’re requesting to blur underneath:

A face

Your home

Car/license plate

A different object

You’ll be asked to provide a bit more detail about what you want blurred in case the image is busy with cars, people and other objects.

Also, be completely sure that what you select is exactly what you want blurred. Google cautions that once you blur something on Street View, it’s blurred permanently.

Finally, enter your email (this is required), verify the captcha (if needed), and click Submit.

You are required to provide additional information about what you want to blur, so be thorough. Screenshot by Nelson Aguilar/CNET

You should then receive an email from Google that says it’ll review your report and get back to you once the request is either denied or approved. You may receive more emails from Google asking for more information regarding your request. Google doesn’t offer any information on how long your request will take to process, so just keep an eye out for any further emails.

For more, take an inside look at how Google built Immersive View for Maps.

Tech.title: 25% of US Adults Are Eyeing the iPhone Ultra, but Not the $2,000 Price Tag
Tech.content:
Apple’s next big thing could be debuting as soon as Wednesday, Sept. 9, at its Surprise and Shine event. CNET’s Big Guessing Game says that most US adults expect Apple to unveil its first foldable iPhone at the event. If so, that means Apple would join the competition alongside other foldable smartphones, including the Galaxy Z Fold 8 and the Google Pixel 11 Pro Fold. The iPhone Ultra could have two rear-facing cameras and a single front-facing camera that works whether it’s folded or not, and come with Apple’s usual features and services.

A CNET survey that polled 2,605 US adults found that 25% are interested in a foldable Apple smartphone, but not the estimated $2,000 price tag analysts predict it could cost. That’s not much more than what other foldable phones would cost, but interested US adults are only willing to spend much less.

Key takeaways

Three out of four US adults (75%) are indifferent about buying a foldable Apple device, such as the rumored Apple iPhone Ultra.

US adults would spend an average of $781 on an Apple foldable device, which is a stark contrast to what analysts say the phone could cost (and $48 less than the base model iPhone 17).

The RAM shortage is affecting nearly half (41%) of US adults’ plans to upgrade their phones. Some are holding onto their current devices longer than originally planned.

1 in 4 US adults want a foldable iPhone

CNET found that while 25% of US adults want a foldable iPhone, most don’t. Older generations (Boomers and Gen X) express the least interest — 83% and 77%, respectively. Younger generations aren’t that excited either, with nearly 70% of Gen Z and millennials (69% and 68%, respectively) not interested in a foldable iPhone. And those who are excited about one aren’t willing to break the bank for it.

Cole Kan/CNET

Patrick Holland, CNET’s director of content, finds it surprising that only 75% weren’t interested in a foldable iPhone. “Foldable phones are niche products, and it’s impressive that 25% might be interested in an Apple folding phone,” said Holland. “That would be a killer product debut if Apple could get that many people to buy one.”

The same thing can be said for the iPhone Mini and Plus models for those who want a smaller or larger screen, but still want an iPhone. Or the E series, which is a budget-friendly model starting at $600 before discounts.

Holland pointed out that the foldable iPhone isn’t meant to replace the baseline model; it’s about expanding the line and offering phone models at an even bigger price range. Apple could have an iPhone model at ever $100 increase between $600 and $2,000.

US adults will spend an average of $781 on a new foldable iPhone

On average, US adults are willing to spend $781 on a new foldable iPhone. That’s less than what most iPhones cost now. For context, the base model of the iPhone 17 starts at $799 (with a $30 carrier discount).

Gen Z is willing to spend the most on a foldable iPhone — an average of $919 — whereas other generations would spend less. Millennials would spend an average of $859, Gen X would spend $690, and Boomers even less — $572.

Cole Kan/CNET

“The fact that people want an average price that’s nearly $50 below the baseline iPhone 17 shows where we’re at financially right now,” said Holland. “A foldable iPhone is going to be expensive to make, and its retail price will likely reflect that.”

But foldable phones haven’t always been this expensive. Holland points out that the price of foldable phones has dropped for years, as with the Motorola Razr line. The first model cost $1,400, but last year you could buy a new one for half that price before discounts. Now those prices have started to rise again (because of the RAM shortage), and the rumored $2,000 price for the iPhone Ultra is proof of that. It’s a few hundred dollars more than foldable phones cost just a couple of years ago, Holland said.

The RAM shortage is affecting iPhone upgrade plans

The evolution of AI and data centers has led to a memory chip shortage — also known as the RAM shortage or RAMageddon. Personal devices, like phones and laptops, need those chips for data storage. However, the shortage has led tech companies to raise prices on their devices.

Apple raised prices on many of its devices in June for this very reason. The RAM shortage and price increases are making 41% US adults rethink their plans to upgrade to a new iPhone — regardless of whether it’s a foldable or another model.

“The very companies investing in AI and building data centers to support new features and tools on phones are the ones passing the higher cost of RAM and chips on to consumers,” said Holland. “There’s a corporate Gift of the Magi happening, and it’s us who are footing the bill while companies rake in record-breaking profits.”

Many contemplating an upgrade are weighing other options due to price increases. Some are considering older or less expensive options (5%) and switching to another brand (4%), while others are considering refurbished or used models (4%) to save money on the upgrade. Others (9%) will only upgrade if a trade-in or a mobile carrier promotion covers the price, which usually comes in the form of account credits or a multiyear commitment to stay with that carrier.

The bigger story is that most US adults aren’t eager to upgrade due to the RAM shortage and device price hikes. Ten percent are planning to delay their upgrade and keep their phone longer, while 9% are holding onto their phone longer than originally planned.

Twenty-two percent of US adults don’t plan to upgrade anytime soon, regardless of Apple’s new devices or the impact of the RAM shortage. By generation, 19% of Gen X and 27% of Boomers don’t have plans to upgrade anytime soon, while 16% of millennials and 21% of Gen Zers share the same sentiment. Here’s a breakdown.

If you have an old phone and the battery is the only issue, replace it instead of getting a new phone, Holland said. “You’ll add another two to three years of life onto your phone and avoid paying hundreds of dollars more for an upgrade or multiyear commitment to a carrier.”

If you’re still thinking of upgrading your phone, Holland said the best deals on phones are typically found when a new model launches or during holiday sales. And even though trading in your old phone is a good way to save money, check with third-party reseller sites, too.

“You might be able to get more money for your old phone than from the carrier or phone-maker is offering,” said Holland. “Used and refurbished phones are definitely worth buying, as are models from a year or two ago, and often discounted by hundreds.”

Lastly, be skeptical about that “free” $1,000-plus phone a carrier is willing to give you. These deals often come with multiyear commitments and are shown as account credit rather than cash. If you switch to a new mobile carrier before the phone is paid off, you’ll have to pay the difference.

Methodology

All figures, unless otherwise stated, are from YouGov Plc. The total sample size was 2,605 adults. Fieldwork was undertaken between Aug. 13 and 17, 2026. The survey was carried out online. The figures have been weighted and are representative of all US adults (aged 18 and older).

Tech.title: Sonos Ace Ultra Headphones Get Upgraded Sound, Noise Canceling and Direct Link to Your Sonos System
Tech.content:
A new pair of Ultra headphones has arrived, and it’s not from Bose. The Sonos Ace Ultra is a follow-up to its Ace premium noise-canceling headphones. The $449 Sonos Ace Ultra is equipped with new Sonos-designed 40-millimeter drivers and upgraded adaptive noise canceling. Sonos says they’re also its first headphones built on its Headphone Engine 2, which lets you link the Ace Ultra directly to your Sonos system with a press of a button, and unlink it with another press.

Available for preorder today and shipping on Sept. 29, the Ace Ultra headphones come in black, soft white, agave or sand colors. They look similar to their predecessors, but Sonos says they have new rebound foam ear cushions that better passively reduce ambient noise — and hopefully they’re more comfortable as well.

Aside from the new drivers, one of the key upgrades is the new 10-microphone array, with five in each earcup. The previous model has eight microphones. That should help not only with noise-canceling performance but voice-calling performance as well.

Weighing in at 322 grams or 10 grams more than the Ace, the Ace Ultra is equipped with Bluetooth 6.0 and an upgraded 5-series Qualcomm chip that supports the SBC, AAC and aptX Adaptive Lossless audio codecs (though the latter is supported by only a relatively small number of phones). Spatial audio and USB-C audio are also on board.

As for battery life, it’s rated at 35 hours with noise canceling on at moderate volume levels. That’s an improvement over the Ace’s 30 hours.

The Sonos Ace Ultra ships on Sept. 29. Sonos

Headphone Engine 2 features redesigned Wi-Fi hardware

The Ace was designed to link up with Sonos soundbars so you could have a personal cinema experience on the headphones and not disturb others in your household. The Ace Ultra’s linking ability is more sophisticated, as Sonos says the Headphone Engine 2 includes redesigned Wi-Fi hardware and secure credential storage that allow the headphone to “connect directly to and participate in the Sonos system.” That means whatever you have playing on your Sonos system will transfer over to the headphones with a press of a button. Another press then returns the audio to your speakers.

The original Ace headphones arrived in June 2024, shortly after Sonos’ problematic redesign of its app, which left off some features and was buggy, angering users. Like some other reviewers, I initially had some trouble linking the Ace headphones with my Sonos Arc soundbar. Though Sonos did have to work out some kinks, I was generally impressed with its first headphones, which featured excellent sound and good noise canceling.

With a couple of years of development behind it, I suspect the Ace Ultra will integrate more smoothly with Sonos systems. But I’ll update this post with some hands-on impressions after spending some time with the new headphones at Sonos’ launch event in New York. Along with the new headphones, Sonos also announced the new Beam Ultra Soundbar ($699) and Sonos 27, the latest version of the audio operating system. The Sonos Beam Ultra is also available for preorder today and ships on Sept. 29.

Tech.title: New Sonos Beam Ultra Gets Dolby Atmos Glow Up for $699
Tech.content:
Sonos has a new soundbar in its streaming-centric lineup: the Dolby Atmos-capable Beam Ultra. It falls between the existing Beam and the flagship Arc Ultra.

The Beam Ultra is the Dolby Atmos upgrade of the Beam Gen 2 — which remains in the lineup– and adds physical, upfiring drivers and “warmer bass” to become a 7.1.2-channel soundbar.

Sonos says it has redesigned the center channel for clearer dialogue, and the speaker comes with four different levels of AI Speech Enhancement as well as a Night Sound mode. The Beam Ultra also comes with the Trueplay feature for tuning the soundbar to any room.

See Also: Best Sonos Speakers for 2026

Connectivity on the Beam Ultra includes Wi-Fi, Bluetooth and HDMI eARC, while the new version of the Sonos app includes Sonos 27voice — the company’s own music assistant — and Sonos 27mcp for connecting an outside AI assistant. The Sonos ecosystem includes compatibility with dozens of streaming apps as well as the ability to add surround speakers and multiroom options.

The Beam is one of CNET’s favorite soundbars, but it has always been limited by its software emulation of Dolby Atmos — something which the Beam Ultra fixes. Adding this option between $500 and $1,000 gives Sonos users more flexibility when building their own home theater systems.

The Beam Ultra is available for preorder starting today for $699, with general availability on Sept. 29, 2026.

Tech.title: People’s Picks ISP Winners: Is Your Internet Service Provider a Flop or Favorite?
Tech.content:
Your internet service provider choice will depend on what’s available in your area, but CNET readers’ survey responses can help narrow down your choice if you have several options. Jeffrey Hazelwood/CNET

The internet service provider you choose hinges on a lot. We rely on the internet for many daily tasks, streaming, shopping, work and social media. Several factors that go into choosing the right one, like cost effectiveness, satisfaction, speed and customer support are important. But Joe Supan, CNET’s broadband principal writer, says a reliable connection is paramount.

We asked CNET readers what they like (and don’t) about their ISP for People’s Picks, CNET’s community awards program. Did your provider make the cut? Here’s what they said and what we didn’t expect to find out.

CNET’s People’s Picks ISP Winners

J. Hazelwood/CNET GFiber GFiber, previously known as Google Fiber, is a household name among internet service providers and a popular fiber internet option. CNET readers give it high scores, making it the overall top pick among ISPs. GFiber has an overall satisfaction score of 4.72 out of 5, and scores highly for reliability (4.70) and plan speed (4.82). GFiber also scores 4.28 out of 5 for price, Verizon Fios and AT&T Fiber are close runners-up to GFiber. Both score highly for reliability (4.39 and 4.48, respectively) and plan speed (4.41 and 4.49, respectively). But GFiber wins by a landslide for its customer support. Most CNET readers who have contacted customer support within the past year rate their experience as “Excellent,” while other GFiber customers say customer service was “Good” and don’t have any negative ratings for the fiber-optic ISP. Winner for: Fiber internet, customer service, price, reliability and speed See at GFiber

J. Hazelwood/CNET T-Mobile Home Internet (5G) T-Mobile is often known as a popular cellphone provider, but it wins CNET’s People’s picks for 5G internet. T-Mobile scores 4.20 out of 5 for customer satisfaction, the highest among 5G internet providers. CNET readers say their T-Mobile internet connection rarely drops, noting only a few times a year. And there’s no noticeable difference in speed during peak hours. T-Mobile readers haven’t experienced unexpected price hikes within the past year and many wouldn’t change providers if a new one moved into their neighborhood. T-Mobile’s 5G internet is a close runner-up to GFiber in terms of price. Verizon’s 5G internet is just behind T-Mobile, with a price score of 4.10 out of 5. T-Mobile won 5G internet by narrowly beating Verizon in speed and reliability. Wins for: 5G internet See at T-mobile

J. Hazelwood/CNET Starlink Starlink wins among major internet companies with a high overall satisfaction rating of 4.47 out of 5, compared to Verizon Fios and T-Mobile, which score 4.16 and 4.20, respectively. And it has the second-highest reliability score among major winners. Starlink scores 4.59 in reliability while GFiber scores 4.70. “A few years ago, it would have been unfathomable that a satellite company would be considered this reliable. This really speaks to how massive Starlink’s technical improvements have been,” said Supan. Satellite internet also scores fairly highly for plan speed (4.41 out of 5), with no noticeable changes during peak hours. However, Starlink falls short on price satisfaction compared to other major internet providers because it has traditionally required an upfront $349 charge for a satellite dish. However, it recently switched to a $10 monthly charge. “Starlink isn’t particularly fast or affordable, but it serves customers who essentially had no modern internet options before it came along,” said Supan. Wins for: Rural satellite internet, overall satisfaction for satellite, reliability for satellite and speed for satellite See at Starlink

CNET’s People’s Picks regional ISP winners

We pored through our readers’ responses to find the best ISP in each region based on the internet service features you rely on every day. Here’s how each regional winner compares to other ISPs in your area and what to know before choosing one.

West: Sonic

Wins for: Customer service, overall satisfaction, price, reliability and speed

J. Hazelwood/CNET

Sonic is a California-based fiber optic ISP that wins in several of CNET’s categories compared to other Western providers. It earns high marks for price (4.65 out of 5), speed (4.80 out of 5) and overall satisfaction (4.85 out of 5) — the highest among other Western providers. It even beats out national ISPs GFiber and Verizon FiOS for its reliability.

Sonic received nearly flawless feedback from CNET readers. Many readers never experience internet drops or need to reset their router. They also report no noticeable speed differences during peak hours. And when it comes to customer service, no readers report poor or fair customer service.

South: EPB (Electric Power Board)

Wins for: Customer service, overall satisfaction, price, reliability and speed

J. Hazelwood/CNET

Electric Power Board is a fiber optic ISP based in Chattanooga, Tennessee that scores highly compared to other southern ISPs. It scores 5 out of 5 for overall satisfaction, speed and reliability, and 4.5 out of 5 for price satisfaction, beating out national ISPs AT&T Fiber, GFiber, Comcast Xfinity and Spectrum.

CNET readers also give EPB an “Excellent” customer satisfaction rating with no lower ratings. They don’t experience connection drops or speed lags, and wouldn’t change providers if another ISP came to their area.

J. Hazelwood/CNET

Northeast: T-Mobile Home Internet 5G

Wins for: Overall satisfaction and price

T-Mobile Home Internet 5G scores the highest overall satisfaction score in the northeast — earning a 4.40 out of 5. Verizon Fios comes as a close contender with a 4.19. CNET readers also give T-Mobile’s 5G home internet 4.60 out of 5. T-Mobile still has solid customer satisfaction scores (4.20), with many readers noting no noticeable difference in speed during peak hours and no unexpected price hikes.

Midwest: Quantum

Wins for: Overall satisfaction, reliability and speed

J. Hazelwood/CNET

Quantum Fiber wins among Midwest ISPs with a satisfaction score of 4.67 out of 5. Quantum has a flawless 5 out of 5 for reliability. CNET readers say the connection rarely drops — only a few times a year and they don’t experience speed lags during peak hours, which earns Quantum another 5 out of 5 score for speed.

Quantum Fiber was acquired by AT&T earlier this year. Even though customers still see Quantum on their bills, they now have some AT&T perks and benefits like bundling wireless discounts.

GFiber is a close second to Quantum with an overall satisfaction score of 4.64. It falls short on reliability, plan speed and price.

These top 4 ISP features matter most

Speed of plan

J. Hazelwood/CNET

Speed and price are the two most important factors when shopping for internet. “The more people and connected devices in your home, the more speed you’ll need,” Supan says.

Supan adds that even though ISPs generally highlight their download speeds, upload speeds are arguably just as important, especially if you work from home or play games online. CNET has an internet speed guide to help you determine whether you’re getting the right amount of speed for your home.

GFiber scores a 4.82 out of 5 for speed, and most users don’t have any speed issues during peak hours. Regionally, Ting scores the highest 5 out of 5 score for speed compared to other regional providers. Your home internet speed will vary depending on your needs and usage.

Price of plan

J. Hazelwood/CNET

Choosing an internet service provider at a reasonable price can be tough, as prices continue to rise due to improvements in internet technology and equipment. How much you can expect to pay depends on your plan’s speed, connection type and which providers are available in your area.

Supan says that pricing isn’t always straightforward because many ISPs, especially cable providers, will hike your price after a year or two. However, providers are required to list increases in a broadband label so you can see exactly how much your bill will increase and when, he says. It’s also worth noting that some providers charge a fee if you exceed your plan’s data cap. And your price may change if an introductory promotional period ends.

T-Mobile Home Internet scores highly with a 4.24 out of 5. It doesn’t have equipment fees, data caps or contracts, which makes its home internet service a more flexible and cost-effective option. Pricing starts at $50 per month, or $35 per month if you bundle with any T-Mobile voice line and 

Reliability

J. Hazelwood/CNET

Earlier this year, CNET found that 86% of US adults experience wonky Wi-Fi connections or drops. And 1 in 5 (19%) regularly have Wi-Fi problems. Internet reliability can depend on a number of factors that may or may not be your ISP’s fault.

Supan says some internet connection types can be more susceptible to drops or disconnections, but your ISP may still be able to help. You may be able to get your router replaced or switch your internet channel from 2.4 to 5GHz. Your connection reliability may also depend on where your router is placed in your home or on the type of router you’re using. Bigger homes can usually benefit from a mesh router system to extend your connection and reduce dead zones.

CNET readers highly recommend GFiber for reliability and give it a 4.70 out of 5. It offers mesh networking and Wi-Fi 7, the newest and fastest router generation, without data caps or throttling. Sonic scores even higher as a regional provider with 4.90 out of 5. Most don’t experience random connection drops, while others say only a few times a year. Sonic also offers a free Wi-Fi check when installing your internet to double-check your connection and Wi-Fi, which could speak to its high reliability score.

Customer service

J. Hazelwood

Trying to troubleshoot your internet troubles on your own can be tough. The right customer support can help — whether it’s extended live assistance hours, online assistance or text message notifications of outages. Some providers even let you schedule in-person appointments online and provide up-to-date articles.

When choosing a provider, review the support options to ensure you’re comfortable with the availability and resources in case you need them. CNET readers give GFiber high marks for its fast, helpful customer support.

GFiber scores a 4.72 out of 5 for CNET readers. It offers a customer support page and several ways to get help, including scheduling a call or an online chat. There’s also a list of FAQs covering topics such as billing, internet support and self-installation. EPB scores a flawless 5 out of 5 for excellent customer service ratings. It offers a comprehensive FAQ page with troubleshooting assistance, live online chat, short videos and phone assistance.

Did you agree with these findings? CNET’s People’s Picks is community-driven and helps us spread the word about the tech and services you love. Take our ongoing TV survey to tell us what you love about yours.

Correction, July 10: An earlier version of this story gave an incorrect starting price for T-Mobile Home Internet.
